idea: Teams choose Rust for a specific combination: **memory safety without a garbage collector**, performance on par with C and C++, **fearless concurrency** (data races are compile errors), and first-class tooling. Use-after-free, double free, null dereferences and buffer overflows, which cause a large share of security vulnerabilities in C and C++ code, are ruled out at compile time in safe Rust. That is why Rust shows up in operating systems, browsers, cloud infrastructure, command-line tools, embedded devices and WebAssembly.

The trade-off is a steeper learning curve and slower compile times: the compiler asks you to make ownership and error handling explicit up front. In exchange, refactoring is safer, and "if it compiles, it usually works" becomes a practical experience rather than a slogan.

A professional setup is the same everywhere: **rustup** for toolchains, **cargo** for building and dependencies, **rust-analyzer** in the editor, **rustfmt** for formatting (`cargo fmt`), **Clippy** for lints (`cargo clippy -- -D warnings` in CI), and `cargo test` and `cargo doc`. Add `cargo-watch` or `bacon` to re-check on every save, and `cargo audit` or `cargo deny` to check dependencies for known vulnerabilities and licences.
how: Install with rustup; editor with rust-analyzer.
`cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, `cargo test`, `cargo doc --open` daily.
`cargo check` (or `bacon`/`cargo watch`) for instant feedback.
`cargo audit` / `cargo deny` for dependency vulnerabilities and licences.
CI runs fmt check, clippy and tests on every push.

examples.title: Clippy and rustfmt catching real problems
examples.note: Clippy flagged four non-idiomatic patterns, each with a suggested fix, and `cargo clippy --fix` applied them while `cargo fmt` normalised the layout. Running both in CI (with `-D warnings` to fail on any lint) keeps a codebase consistent without arguments in review. Output abridged from a real run.

check.q: Which command makes CI fail on any Clippy warning?
check.explain: `-D warnings` turns every warning into an error, so the CI step fails. `--fix` applies suggestions locally, and `cargo fmt --check` checks layout, not lints.

examples.title: The same function, idiomatic, and why it matters
examples.note: Taking `&[f64]` instead of `&Vec<f64>` lets the function accept vectors, arrays and sub-slices, and `iter().sum()` replaces the manual index loop with no bounds checks to get wrong. The "-0" for an empty slice is a floating-point quirk: float sums start from negative zero, so that summing only negative zeros stays negative. These are exactly the changes Clippy suggested, and they make the API more useful as well as more idiomatic.

check.q: Why is `fn mean(values: &[f64])` better than `fn mean(values: &Vec<f64>)`?
options: A slice accepts vectors, arrays and sub-slices, so callers aren't forced to build a Vec.
Slices can be resized inside the function.
check.explain: A `&Vec<T>` coerces to `&[T]` automatically, but not the other way round. Taking the slice keeps the function as flexible as possible.

mistakes: **Skipping Clippy.** It catches bugs and teaches idioms; run it in CI with `-D warnings`.
**Fighting the borrow checker with clones everywhere.** Learn the ownership patterns instead (module A03).
**Judging Rust by compile errors in week one.** The errors are the safety checks other languages skip.
keys: Rust offers memory safety without GC, C-like speed and compile-time data-race freedom.
The cost is a learning curve and longer compiles.
Daily tools: cargo, rust-analyzer, rustfmt, Clippy, cargo test/doc.
Audit dependencies and enforce fmt and Clippy in CI.

idea: This self-test runs through the core of the language in one program, so you can spot gaps quickly. **Bindings** are immutable unless `mut`; shadowing creates new bindings. **Types** are inferred locally but always explicit in function signatures; integers don't convert implicitly. **Expressions** produce values, including blocks, `if` and `match`; the last expression without a semicolon is a block's value.

**Ownership**: every value has one owner; assigning or passing a heap-owning value moves it; `Copy` types are copied; `.clone()` is explicit. **Borrowing**: `&T` many at once or `&mut T` alone, and references never outlive their data. **Slices** (`&str`, `&[T]`) borrow parts of collections, and idiomatic functions take them as parameters. **Errors**: `Option` for absence, `Result` for failure, `?` to propagate, panics only for bugs.

If any line of the example surprises you, or any of the compile errors below are not immediately clear, revisit the matching chapter of Track 1 before continuing: everything in Track 2 builds on these rules being second nature.
how: Immutable by default; `mut` when needed; shadow to transform.
Signatures are explicit; no implicit numeric conversion.
Moves for heap types, copies for `Copy` types, clones explicit.
Borrow with `&`/`&mut`; take `&str`/`&[T]` parameters.
`Option`/`Result` with `?`; panic only on bugs.

Bad lines become errors instead of crashes.

check.explain: Borrow the input as a slice, return a borrow tied to it, and use Option for the empty case. Taking the Vec by value leaves nothing to borrow from once the function returns.

**Moving out of a vector with indexing.** Borrow (`&names[0]`) or clone.
**Returning references to locals.** Return owned values, or borrow from an input.

Ownership and moves; borrowing rules; slices as parameters.

idea: Structs and enums together model a domain precisely. **Structs** group fields that always exist together ("a product has a name and a price"). **Enums** model alternatives ("a payment is cash, card or gift card"), and each variant carries exactly the data that case needs, so impossible combinations (a card payment without a card number) cannot be represented. Recursive enums (with `Box`) model trees such as expressions, file systems or JSON values.

**`match`** handles every variant, and exhaustiveness checking makes enums safe to extend: add a variant and the compiler lists every `match` that must handle it. Methods in `impl` blocks keep behaviour next to the data, and returning `Result` from operations that can fail (division by zero, unknown variables) keeps the model honest.

The example builds a tiny **expression evaluator**: `Expr` is an enum with number, variable and operation variants; evaluation is a recursive `match`. It is a classic exercise because it combines recursion, Box, pattern matching with nested destructuring, error handling and `Display` in under fifty lines.
how: Struct for "all of these"; enum for "one of these", with per-variant data.
Recursive enums need `Box` (or `Vec`, `Rc`) for indirection.
`match` exhaustively; avoid `_` on your own enums so new variants are flagged.
Methods return `Result` for failures; implement `Display` for user output.
Make illegal states unrepresentable.

examples.title: A tiny expression evaluator
examples.note: Each variant carries exactly what it needs, `Box` makes the recursive type sized, and `eval` is one exhaustive `match` using `?` to propagate errors from sub-expressions. The same structure gives a `Display` implementation for free-form printing. Division by zero and unknown variables become typed errors, not panics.

check.q: Why does idiomatic code avoid a `_ =>` catch-all when matching on its own enums?
options: Catch-alls disable exhaustiveness checking for the whole crate.
Without it, adding a variant makes the compiler flag every match that must handle the new case.
check.explain: A catch-all silently absorbs new variants. Listing variants explicitly turns the compiler into a checklist of places to update.

mistakes: **Structs full of optional fields for "kinds".** Use an enum with per-variant data.
**`_ =>` on your own enums.** You lose the compiler's help when variants are added.
**Panicking in evaluation code.** Return a typed error.
keys: Structs for "and", enums for "or"; make illegal states unrepresentable.
Recursive enums use Box.
Exhaustive matches turn new variants into compiler checklists.
Return typed errors; implement Display for output.

idea: `Vec<T>` is the default collection, and knowing how it grows helps you use it well. A vector has a **length** (elements in use) and a **capacity** (allocated space). When a push exceeds the capacity, it allocates a bigger buffer (roughly doubling) and moves the elements, so `push` is **amortised O(1)**. If you know the final size, `Vec::with_capacity(n)` or `reserve(n)` avoids the repeated reallocations; `shrink_to_fit` releases unused space.

A `Vec` is a perfect **stack** (`push`/`pop`/`last`), and `insert(0, x)` or `remove(0)` are O(n) because everything shifts. For a **queue**, use **`VecDeque<T>`**, a ring buffer with O(1) `push_back`, `push_front`, `pop_front` and `pop_back`; it is the right tool for breadth-first search, job queues and sliding windows. Other useful methods: `retain` (filter in place), `dedup` (remove consecutive duplicates), `drain(range)` (remove and iterate), `swap_remove` (O(1) removal that doesn't keep order), `sort_unstable` (faster when stability doesn't matter), `binary_search` on sorted data, and `chunks`/`windows`.
**`LinkedList`** exists but is rarely the right choice: each node is a separate allocation, cache behaviour is poor, and VecDeque does most of its jobs faster.
how: `with_capacity(n)` / `reserve(n)` when the size is known; `len()` vs `capacity()`.
Stack: `push`, `pop`, `last`; avoid `insert(0)` and `remove(0)` on large vectors.
Queue/deque: `VecDeque` with `push_back`, `pop_front`, etc.
In-place tools: `retain`, `dedup`, `drain`, `swap_remove`, `sort_unstable`, `binary_search`.
`chunks(n)`, `windows(n)` for grouped and sliding views.

examples.title: Capacity, stacks, queues and in-place tools
examples.note: Capacity grew in jumps (4, 8, 16, 32), so 20 pushes needed only four reallocations. The Vec served as an undo stack, and VecDeque served as a queue with a priority job pushed to the front. `retain` and `dedup` cleaned the data in place; `binary_search` returns `Ok(index)` when found and `Err(insertion_point)` when not.

check.explain: `Ok(index)` means found. `Err(i)` means not found, with `i` the position where the value would be inserted to keep the order: 8 belongs between 7 and 12, at index 2.

examples.title: Why queues shouldn't use Vec::remove(0)
examples.note: Removing from the front of a Vec shifts all remaining elements, so draining it is O(n²), while VecDeque's ring buffer pops from the front in O(1). Exact times vary, so only the comparison is printed; the gap grows with the size of the queue.
examples.output: VecDeque at least 20x faster at draining from the front: true

check.q: Why is draining a queue with `Vec::remove(0)` slow?
options: Vec doesn't allow removing the first element.
`remove(0)` allocates a new Vec each time.
It locks the Vec on every call.
Each removal shifts every remaining element, so draining is O(n²); VecDeque pops the front in O(1).
check.explain: A Vec stores elements contiguously from the start. VecDeque's ring buffer can move its start point instead of moving the data.

mistakes: **`remove(0)` in a loop.** Quadratic time. Use VecDeque.
**Pushing thousands of items without `with_capacity` when the size is known.** Extra reallocations.
**`binary_search` on unsorted data.** Results are meaningless. Sort first.
keys: Vec grows by reallocating; push is amortised O(1); reserve when size is known.
Vec is a stack; VecDeque is the queue/deque.
`retain`, `dedup`, `drain`, `windows`, `chunks` work in place or as views.
LinkedList is rarely the right choice.

idea: `HashMap<K, V>` and `HashSet<T>` are hash tables: average O(1) insert, lookup and removal. Keys must implement **`Eq` and `Hash`**, and they must agree: values that are equal must hash the same. For your own types, `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]` gets this right automatically, hashing every field that equality compares; if you implement `PartialEq` by hand (say, case-insensitive), implement `Hash` consistently too, or lookups will silently fail.

**`HashSet`** stores unique values and supports set algebra: `union`, `intersection`, `difference` and `symmetric_difference` return iterators, and `is_subset`/`is_disjoint` answer relationship questions. Collecting into a HashSet is the idiomatic way to deduplicate.

Two properties matter in practice. **Iteration order is arbitrary** and differs between runs (std uses randomly seeded SipHash to resist hash-flooding attacks), so never depend on it: sort, or use `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet`, or `IndexMap` (crate) when insertion order matters. And for performance-critical code with trusted keys, a faster non-cryptographic hasher (`rustc-hash`'s FxHashMap, `ahash`) can make maps noticeably quicker. The **entry API** remains the tool for update-or-insert.
how: `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]` for key types; keep manual Eq and Hash consistent.
HashSet: `insert` returns false for duplicates; `union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `is_subset`.
Never rely on iteration order; sort or use BTree collections.
Entry API for counting and grouping.
Faster hashers for trusted keys; default SipHash resists DoS.

examples.title: Custom keys and set algebra
examples.note: Deriving `Hash` and `Eq` made `Seat` usable as a key, and a freshly built equal Seat finds the booking. Set operations return iterators, collected and sorted here because hash order is arbitrary. `insert` returning false is a one-line duplicate detector. Sorting the keys (thanks to the derived `Ord`) gives stable output.

check.q: What do you need to use your own `Seat` struct as a HashMap key?
options: Nothing: any struct can be a key.
check.explain: The map hashes keys to find a bucket and compares them for equality, so it needs `Hash` and `Eq` that agree with each other.

examples.title: Inconsistent Eq and Hash break lookups
examples.note: The two emails compare equal, yet the set cannot find one when given the other, because they hash to different buckets: equal values must have equal hashes. The robust fix is to normalise the data once in a constructor and derive everything, so equality and hashing can never disagree.

equal? true
buggy set contains the equal value? false
fixed set contains it? true

check.q: Two values compare equal but hash differently. What happens with a HashSet?
options: Lookups fail: the set can't find an equal value because it searches the wrong bucket.
check.explain: The rule is that equal values must have equal hashes. Normalising data in a constructor and deriving both traits keeps them consistent.

mistakes: **Depending on HashMap iteration order.** It changes between runs. Sort or use BTreeMap.
**Manual `PartialEq` without a matching `Hash`.** Lookups fail silently. Normalise and derive.
**Mutating a key's fields while it is in a map.** Its hash changes and it gets lost. Keys should be immutable.
keys: Keys need consistent `Eq` and `Hash`; derive them.
HashSet provides deduplication and set algebra.
Iteration order is arbitrary; sort for stable output.
Normalise data before hashing when equality is custom.

idea: The **B-tree** collections keep keys **sorted**. `BTreeMap<K, V>` and `BTreeSet<T>` have O(log n) operations (instead of a hash map's average O(1)), and in return iteration is always in key order, and **range queries** are efficient: `map.range("b".."d")` or `set.range(10..=20)` visit only the keys in that interval. `first_key_value`/`last_key_value` give the minimum and maximum. Keys need `Ord` rather than `Hash`. Choose BTree collections when you need ordered output, ranges, or deterministic iteration (reports, tests, serialised output).

**`BinaryHeap<T>`** is a priority queue: `push` adds in O(log n) and `pop` always removes the **largest** element (it is a max-heap). For a min-heap, wrap values in **`std::cmp::Reverse`**: `heap.push(Reverse(cost))`. Tuples order field by field, so `(priority, name)` or `Reverse((distance, node))` give natural multi-key priorities.

Priority queues power schedulers, "top k" queries, merging sorted streams and graph algorithms. **Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm** is the classic: a min-heap of `(distance, node)` always expands the closest unvisited node next.
how: `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet`: sorted iteration, `range(a..b)`, `first_key_value`, `last_key_value`; keys need `Ord`.
Use them for ordered or deterministic output and range queries.
`BinaryHeap`: max-heap; `push`, `pop`, `peek`, `into_sorted_vec`.
Min-heap: `Reverse(x)`; tuples order lexicographically.
Top-k: keep a min-heap of size k.

examples.title: Sorted data, ranges and a priority queue
examples.note: The BTreeMap iterated in date order regardless of insertion order, and `range` returned just the days requested. The BinaryHeap popped the highest priority first, breaking the tie between the two 9s by name (tuples compare field by field). Wrapping in `Reverse` turned it into a min-heap for an efficient top-3.

check.q: In what order does a BTreeMap iterate its entries?
options: In sorted key order, regardless of insertion order.
In an arbitrary order that changes between runs.
check.explain: A BTreeMap keeps keys sorted, which also makes range queries like `range("2026-11-02"..="2026-11-04")` efficient.

examples.title: Dijkstra's shortest paths with a min-heap
examples.note: The min-heap always expands the closest unsettled city, so each city's first appearance is its shortest distance; later, longer entries are skipped. Toronto is reached directly at 540 km rather than via Ottawa (650) or Kingston (660). Using BTreeMap makes the output order deterministic.

Montréal     0 km
Ottawa     200 km

check.q: Montréal–Toronto is 540 km directly, Montréal–Ottawa 200 then Ottawa–Toronto 450, and Montréal–Kingston 400 then Kingston–Toronto 260. What does Dijkstra report for Toronto?
check.explain: The direct road (540) beats both detours (650 and 660). The min-heap settles each city at its shortest distance and skips longer entries found later.

mistakes: **HashMap when output order matters.** Use BTreeMap or sort.
**Expecting BinaryHeap to pop the smallest.** It's a max-heap; use `Reverse`.
**Sorting a whole list to get the top k.** A size-k heap is cheaper for large inputs.
keys: BTreeMap/BTreeSet keep keys sorted, with efficient range queries.
They give deterministic iteration, at O(log n) per operation.
BinaryHeap is a max-heap priority queue; `Reverse` makes a min-heap.
Heaps power schedulers, top-k and Dijkstra.

idea: Knowing where data lives makes ownership feel physical. The **stack** holds each function's local variables in a frame that is pushed on call and popped on return: allocation is just moving a pointer, so it is extremely fast, but sizes must be known at compile time. The **heap** holds data whose size is decided at run time or that must outlive a function call; allocating there means asking the allocator for memory and later freeing it.

Common types have small, fixed **stack** parts. A `String` or `Vec<T>` is three words (pointer, capacity, length: 24 bytes on 64-bit) pointing at a heap buffer; a `&str` or `&[T]` is two words (pointer, length); `Box<T>` and `&T` are one word; `Option<Box<T>>` and `Option<&T>` are also one word thanks to the **niche optimisation** (null means None). `std::mem::size_of` tells you.

A **move** copies only the stack part (those few words) and marks the old variable as unusable; the heap data never moves. That is why moving a huge `Vec` is cheap, and why using the old variable is forbidden: two owners of one buffer would free it twice. **Drop** runs when the owner goes out of scope, freeing heap memory deterministically, without a garbage collector.
how: Stack: fixed-size locals, fast push/pop; heap: run-time-sized or long-lived data.
`size_of::<T>()`: String/Vec = 24, &str/&[T] = 16, Box/& = 8 bytes on 64-bit.
Moves copy the stack part; heap buffers stay put.
`Option<Box<T>>`/`Option<&T>` cost nothing extra (niche optimisation).
Drop frees deterministically at the end of scope.

Moving a million-element vector copied only its 24-byte header: the heap buffer did not move.

check.q: Moving a vector of a million elements into a function copies how much data?
options: Only the 24-byte header (pointer, length, capacity); the heap buffer stays where it is.
Half the elements, the other half are shared.
check.explain: A move transfers ownership of the existing buffer. That's why moves are cheap, and why the old variable can't be used afterwards.

**Boxing small values for "performance".** It adds an allocation and an indirection.
**Large arrays on the stack** (`[u8; 10_000_000]`). They can overflow the stack; use `Vec` or `Box<[T]>`.
keys: Stack frames are fast and fixed-size; the heap holds run-time-sized data.
String/Vec are 24-byte headers pointing at heap buffers.
Moves copy headers; the old variable becomes invalid.
Drop frees deterministically; niche optimisation makes `Option<Box<T>>` free.

idea: Some borrowing situations come up constantly; knowing the patterns avoids most fights with the borrow checker. **Split borrows**: the compiler tracks struct fields separately, so you can borrow `self.items` mutably while reading `self.limit`, as long as you access the fields directly rather than through methods that borrow all of `self`. Destructuring (`let Self { items, limit } = self;`) makes this explicit.

**Getting a value out of a `&mut`**: you cannot move out of a borrowed place, but you can swap something in. `std::mem::take(&mut x)` replaces `x` with its `Default` value (an empty Vec or String) and returns the old one; `mem::replace(&mut x, new)` puts in a value you choose; `mem::swap` exchanges two. `Option::take()` is the same idea for options. These are the standard way to move out of fields, transform state machines, or reuse buffers.

**Avoiding clones**: `Cow<'a, str>` (clone on write) holds either a borrowed `&str` or an owned `String`, and only allocates when a change is actually needed, ideal for functions that usually return their input unchanged (escaping, normalising). **Iterating while modifying**: collect what you need first, use `retain`, or iterate over indices; the borrow checker is right that changing a collection while iterating over it is dangerous.
how: Borrow disjoint fields separately; destructure `self` to make it obvious.
`mem::take(&mut x)` (leaves Default), `mem::replace(&mut x, v)`, `mem::swap(&mut a, &mut b)`, `option.take()`.
`Cow<'a, str>`: `Cow::Borrowed(s)` when unchanged, `Cow::Owned(new)` when changed.
Modify collections with `retain`, `iter_mut`, or a collect-then-apply pass.
Clone only when you truly need two owners.

examples.title: Split borrows, mem::take and Cow
examples.note: Destructuring `self` let the loop mutate `messages` while reading `max_len`. `mem::take` moved the whole message list out of `&mut self`, leaving an empty Vec, and `mem::replace` swapped in a new state while returning the old. `escape_html` returned the input borrowed when nothing needed escaping and only allocated when it did.

check.q: What does `std::mem::take(&mut self.messages)` do?
options: It borrows the Vec for the rest of the function.
It deletes the Vec and leaves the field uninitialised.
It moves the Vec out and leaves an empty Vec (its Default) in its place.
check.explain: You can't leave a field empty behind a `&mut`, so `take` swaps in a default value. `mem::replace` does the same with a value you choose.

check.q: Which line correctly returns the log from `fn drain_log(&mut self) -> Vec<String>`, leaving it empty?
check.explain: Returning `self.log` would move a field out of a borrowed struct. `take` hands back the log and leaves an empty Vec in its place.

mistakes: **Calling a `&mut self` method while holding a field borrow.** Access fields directly, or destructure.
**Cloning to get a value out of `&mut`.** Use `mem::take`/`replace` or `Option::take`.
**Always returning `String` from transformation functions.** `Cow` avoids allocating when nothing changes.
keys: The compiler tracks disjoint field borrows; destructure to use them.
`mem::take`, `mem::replace`, `mem::swap` and `Option::take` move values out of `&mut`.
`Cow` borrows when possible and allocates only on change.
Prefer these patterns to reflexive cloning.

idea: Lifetimes become interesting in structs and generic code. A struct holding references needs lifetime parameters, and sometimes **more than one**: a `Parser<'src, 'cfg>` that borrows its input text and a separate configuration lets callers drop the configuration while still using slices of the input, which a single shared lifetime would forbid. Methods in `impl<'a> S<'a>` can return references tied to `'a` (the data the struct borrows), which then outlive the struct itself.

The **elision rules**, applied by hand: (1) each reference parameter gets its own lifetime; (2) if there is exactly one input lifetime, it is assigned to all outputs; (3) if one of the inputs is `&self` or `&mut self`, its lifetime is assigned to the outputs. When none of these determines the output, you must annotate.

**`T: 'static`** is commonly misread. It does not mean "lives forever"; it means "contains no non-static references", so the value *could* be kept as long as you like. Every owned type (`String`, `Vec<u8>`, your own structs without references) satisfies `'static`. That is why `thread::spawn` requires `'static`: the thread may outlive the caller, so the closure must own its data. `&'static str` is a different thing: a reference valid for the whole program, like a string literal.
how: Several lifetimes (`'a`, `'b`) when borrows are independent.
Methods returning `&'a T` borrow from the struct's data, not from `&self`.
Elision: one input lifetime → output; `&self` → output; otherwise annotate.
`T: 'static` = owns its data (no short-lived references); owned types qualify.
`&'static T` = reference valid for the whole program.

examples.title: Two lifetimes and a 'static bound
examples.note: Because the tokens are tied to `'src` only, `first_tokens` could return them after its local separator list and tokenizer were dropped; with a single lifetime for both borrows, this would not compile. `keep_forever` accepted an owned String and Vec as `'static`, since they contain no borrowed data, and a string literal, which is a `&'static str`.

check.q: Why can a `String` or a `Vec<u32>` satisfy a `T: 'static` bound?
options: They are stored in static memory.
They contain no borrowed data, so they can live as long as needed.
check.explain: `T: 'static` means "holds no short-lived references", not "lives forever". Owned data qualifies; a `&str` borrowed from a local doesn't.

examples.title: A borrowed value is not 'static
examples.note: `&str` borrowed from a local String is not `'static`: the thread could outlive `name`. The compiler explains that `name` does not live long enough for the `'static` requirement. Passing the String itself (`keep_forever(name)`) satisfies the bound, because an owned String contains no short-lived references.

check.q: `keep_forever(&name)` fails because a thread needs `'static` data. What is the simplest fix?
options: Add `'static` to the variable: `let name: &'static String`.
Join the thread before `name` is dropped, without changing anything else.
check.explain: An owned String moves into the thread, so nothing borrowed can expire. A reference to a clone is still a reference to a local.

mistakes: **One lifetime for independent borrows.** Callers get needlessly restricted; use separate lifetimes.
**Reading `T: 'static` as "never freed".** It means "owns its data"; owned values are dropped normally.
**Adding `'static` to references to silence errors.** Usually the fix is to own the data.
keys: Structs can have several lifetimes for independent borrows.
Methods can return references tied to the borrowed data, outliving the struct.
Elision rules: single input, or `&self`, decide the output lifetime.
`T: 'static` means no short-lived references; owned types qualify.

idea: Good error handling starts with a good **error type**. For a library or a module with distinct failure modes, define an **enum with one variant per failure**: `ConfigError::Io(io::Error)`, `ConfigError::Parse { line: usize, message: String }`, `ConfigError::Missing(&'static str)`. Callers can `match` on it and react differently to each case: retry an I/O error, show the line number for a parse error.

To be a proper error, the type implements **`Display`** (the human-readable message, without a trailing period and without repeating the cause) and **`std::error::Error`**, whose **`source()`** method returns the underlying error, so tools can print the whole chain: "failed to load config: cannot read settings.toml: No such file or directory". `Debug` is derived.

**`From` implementations** let the `?` operator convert automatically: `impl From<io::Error> for ConfigError` means a `fs::read_to_string(path)?` inside a function returning `Result<_, ConfigError>` wraps the I/O error in the right variant with no extra code. Writing all this by hand once makes clear what the `thiserror` crate (next lesson) generates for you.
how: `#[derive(Debug)] enum MyError { Io(io::Error), Parse { line: usize, msg: String }, ... }`.
`impl Display` with a concise message; don't repeat the source's message.
`impl std::error::Error` with `source()` returning the wrapped error.
`impl From<io::Error> for MyError` so `?` converts automatically.
Walk the chain with `source()` to print full context.

check.q: What makes `fs::read_to_string(path)?` work in a function returning `Result<_, AppError>`?
check.explain: `?` calls `From::from` on the error. Without that conversion (or a `map_err`), the compiler can't turn an io::Error into your type.

mistakes: **One string error for everything.** Callers can't react to specific failures. Use an enum.
**Display messages that repeat the cause.** Chains then print it twice; let `source()` carry it.
**`map_err` everywhere.** Implement `From` for common conversions so `?` does it.
keys: An error enum with a variant per failure lets callers match.
Implement Display (message) and Error (with `source()`).
`From` impls let `?` convert automatically.
Walk `source()` to print the full error chain.

idea: Writing `Display`, `Error` and `From` by hand is repetitive, and **thiserror** generates exactly that code from attributes, with no run-time cost and no trace in your public API. `#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]` on the enum, then on each variant: `#[error("line {line}: expected a number")]` provides the Display message (fields can be interpolated), `#[source]` marks the underlying error for `source()`, and **`#[from]`** additionally generates the `From` impl so `?` converts automatically. `#[error(transparent)]` forwards both message and source to a wrapped error, useful for "other" variants.

thiserror is meant for **libraries** (and for modules inside applications that want typed errors). Libraries should expose **typed errors** because their callers need to make decisions: is the failure retryable? did the user give bad input? A library that returns `Box<dyn Error>` or a string forces callers to parse messages, which breaks every time the wording changes.

A common refinement is `#[non_exhaustive]` on public error enums, so the library can add variants later without a breaking change (callers must then include a catch-all arm). Keep variants meaningful to the caller, not a mirror of every internal function.
how: `#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)] pub enum MyError { ... }`.
`#[error("message {field}")]` for Display; `{0}` for tuple fields; `{source}` to include the cause (usually avoid).
`#[from]` generates From (and implies `#[source]`); `#[source]` alone for source without From.
`#[error(transparent)]` to wrap another error entirely.
Libraries expose typed errors; consider `#[non_exhaustive]`.

examples.title: The config error, rewritten with thiserror

Callers still match on variants, here to decide whether a failure is retryable.

check.q: What does `#[from]` on a thiserror variant generate?

check.explain: thiserror writes the boilerplate: `#[error(...)]` for Display, `#[from]` for From (and source), `#[source]` for the chain.

check.q: Why do library callers benefit from a typed error enum rather than a String?
options: Strings can't be returned in a Result.
Typed errors are printed in colour.
They can match on variants to decide what to do (retry, skip, give up) without parsing messages.
check.explain: Messages are for humans and can change. Variants are a stable contract that code can branch on.

mistakes: **Returning `Box<dyn Error>` or strings from library APIs.** Callers can't react to specific failures.
**Including `{source}` in messages.** The chain then repeats it. Let `source()` carry the cause.
**A variant for every internal function.** Model what the caller needs to distinguish.
keys: thiserror derives Display, Error and From from attributes, at no run-time cost.
`#[error]`, `#[source]`, `#[from]` and `transparent` cover most needs.
Libraries expose typed errors so callers can decide what to do.
`#[non_exhaustive]` leaves room to add variants.

idea: Applications have different needs from libraries. The binary is the final caller: it rarely matches on specific error variants; it mostly wants to stop, report clearly what went wrong and why, and exit with an error code. **anyhow** is built for that. **`anyhow::Result<T>`** (an alias for `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`) accepts any error type through `?`, so functions that call several libraries don't need a combined error enum.

The key feature is **context**. `.context("reading settings.toml")` or `.with_context(|| format!("parsing line {n}"))` wraps an error with a message describing what the program was doing, building a chain from high-level intent down to the root cause. Printing with `{:#}` shows the chain on one line; returning the error from `main` prints "Error: ..." with a "Caused by:" list. Context works on `Option` too, turning `None` into a descriptive error.

`anyhow!("...")` creates an ad-hoc error, `bail!("...")` returns one early, and `ensure!(condition, "...")` checks a condition. When a caller does need to inspect a specific error, `err.downcast_ref::<io::Error>()` recovers the original type. The usual split: **thiserror in libraries, anyhow in binaries**.
how: `fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()>`; `?` accepts any error type.
`.context("doing X")?`, `.with_context(|| format!(...))?` on Result and Option.
`bail!("...")`, `ensure!(cond, "...")`, `anyhow!("...")` for ad-hoc errors.
`{:#}` prints the chain on one line; returning from main prints "Caused by".
`downcast_ref::<T>()` to inspect the root cause when needed.

check.explain: `ensure!(cond, msg)` returns an error when the condition is false. `bail!(msg)` returns an error unconditionally, and `anyhow!` just builds one.

mistakes: **anyhow in a library's public API.** Callers lose the ability to match on errors. Use thiserror there.
**`?` without context in application code.** "No such file or directory" with no file name helps nobody.
**Matching on error message strings.** Use `downcast_ref` or typed errors.
keys: anyhow is for applications: one error type that accepts any error.
`context`/`with_context` build chains from intent to root cause.
`bail!`, `ensure!`, `anyhow!` create ad-hoc errors.
thiserror for libraries, anyhow for binaries.

idea: Flexible generic APIs come from choosing the right bounds. To accept "anything I can iterate over", bound on **`IntoIterator`** rather than `Iterator` or a concrete collection: `fn total<I: IntoIterator<Item = u32>>(items: I)` accepts a `Vec`, an array, a range, a `HashSet` or an iterator chain. Bounds can constrain **associated types**: `I: IntoIterator, I::Item: Display` says "the items must be displayable", and `Item = &'a str` pins them exactly.

**`where` clauses** keep complex bounds readable and can express things inline bounds can't, such as bounds on associated types or on types that aren't parameters (`where Vec<T>: Debug`). `impl Trait` in argument position is shorthand for an anonymous type parameter; in return position it hides a concrete type (essential for returning iterator chains and closures).

**Conditional `impl` blocks** add methods only when type parameters meet extra bounds: `impl<T: Display + PartialOrd> Pair<T> { fn largest(&self) ... }`. **Blanket implementations** implement a trait for every type that satisfies a bound (`impl<T: Display> ToString for T` is how every displayable type gets `to_string()`). Together these let a small amount of generic code serve many types precisely.
how: Accept iterables with `I: IntoIterator<Item = T>`; constrain `I::Item` in `where`.
Return iterator chains with `impl Iterator<Item = T> + '_` when borrowing.
`where` for long or associated-type bounds.
Conditional impls: `impl<T: Bound> Type<T> { ... }`.
Blanket impls: `impl<T: Bound> MyTrait for T { ... }`.

mistakes: **Concrete collection parameters** (`&Vec<T>`, `HashSet<T>`). Accept `IntoIterator` or slices.
**Forgetting `+ 'a` on returned iterators that borrow.** The compiler asks for the lifetime.
**Bounds that are stricter than needed.** Every extra bound excludes callers.
keys: `IntoIterator<Item = T>` accepts any iterable.
Constrain associated types in `where` clauses.
Conditional impls add methods only when bounds hold.
Blanket impls give a trait to every type meeting a bound.

idea: A handful of standard traits make your types feel native. **`From`/`Into`** express infallible conversions: implement `From<A> for B` and you get `Into<B> for A` for free, plus `?` conversions for errors. **`TryFrom`/`TryInto`** are the fallible versions, returning a `Result` (`u8::try_from(300)` fails). **`FromStr`** powers `"1.2.3".parse::<Version>()`. **`Display`** gives `{}` and `to_string()`. **`Default`** provides a sensible starting value (derivable), used by `..Default::default()` in struct literals and by `unwrap_or_default`.

**`AsRef<T>`** makes parameters flexible: `fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path>)` accepts `&str`, `String`, `PathBuf` and `&Path`, which is how std's file functions work. **`Borrow`** is similar but promises equal hashing and ordering, which is why a `HashMap<String, V>` can be looked up with a `&str`.

For comparisons: **`PartialEq`/`Eq`** (equality; Eq means it is reflexive, which floats are not because NaN ≠ NaN), **`PartialOrd`/`Ord`** (ordering; Ord is total and required by sort and BTreeMap). Derived comparisons go field by field in declaration order, so ordering fields from most to least significant (major, minor, patch) gives correct semantics for free.
how: `impl From<A> for B` (gives `Into`); `TryFrom` for fallible conversions.
`impl FromStr` for `.parse()`; `impl Display` for `{}`.
`#[derive(Default)]` or impl it; `..Default::default()`.
Parameters: `impl AsRef<str>`, `impl AsRef<Path>`, `impl Into<String>`.
Derive `PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash`; field order decides ordering.

check.q: Why can a `HashMap<String, u32>` be queried with `stock.get("tea")`?
options: `get` converts the `&str` into a new String first.
HashMap keys are always compared as `&str`.

**Implementing `Into` directly.** Implement `From`; you get `Into` for free.

idea: Rust's type system can carry information that never exists at run time. A **zero-sized type** (ZST), such as a unit struct `struct Meters;`, takes no memory, and **`PhantomData<T>`** lets a struct mention a type parameter it doesn't store, purely to make the compiler track it. Together they encode **units** (`Length<Meters>` vs `Length<Feet>` cannot be added by mistake), **ownership markers** and **states**, all at zero run-time cost.

The **typestate pattern** encodes an object's state in its type: `Connection<Disconnected>`, `Connection<Connected>`, `Connection<Authenticated>`. Each state has only the methods valid in it, and transitions consume `self` and return the next state's type. Calling `send` before `login` is then a compile error, not a run-time check, and the states vanish from the compiled code.

**Const generics** parameterise types by **values**: `struct Matrix<const R: usize, const C: usize>` makes dimensions part of the type, so multiplying a 2×3 by a 2×3 matrix is a compile error while 2×3 by 3×2 type-checks and yields a 2×2. Arrays use this (`[T; N]`), and `fn sum<const N: usize>(a: [i32; N])` works for every array length.
how: `PhantomData<T>` to tag a struct with a type it doesn't store.
Unit structs as markers: `struct Meters; struct Feet;`.
Typestate: `struct Conn<S> { ..., _state: PhantomData<S> }`; methods in `impl Conn<StateA>`.
Transitions take `self` and return `Conn<NextState>`.
Const generics: `struct M<const N: usize>`, `fn f<const N: usize>(a: [T; N])`.

examples.title: Units, typestate and const generics
examples.note: `Length<Meters>` and `Length<Feet>` are different types, so feet had to be converted before adding, yet a Length is just 8 bytes: the unit costs nothing at run time. The timer's state lives in its type (`start` only exists when idle, `stop` only when running), and `Idle` is zero-sized. The matrix dimensions are checked by the compiler.

idea: Visibility in Rust is more fine-grained than public versus private. **`pub`** exposes an item to everyone who can reach its module. **`pub(crate)`** exposes it anywhere in the current crate but not to users of the library, perfect for helpers shared between modules. **`pub(super)`** exposes it to the parent module only, and `pub(in path)` to a chosen ancestor. Private (the default) means the current module and its descendants.

Getting visibility right keeps a library's **public API** small and stable: everything `pub` (and reachable) is a promise you can't change without a major version bump, while `pub(crate)` items can be refactored freely. Many crates add a **prelude** module that re-exports the most common items (`pub use crate::{Client, Config, Error};`), so users write `use mylib::prelude::*;`.

**Organise by feature**, not by kind. A `orders/` module containing the order types, validation, storage and tests for orders beats separate `models/`, `services/` and `utils/` folders, because most changes touch one feature and the module boundary becomes a natural encapsulation boundary. Tools: `cargo doc` shows exactly what is public; Clippy's `unreachable_pub` lint flags `pub` items that aren't actually exported.
how: `pub` (everyone), `pub(crate)` (this crate), `pub(super)` (parent), private (this module).
Keep the public API minimal; use `pub(crate)` for internal sharing.
A `prelude` module re-exports common items.
Organise modules by feature; each feature module hides its internals.
Check the public surface with `cargo doc`.

idea: Dependencies are declared with **semantic version requirements**. `serde = "1.0"` (the same as `^1.0`) means "any compatible version": at least 1.0.0 and below 2.0.0; for 0.x crates the minor number is the breaking one, so `"0.4"` means below 0.5.0. Other forms: `"~1.2"` (patch updates only), `"=1.2.3"` (exactly), `">=1.2, <1.5"`. Cargo picks the newest matching versions and records them in `Cargo.lock`; **`cargo update`** moves to newer compatible versions on purpose, `cargo update -p serde` for one crate. **`cargo tree`** shows the dependency graph, and `cargo tree -d` finds crates compiled in two versions (a common source of bloat).

Dependency kinds: **`[dev-dependencies]`** are used only by tests, examples and benchmarks (proptest, criterion); **`[build-dependencies]`** by build scripts. **Optional dependencies** (`optional = true`) are compiled only when a feature enables them.

**Features** are named switches for conditional compilation. `[features] default = ["json"]` and `json = ["dep:serde_json"]` define them; code uses `#[cfg(feature = "json")]`. Features must be **additive**: enabling one must never break code that worked without it, because Cargo unifies features across the whole dependency graph. Users opt out with `default-features = false` and pick what they need.
how: `cargo update` (all) / `cargo update -p name`; `cargo tree`, `cargo tree -d`.
`[dev-dependencies]` for tests and benches; `[build-dependencies]` for build.rs.
`optional = true` + `[features] x = ["dep:name"]`; `#[cfg(feature = "x")]` in code.
Features are additive; `default-features = false` to slim down.

[package]
name = "reportgen"
version = "0.3.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
anyhow = "1"                                   # >= 1.0.0, < 2.0.0
chrono = { version = "0.4", default-features = false, features = ["clock"] }
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"], optional = true }
serde_json = { version = "1", optional = true }
csv = { version = "1.3", optional = true }

[features]
default = ["json"]
json = ["dep:serde", "dep:serde_json"]         # enabling "json" pulls in two optional crates
csv = ["dep:csv", "dep:serde"]
all-formats = ["json", "csv"]

[dev-dependencies]
proptest = "1"                                  # only for tests
criterion = "0.5"                               # only for benchmarks

# cargo build                                   -> default features (json)
# cargo build --no-default-features --features csv
# cargo build --all-features
# cargo tree -e features                        -> which feature enabled what
examples.note: `chrono` is used with its default features turned off and only `clock` enabled, a common way to slim a dependency. `serde`, `serde_json` and `csv` are optional and appear only when a feature asks for them, and both `json` and `csv` can be on at once because features are additive. Dev-dependencies never reach users of the crate.

idea: **rustdoc** turns doc comments into documentation, and good docs are part of a professional crate. Beyond the basics (`///` for items, `//!` for modules and the crate, Markdown, sections like `# Examples`, `# Errors`, `# Panics`, `# Safety`), a few features make docs much better.

**Intra-doc links** reference other items by path: `[`Config`]`, `[`Client::send`]` or `[`std::io::Error`]` become links checked at build time, so they never go stale. **Doc tests** run every code block as a test; to keep examples realistic, use the `?` operator (end the block with `Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())`), and hide setup lines from the rendered page by starting them with `# ` (they still run). Code-block annotations change behaviour: `no_run` (compile but don't run, for network examples), `should_panic`, `compile_fail` (demonstrate a mistake), `ignore`.

At the crate root, **`#![warn(missing_docs)]`** makes every undocumented public item a warning, a cheap way to keep coverage complete. `cargo doc --open` builds the site locally; publishing to crates.io builds it automatically on **docs.rs**. A crate-level `//!` comment with a short overview and a quick-start example is the most-read page of any library.
how: Intra-doc links: `[`Type`]`, `[`Type::method`]`, `[`crate::module`]`.
Doc tests with `?`: end with `Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())`.

idea: Beyond `Mutex`, std offers synchronisation tools for specific patterns. **`RwLock<T>`** allows **many readers or one writer**: `read()` returns a shared guard and several threads can hold one at once, while `write()` waits for exclusive access. It suits read-heavy data such as configuration or caches. For short critical sections a Mutex is often just as fast, so measure before switching.

**`Condvar`** (condition variable) lets threads **wait for a condition** without busy-looping: a thread locks a Mutex, checks a condition, and calls `condvar.wait(guard)` (or `wait_while`), which releases the lock and sleeps until another thread calls `notify_one`/`notify_all`. It is the building block of bounded queues, barriers and "wait until ready" logic; always re-check the condition after waking, because wakeups can be spurious.

**One-time initialisation**: **`OnceLock<T>`** holds a value set at most once, safely from any thread (`get_or_init(|| ...)`), and **`LazyLock<T>`** wraps that in a static that initialises on first access: `static TABLE: LazyLock<HashMap<..>> = LazyLock::new(|| build())`. They replace the `lazy_static` and `once_cell` crates for global caches, compiled regexes and configuration loaded once.
how: `RwLock`: `read()` for shared access, `write()` for exclusive; best for read-heavy data.
`Condvar` with a `Mutex`: `wait_while(guard, |state| condition)`, `notify_one`/`notify_all`.
Re-check conditions after waking (spurious wakeups); `wait_while` does it for you.
`OnceLock::get_or_init` for set-once values; `static X: LazyLock<T> = LazyLock::new(...)` for lazy globals.
Avoid holding guards across slow work.

idea: **Atomic types** (`AtomicBool`, `AtomicUsize`, `AtomicI64`, `AtomicPtr`...) can be shared between threads and updated **without a lock**, using special CPU instructions. Operations include `load`, `store`, `fetch_add`/`fetch_sub` (add and return the old value), `swap`, and **`compare_exchange(expected, new)`**, which updates only if the current value is still `expected` and reports whether it succeeded; it is the foundation of lock-free algorithms (retry in a loop until it succeeds). Share atomics with `Arc` or as `static`s.

Each operation takes a **memory ordering**, which controls how it is ordered relative to *other* memory operations. **`Relaxed`** guarantees only that the atomic itself is updated correctly: fine for counters and statistics where nothing else depends on the value. **`Release`** (on a store) and **`Acquire`** (on a load) form a pair: everything a thread wrote before a Release store is visible to a thread that Acquire-loads the new value. That is how a "data ready" flag safely publishes data. **`SeqCst`** adds a single global order of all SeqCst operations; it is the safest default when unsure.

Atomics are fast for simple shared counters and flags (a stop signal, request counts, IDs). For anything involving several related values, a Mutex is simpler and much less error-prone: correctness reasoning about orderings is genuinely hard.
how: `AtomicUsize::new(0)`; `fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)` for counters.
`store(true, Release)` / `load(Acquire)` to publish data with a flag.
`compare_exchange(old, new, AcqRel, Acquire)` in a retry loop for lock-free updates.
`SeqCst` when unsure; Relaxed only for independent counters.
Several related values: use a Mutex.

Prefer a Mutex for anything involving several values.

idea: **rayon** makes data parallelism almost effortless. Replace `.iter()` with **`.par_iter()`** (or `into_par_iter()`, `par_iter_mut()`) and the iterator chain runs on a pool of worker threads, one per core, with work stealing to balance load. The rest of the chain looks the same: `map`, `filter`, `sum`, `collect`, `for_each`. Rayon also offers `par_sort` and `par_sort_unstable`, `par_chunks`, and **`rayon::join(a, b)`** to run two closures in parallel (handy for divide-and-conquer like parallel quicksort).

It is safe for the same reason threads are: closures must be `Send + Sync`, so the compiler rejects chains that would share mutable state without synchronisation. Reductions are expressed with `sum`, `reduce` or `fold`, never by mutating an outer variable.

Parallelism helps when there is **enough CPU work per item** and many items: image processing, parsing many files, simulations, heavy maps over large collections. It does **not** help, and can hurt, for tiny workloads (thread coordination costs more than the work), for I/O-bound work (use async), or when the chain is dominated by a sequential step. Measure in release mode before and after.
how: `use rayon::prelude::*;` then `.par_iter()`, `.into_par_iter()`, `.par_iter_mut()`.
Same adaptors: `map`, `filter`, `sum`, `reduce`, `collect`, `for_each`.
`par_sort_unstable`, `par_chunks`; `rayon::join(a, b)` for two tasks.
Closures must be `Send + Sync`; reduce instead of mutating shared variables.
Worth it for CPU-heavy items; measure in release mode.

idea: In Tokio, a **task** is a lightweight unit of concurrent work, created with `tokio::spawn` and scheduled by the runtime. The default **multi-threaded runtime** (from `#[tokio::main]`) runs tasks on a pool of worker threads with work stealing; `#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]` runs everything on one thread (simpler, and fine for many I/O-bound programs). Spawned tasks must be `Send + 'static` on the multi-threaded runtime.

**`JoinSet`** manages a dynamic group of tasks: spawn into it, then `join_next().await` returns results in **completion order**; dropping the set **aborts** any tasks still running, which makes cleanup automatic. Use it for "fetch these N things concurrently and handle each as it finishes".

The cardinal rule of async is: **never block the runtime**. Each worker thread runs many tasks by switching at `.await` points; a blocking call (`std::thread::sleep`, synchronous file or database I/O, a long CPU loop) freezes every task on that thread. Move such work to **`tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| ...)`**, which runs it on a separate pool of threads meant for blocking and returns a future of the result; for heavy CPU parallelism, rayon inside `spawn_blocking` is a common combination.
how: `tokio::spawn(async move { ... })` returns a `JoinHandle<T>`; await it for the result.
`JoinSet`: `set.spawn(fut)`, `while let Some(res) = set.join_next().await`; dropping aborts.
Multi-thread (default) vs `flavor = "current_thread"` runtimes.
`spawn_blocking(|| heavy())` for blocking or CPU-heavy work.
Never call blocking functions directly in async code.

examples.title: What a blocking call does to other tasks
examples.note: On a single-threaded runtime, `std::thread::sleep` froze the only worker thread, so the heartbeat task, due after 10 ms, could not run until the blocking call ended 200 ms later. On a multi-threaded runtime the damage is smaller but real. Use `tokio::time::sleep` or `spawn_blocking` instead.
examples.output: a 10 ms timer fired after at least 200 ms: true

check.q: What does `std::thread::sleep` inside async code do on a single-threaded runtime?
options: It pauses only the current task.
It blocks the only worker thread, so no other task can run until it returns.
check.explain: The runtime switches tasks only at `.await` points. A blocking call holds the thread; use `tokio::time::sleep` or `spawn_blocking` instead.

mistakes: **Blocking calls in async code.** Every task on the thread stalls. Use async APIs or `spawn_blocking`.
**Forgetting that dropping a JoinSet aborts its tasks.** Keep it alive until the work is done.
**Spawning non-`Send` futures on the multi-thread runtime.** Holding an `Rc` or a std MutexGuard across `.await` makes the future non-Send.
keys: Tasks are cheap; `tokio::spawn` runs them on the runtime's workers.
JoinSet collects results as tasks finish and aborts on drop.
Never block the runtime; `spawn_blocking` for blocking or heavy CPU work.
Choose multi-thread or current-thread runtimes deliberately.

idea: Async shines for network services. **`tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(addr).await`** opens a listening socket, and `listener.accept().await` waits for the next connection, returning a `TcpStream` and the client's address. The idiomatic server **spawns one task per connection**, so thousands of mostly idle connections cost little memory.

Reading and writing use the `AsyncReadExt`/`AsyncWriteExt` traits (`read`, `write_all`, `read_to_end`). For line-based protocols, wrap the read half in **`BufReader`** and use `.lines()` (`next_line().await` returns `Ok(Some(line))`, or `Ok(None)` when the client disconnects). **`stream.into_split()`** (or `split` for borrowed halves) separates the read and write halves so a task can read while another writes.

Clients use **`TcpStream::connect(addr).await`**. Real protocols need **framing**: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries, so messages are delimited by newlines, length prefixes or a format's own structure. For anything beyond simple line protocols, `tokio_util::codec` provides framing (`LinesCodec`, `LengthDelimitedCodec`), and higher-level crates (hyper, axum, tonic) build HTTP and gRPC on top.
how: `let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").await?;` `let (socket, addr) = listener.accept().await?;`
One task per connection: `tokio::spawn(handle(socket))`.
`let (r, mut w) = socket.into_split();` `BufReader::new(r).lines()`.
`next_line().await` → `Ok(None)` when the peer disconnects.
Frame messages: newline, length prefix, or `tokio_util::codec`.

examples.title: A line-based echo server and two clients in one program
examples.note: The accept loop spawned a task per connection, and two clients talked to the server concurrently through `join!`. Each connection split its stream to read lines and write replies, and `next_line` returning `None` would end the handler when a client disconnects. Connection numbers depend on timing, so they are stripped and the replies sorted for stable output.

Close it immediately and reopen it in a task.

mistakes: **Handling connections sequentially in the accept loop.** One slow client blocks all others. Spawn a task each.
**Assuming one `read` equals one message.** TCP has no boundaries; frame your protocol.
**Ignoring write errors.** The client may have gone; stop the handler cleanly.

Split streams into read and write halves; BufReader for lines.
`next_line` returning `None` means the peer disconnected.
Frame messages explicitly; TCP is a byte stream.

idea: Async code needs async-aware synchronisation. **`tokio::sync::Mutex`** can be held across `.await` points (its `lock()` is itself async), while **`std::sync::Mutex`** must not be held across an await: its guard isn't `Send`, and holding it while the task sleeps blocks other tasks. The common advice: use std's Mutex for short, synchronous critical sections (it is faster), and Tokio's when you truly must hold the lock across an await. `tokio::sync::RwLock` is the async read-write lock.

**`Semaphore`** limits concurrency: create one with N permits, and each task `acquire()`s a permit before doing limited work (calling an API, opening a file); the permit is released when dropped. It is the standard tool for rate limiting and for capping parallel connections.

Tokio's channels cover the common patterns: **`mpsc`** (many producers, one consumer, bounded for back-pressure), **`oneshot`** (a single reply, for request/response between tasks), **`broadcast`** (every receiver gets every message: events, chat), and **`watch`** (receivers see the latest value only: configuration, status, shutdown). **Graceful shutdown** combines them: listen for Ctrl+C with `tokio::signal::ctrl_c()`, send a shutdown signal on a `watch` or `broadcast` channel (or a `CancellationToken`), have tasks `select!` on it, and wait for them to finish before exiting.
how: std `Mutex` for short sync sections; `tokio::sync::Mutex` when held across `.await`.
`Semaphore::new(n)`; `let _permit = sem.acquire().await?;` limits concurrency.
Channels: `mpsc` (queue), `oneshot` (one reply), `broadcast` (fan-out), `watch` (latest value).
Shutdown: `ctrl_c()` → signal via `watch`/`broadcast` → tasks `select!` → await them.
Keep critical sections short; never block inside them.

examples.title: A semaphore, a oneshot reply and a graceful shutdown
examples.note: The semaphore capped concurrent "API calls" at two even though six tasks were spawned. The oneshot channel carried a single reply from one task to another. For shutdown, a `watch` channel told every worker to stop; each was in a `select!` between its work and the signal, finished its loop, and was awaited before the program ended.

check.q: Six tasks call an API through a `Semaphore::new(2)`. What does the first line report?
options: `6 calls, never more than 1 at once`

Copy the value out and drop the guard before awaiting, or use `tokio::sync::Mutex` if the lock really must be held across the await.

mistakes: **Holding std locks across `.await`.** Non-Send futures and stalled tasks. Drop the guard first.
**Unlimited concurrency against external services.** Use a Semaphore.
**Exiting without waiting for tasks.** Signal shutdown, then await them.
keys: std Mutex for short sync sections; Tokio's Mutex across awaits.
Semaphores cap concurrency for rate limiting.
mpsc, oneshot, broadcast and watch channels fit different patterns.
Graceful shutdown: signal, select, then await every task.

idea: A declarative macro (`macro_rules!`) is a set of **rules**, each a pattern and an expansion. The compiler tries the rules in order and uses the first whose pattern matches the tokens it was given. Patterns capture pieces with **fragment specifiers**: `$e:expr` (an expression), `$i:ident` (a name), `$t:ty` (a type), `$p:pat` (a pattern), `$l:literal`, `$b:block`, `$v:vis` (a visibility such as `pub`), `$m:meta` (an attribute's contents), and `$t:tt`, a single **token tree** (one token, or a bracketed group), which matches almost anything and powers the most flexible macros.

**Repetition** is written `$( ... ),*` (zero or more, comma-separated) or `$( ... );+` (one or more, semicolon-separated); the expansion repeats the same way, and repetitions can nest. Macros can call themselves **recursively**, consuming input a piece at a time, and **internal rules** (by convention starting with `@name`) hide helper steps inside one macro.

Macros are **hygienic** for local variables: a `let x` inside an expansion can't clash with the caller's `x`. Item names (functions, types) are not hygienic, so macros that generate items take the names as `$name:ident`. In a library, mark a macro `#[macro_export]` to make it available at the crate root, and refer to your own items inside it as **`$crate::path`** so the macro works wherever it's called from.
how: `macro_rules! name { (pattern) => { expansion }; ... }`; rules are tried top to bottom.
Specifiers: `expr ident ty pat literal block vis meta tt`.
Repetition: `$( $x:expr ),*`, `$( ... );+`, `$(,)?` for an optional trailing comma.
Recursion and internal rules (`(@step ...) => ...`) for multi-stage macros.
`#[macro_export]` and `$crate::` in libraries.

examples.title: Generating an enum with string conversions
examples.note: One declaration produced the enum, a list of all variants, `as_str` and a `FromStr` implementation, keeping the names and strings in a single place. `max_of!` handled any number of arguments by recursing on the tail. Hygiene kept the macro's internal `first` separate from the caller's `first`.

check.explain: The macro compares the first value with the maximum of the rest, recursively, until one value remains.

examples.note: The only rule expects exactly two expressions, so the third argument produces "no rules expected the token" with an arrow at the extra comma. check.q: How can a macro give a friendlier message for a common misuse?
options: Add a final rule that matches the wrong form and calls `compile_error!("...")`.
Write the message in a doc comment.
check.explain: `compile_error!` produces a compile-time error with your text, instead of the generic "no rules expected the token".

mistakes: **Macros where a function would do.** Use a macro only for what functions can't express (variable arguments, generating items, new syntax).
**Using `tt` everywhere.** Specific specifiers like `expr` and `ident` give better errors.
**Bare paths in exported macros.** Use `$crate::` so the macro works in other crates.
keys: Rules are tried in order; fragment specifiers capture typed pieces of syntax.
Repetition and recursion handle any number of inputs.
Local variables are hygienic; item names are not.
Export with `#[macro_export]` and refer to items via `$crate`.

idea: **Procedural macros** are Rust functions that run at compile time, receive the code they're applied to as a stream of tokens, and return new tokens. There are three kinds: **derive macros** (`#[derive(Describe)]`, which add code next to a type), **attribute macros** (`#[route(GET, "/")]`, which transform the item they're attached to) and **function-like macros** (`sql!(...)`). They must live in their own crate with `[lib] proc-macro = true`, which is why crates like serde ship a separate `serde_derive`.

Three crates do the heavy lifting. **`proc-macro2`** provides token types usable outside the compiler (so the logic can be unit-tested). **`syn`** parses tokens into a syntax tree: `syn::parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput)` gives the type's name, generics, attributes and fields. **`quote`** turns Rust-like templates back into tokens: `quote! { impl #name { ... } }` interpolates variables with `#var` and repetitions with `#(...)*`.

Good macros produce **good errors**: instead of panicking, build a `syn::Error::new_spanned(node, "message")` and return `err.to_compile_error()`, so the compiler underlines the user's offending code. Use `cargo expand` (a cargo plugin) to see what any macro generates, which is the best debugging tool for both writing and using macros.
how: A separate crate: `[lib] proc-macro = true`; deps `syn`, `quote`, `proc-macro2`.
`#[proc_macro_derive(Describe)] pub fn derive(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream`.
Parse with `syn::parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput)`; inspect `data`, `fields`, `attrs`.
Generate with `quote! { ... #name ... #(#items)* }`.
Errors: `syn::Error::new_spanned(node, msg).to_compile_error()`; inspect output with `cargo expand`.

examples.note: This is exactly the code a `#[proc_macro_derive(Describe)]` function would call; running it as a normal program shows what it produces. `syn` parsed the struct's name and fields, and `quote!` generated an `impl` block (repeating one `push` per field) plus a helper function named with `format_ident!`. The enum produced a proper `syn::Error`, which in a real macro becomes a compiler error pointing at the enum's name.

options: Return `syn::Error::new_spanned(...)` converted with `to_compile_error()`, so the compiler points at the user's code.

examples.title: The two-crate layout and how users call it
examples.note: The derive function itself is tiny: parse, delegate to testable logic, and convert errors with `to_compile_error`. The trait (`Describe`) lives in a normal crate, and the macro in a `proc-macro = true` crate, which is the same split as serde and serde_derive. options: So users can choose a different derive syntax.
Because derive macros are licensed differently.
Procedural macros must live in their own crate with `proc-macro = true`.

mistakes: **Panicking in a macro.** Users get an unhelpful "proc macro panicked". Return `syn::Error`.
**All logic inside the `#[proc_macro_derive]` function.** Put it in a `proc_macro2` function you can unit-test.
**Hard-coding paths like `Describe` in output.** Prefer full paths (`::describe::Describe`) so user imports don't matter.
keys: Proc macros transform token streams at compile time, in a dedicated crate.
syn parses, quote generates, proc-macro2 makes it testable.
Report errors with `syn::Error` spans, never panics.
`cargo expand` reveals generated code.

idea: A **domain-specific language** (DSL) built with macros lets code read like the problem domain: a routing table, an HTML template, a state machine or a test table. Well-known examples are `vec![]`, `println!`, `html!` in Yew and `sqlx::query!`. A DSL is worth it when the same structure is written many times and the plain-Rust version is noisy; it is not worth it for one-off code, because every DSL is new syntax that readers, tools and error messages must cope with.

Design principles: keep the syntax close to Rust so it's guessable; **expand to ordinary Rust** (functions, match arms, structs), so the type checker validates everything the user wrote; and produce clear errors for common mistakes with `compile_error!`.

The core technique for declarative DSLs is **tt munching**: the macro matches the first piece of its input, emits code for it, and recursively calls itself on the rest (`$($rest:tt)*`), often accumulating output in an internal rule. Before reaching for a DSL, consider a **builder API** (`Router::new().route("/", get(index))`): it is plain Rust with full IDE support and good errors, and it's what axum and most libraries choose.
how: Use a DSL for repeated structure; otherwise prefer functions and builders.
Expand to plain Rust so types are checked.
tt munching: handle one item, recurse on `$($rest:tt)*`.
Accumulate output with internal rules (`(@acc [...] ...)`).
Add `compile_error!` rules for common mistakes.

The table reads like a configuration file but costs nothing at run time.

idea: Code is easy to test when its **dependencies are injected** rather than hard-wired. If a function sends email through a concrete SMTP client and reads `SystemTime::now()` directly, a test must send real email at the real time. If it depends on **traits** (`Mailer`, `Clock`) and receives implementations, production passes the real ones and tests pass **fakes**: a mailer that records messages, a clock that returns a fixed time. The same applies to randomness (inject a seeded RNG), the filesystem and HTTP.

Two styles of injection: **generics** (`struct Service<M: Mailer, C: Clock>`), which are zero-cost and resolved at compile time, and **trait objects** (`Box<dyn Mailer>`), which are flexible at run time. Both are fine; generics are the default when there's one implementation per program.

Fakes are hand-written test implementations with simple behaviour; **mocks** additionally verify how they were called. The `mockall` crate generates mocks with `#[automock]`, but simple hand-written fakes (often using `RefCell` or `Mutex` to record calls) are usually clearer. Organise tests in layers: unit tests in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` next to the code, integration tests in `tests/` against the public API, and doc tests for examples.
how: Define small traits for side effects: `trait Clock { fn now(&self) -> u64; }`.
Inject through generics or `Box<dyn Trait>`; production passes real implementations.
Fakes record calls (`RefCell<Vec<_>>`) and return canned data.
Control time and randomness: fixed clocks, seeded RNGs.
Unit tests beside code; integration tests in `tests/`; doc tests for examples.

mistakes: **Calling `now()`, `random()` or the network deep inside logic.** Inject them.
**Huge traits mirroring a whole client.** Define the few methods your code needs.

Generics or trait objects both enable injection.
Fakes record calls and return canned results.
Control time and randomness for deterministic tests.

idea: Example-based tests check the cases you thought of. **Property-based tests** state something that must hold for **all** inputs, and a library generates hundreds of random inputs to try to break it. In Rust, **proptest** is the standard: inside `proptest! { #[test] fn name(x in strategy) { ... } }`, a **strategy** describes the inputs (`0..100u32`, `any::<String>()`, `"[a-z]{1,8}"` regex strings, `prop::collection::vec(any::<u8>(), 0..50)`), and `prop_assert!` checks the property.

When a case fails, proptest **shrinks** it: it simplifies the input step by step while it still fails, then reports the **minimal** failing case (often an empty string or a single number), which makes the bug obvious. Failing seeds are saved to `proptest-regressions/` so the case is re-run on every future test run; commit that folder.

Useful property shapes: **round-trip** (`decode(encode(x)) == x`, perfect for parsers and serializers), **oracle** (your fast implementation agrees with a slow obvious one), **invariants** (output is sorted, length is preserved, no item lost), and **idempotence** (`normalise(normalise(x)) == normalise(x)`).
how: `proptest! { #[test] fn prop(x in strategy) { prop_assert!(...); } }`.
Strategies: ranges, `any::<T>()`, regex strings, `prop::collection::vec(s, 0..n)`.
Properties: round-trip, oracle, invariant, idempotence.
Read the shrunk minimal case when a property fails.
Commit `proptest-regressions/`.

In a normal `proptest!` test the same minimal case appears in the failure message and is saved to `proptest-regressions/`. The fix is to sum as `u64`.

options: It shrinks the input to a minimal case that still fails, and reports that.
It retries with a different seed until the test passes.
It stops and prints the first random input.
check.explain: Shrinking turns a big random failure into the smallest example, often an empty string or two numbers, which makes the bug obvious.

mistakes: **Re-implementing the function inside the property.** Test properties (round trip, invariants), not the same logic twice.
**Strategies that are too narrow.** Include empty, huge and Unicode inputs.
**Ignoring the regressions folder.** Commit it so found bugs stay tested.
keys: Properties must hold for all inputs; proptest generates and checks them.
Failing inputs are shrunk to minimal examples.
Round-trip, oracle, invariant and idempotence properties are the usual shapes.
Regression files keep found cases in the suite.

idea: **`tracing`** is Rust's structured logging and diagnostics framework. Instead of formatted strings, you emit **events** with fields: `info!(user_id = 42, items = 3, "order placed")`, and group work in **spans** (`#[instrument]` on a function, or `info_span!("request", id)`) so every event inside carries its context. A **subscriber** decides what to do with them: `tracing_subscriber::fmt()` prints readable lines or JSON, with a level filter from `RUST_LOG` (e.g. `RUST_LOG=info,myapp=debug`). Libraries only emit; the application installs the subscriber.

**Debuggers** remain the fastest way to understand a confusing state. `rust-gdb` and `rust-lldb` wrap gdb/lldb with Rust pretty-printers; most editors (VS Code with CodeLLDB, RustRover) offer breakpoints, stepping and variable inspection on debug builds. `dbg!(expr)` is the quick alternative: it prints the file, line, expression and value to stderr and returns the value.

To make code faster, **measure first**. **criterion** runs benchmarks many times and reports statistically meaningful timings and changes since the last run (`cargo bench`). **Flamegraphs** (`cargo flamegraph`) show where time goes across the whole program. Always profile release builds (`--release`, or `debug = true` in the release profile for symbols).
how: `tracing::{info, warn, debug, error}` with fields: `info!(id, ?config, "msg")`.
`#[instrument]` to create spans automatically, including arguments.
`tracing_subscriber::fmt().with_env_filter(...)` in `main` only.
`dbg!(x)` for quick inspection; rust-gdb/rust-lldb or the editor for stepping.
`cargo bench` with criterion; `cargo flamegraph`; always release mode.

Fields like `item` and `remaining` are structured data that a JSON subscriber would emit as keys. `dbg!` printed the expression and value with its source location (to stderr) and passed the value through.

[src/main.rs:38:17] stock["tea"] * 2 = 6

check.explain: Libraries only emit events. The application chooses how to format and filter them, once, at start-up.

examples.title: Benchmarking with criterion and finding hot spots

It makes timings more accurate by disabling the CPU cache.
It hides the benchmark from the report.

mistakes: **`println!` debugging left in code.** Use tracing with levels, or `dbg!` removed before committing.
**Installing a subscriber in a library.** Only the application chooses how to log.

`#[instrument]` adds context automatically.
`dbg!` and debuggers inspect state; criterion and flamegraphs measure speed.

idea: **serde** is Rust's serialisation framework: it separates **data structures** (which derive `Serialize` and `Deserialize`) from **formats** (separate crates: `serde_json`, `toml`, `serde_yaml`, `csv`, `bincode`...). Derive once, and the same type reads and writes every format, with conversions generated at compile time, so there is no reflection and no run-time cost.

**Attributes** adapt the mapping without changing your Rust names: `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` on a struct, `#[serde(rename = "type")]` on a field, `#[serde(default)]` to fill a missing field with its Default, `Option<T>` for optional fields (with `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` to omit them), `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` to reject typos in config files, and `#[serde(flatten)]` to inline a nested struct.

**Enums** have several representations: externally tagged by default (`{"Card": {...}}`), internally tagged with `#[serde(tag = "type")]` (`{"type": "card", ...}`, common in APIs), adjacently tagged, or untagged. Deserialising **validates the shape**: missing required fields, wrong types and unknown variants produce errors with line and column numbers. For untyped data, `serde_json::Value` represents any JSON.
how: `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`; `serde_json::to_string_pretty`, `from_str`; `toml::from_str`.
Field attributes: `rename`, `default`, `skip_serializing_if`, `alias`.
Container attributes: `rename_all = "camelCase"`, `deny_unknown_fields`.
Enums: `#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "snake_case")]` for API-style tags.
Errors report what and where; `serde_json::Value` for dynamic JSON.

examples.title: JSON and TOML from the same types
examples.note: The TOML file omitted `port`, so `default_port` filled it in, and the camelCase keys mapped onto snake_case fields. Serialising to JSON skipped the empty `pool` thanks to `skip_serializing_if`. The payment enum used an internal `type` tag, the format most web APIs use, in both directions.

check.q: The TOML file omits `port`, and the field has `#[serde(default = "default_port")]`. What happens?
options: `default_port()` fills it in, so the config parses with port 8080.
check.explain: `default` attributes supply values for missing fields. Without one, a required field missing from the input is an error.

examples.title: What invalid data looks like
examples.note: Each error names the problem and its position: a missing field, a negative number for an unsigned type, an unknown field (rejected because of `deny_unknown_fields`) and truncated input. Validation happens during parsing, so the program never holds a half-valid `Item`. `serde_json::Value` handles JSON whose shape isn't known ahead of time.

ok:    Item { name: "tea", price_cents: 450, tags: None }
error: missing field `price_cents` at line 1 column 15
error: invalid value: integer `-5`, expected u32 at line 1 column 33
error: unknown field `colour`, expected one of `name`, `price_cents`, `tags` at line 1 column 44
error: EOF while parsing a value at line 1 column 35
