error: unknown field `colour`, expected one of `name`, `price_cents`, `tags` at line 1 column 44
check.explain: `deny_unknown_fields` turns an unexpected key into an error with its position, instead of silently ignoring a possible typo.

mistakes: **Parsing JSON by hand with string operations.** Derive and let serde validate.
**Renaming Rust fields to match a format.** Use `rename`/`rename_all` and keep idiomatic names.
**Silently ignoring typos in config files.** Add `deny_unknown_fields`.
keys: Derive once; any serde format can read and write the type.
Attributes adapt names, defaults and optional fields.
Internally tagged enums match common API shapes.
Deserialising validates shape and reports precise errors.

idea: **clap** is the standard crate for command-line parsing. With its **derive API**, you describe the interface as a struct: each field becomes an argument, its type decides parsing and validation (`u16`, `PathBuf`, `bool` flags, `Option<T>` optional, `Vec<T>` repeated), doc comments become help text, and `#[derive(Parser)]` generates `Cli::parse()`, which reads `std::env::args`, prints errors and help, and exits with the right code.

Attributes control the details: `#[arg(short, long)]` for `-v`/`--verbose`, `default_value_t`, `value_enum` for a fixed set of choices, `value_parser = clap::value_parser!(u8).range(1..=10)` for ranges, `env = "TODO_FILE"` to fall back to an environment variable (with the `env` feature), and `#[command(version, about)]` for `--version` and the description. **Subcommands** (`git commit`, `cargo build`) are an enum deriving `Subcommand`, each variant with its own arguments.

clap gives users consistent behaviour for free: `--help` and `-h`, suggestions for typos ("did you mean"), clear errors for missing or invalid values, and exit code 2 for usage errors. For tests, **`Cli::try_parse_from([...])`** parses a given list instead of the real arguments and returns errors instead of exiting.
how: `#[derive(Parser)] #[command(version, about)] struct Cli { ... }`; `Cli::parse()`.
Fields: `#[arg(short, long)]`, `default_value_t`, `Option<T>`, `Vec<T>`, `bool` flags.
Subcommands: `#[command(subcommand)] cmd: Command` with `#[derive(Subcommand)] enum Command`.
Validation: types, `value_enum`, `value_parser!(...).range(..)`; `env = "VAR"` with the env feature.
Test with `Cli::try_parse_from(["prog", "add", "milk"])`.

The usage line and the "For more information, try --help" hint that clap adds are filtered out here to keep the output short.

**Stringly typed options.** Use numeric types, `PathBuf` and value enums so clap validates them.
**Calling `parse()` in tests.** Use `try_parse_from` with explicit arguments.

Types and attributes provide validation, defaults and env fallbacks.

idea: **reqwest** is the most popular HTTP client. Its async API (on Tokio) starts with a **`Client`**, which holds a connection pool, so create one and reuse it for many requests. Build requests with `client.get(url)` or `.post(url)`, add `.query(&[("q", "rust")])`, `.header(...)`, `.bearer_auth(token)`, `.json(&body)` (serialises with serde and sets the content type) and `.timeout(Duration)`, then `.send().await`.

The **response** has a `status()`, `headers()`, and body methods: `.text().await`, `.bytes().await`, or **`.json::<T>().await`** to deserialise straight into your serde types. An important detail: reqwest treats any **HTTP status** as a successful request; a 404 or 500 is still `Ok(response)`. Call **`.error_for_status()?`** to turn 4xx/5xx into errors when that's what you want. Network failures (DNS, refused connection, timeout) are `Err`, and `e.is_timeout()`, `e.is_connect()` and `e.status()` tell them apart.

Set **timeouts** on every client used in production (`Client::builder().timeout(...)`), because the default is to wait forever. Underneath, reqwest uses **hyper**, a lower-level HTTP library that also powers axum; you rarely need hyper directly. A `blocking` feature offers a synchronous API for scripts.
how: `let client = Client::builder().timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)).build()?;` and reuse it.
`client.get(url).query(&[..]).bearer_auth(t).send().await?`.
`.json(&body)` to send; `.json::<T>().await?` to receive.
`.error_for_status()?` to treat 4xx/5xx as errors.
Distinguish errors with `is_timeout()`, `is_connect()`, `status()`.

examples.note: A small axum server on a random local port stood in for a real API, so the example runs without internet access. The client decoded JSON into `Vec<Book>`, sent a JSON body, and showed that a 404 is a normal response until `error_for_status` converts it, while the slow endpoint produced a timeout error thanks to the client-wide timeout.

search 'dun': [Book { id: 1, title: "Dune" }]
POST status 201 Created -> Book { id: 3, title: "Kindred" }
404 is still Ok(response): status 404 Not Found
after error_for_status: error with status Some(404)

options: `404 is still Ok(response): status 404 Not Found`
check.explain: reqwest treats any HTTP status as a successful request. Only `error_for_status()` turns 4xx and 5xx into errors.

examples.title: Retrying only what's worth retrying
examples.note: Client errors such as 404 won't succeed on a second attempt, so only timeouts, refused connections, 429 and 5xx responses are retried, with exponential backoff capped at five seconds. With reqwest you'd map `e.is_timeout()`, `e.is_connect()` and `resp.status()` into this decision; crates like `reqwest-retry` package the same policy.

Status(404)    retry? false

mistakes: **A new Client per request.** It throws away the connection pool. Create one and reuse it.
**Assuming `Ok` means success.** Check the status or call `error_for_status`.
**No timeout.** A stuck server can hang your program forever.
keys: Reuse one Client; build requests fluently and `send().await`.
`.json()` sends and receives serde types.
HTTP error statuses are responses; `error_for_status` makes them errors.
Always set timeouts; retry only transient failures.

idea: **axum** is a web framework built on Tokio, hyper and tower. An application is a **`Router`** that maps paths and methods to **handlers**: `Router::new().route("/notes", get(list).post(create)).route("/notes/{id}", get(show))`. A handler is just an async function whose **arguments are extractors** and whose **return value implements `IntoResponse`**.

**Extractors** pull typed data from the request: `Path(id): Path<u32>` (from `/notes/{id}`), `Query(params): Query<Filter>` (the query string into a serde struct), `Json(body): Json<NewNote>` (the body, rejected with a 4xx if invalid), `State(state): State<AppState>` (shared application state), and `HeaderMap`. Failing extractors respond with an error automatically, so handlers only see valid input.

**Responses**: return `Json(value)`, a `String`, a `StatusCode`, a tuple like `(StatusCode::CREATED, Json(note))`, or `Result<T, AppError>` where your error type implements `IntoResponse`. **Shared state** is typically an `Arc` around a struct with a `Mutex` or a database pool, attached with `.with_state(state)`. Because a Router is a tower `Service`, you can **test handlers without a network** by calling `app.oneshot(request).await`.
how: `Router::new().route("/path/{id}", get(h).post(h2)).with_state(state)`.
Extractors: `Path`, `Query`, `Json`, `State`, `HeaderMap`; the body extractor goes last.
Return `Json`, `StatusCode`, tuples or `Result<_, E: IntoResponse>`.
State: `#[derive(Clone)] struct AppState { notes: Arc<Mutex<..>> }`.
Tests: `app.oneshot(Request::builder().uri("/").body(Body::empty())?).await`.

examples.title: A notes API, exercised without a network
examples.note: Every request went straight into the router with `oneshot`, so the whole API was tested without opening a port. The handlers stayed small because extractors did the parsing: a body with the wrong field and a non-numeric id were rejected automatically with 422 and 400 responses, while the empty-text check and the 404 came from the handlers' own `Result` returns.

check.q: A request body `{"txt":"typo"}` is sent to `POST /notes`, whose handler expects `{"text": ...}`. What comes back?
options: A 422 response from the `Json` extractor saying the field `text` is missing; the handler never runs.
A 500 response because the handler panicked.
A 201 response with an empty note.
A 422 response from the handler saying "text must not be empty".
check.explain: Extractors validate the request before the handler is called, so a body of the wrong shape is rejected automatically. The handler's own empty-text check only sees well-formed bodies.

examples.title: An error type that becomes a response
examples.note: Handlers can now return `Result<Json<T>, AppError>` and use `?`; each error variant maps to a status code and a consistent JSON body. Internal errors are logged in full but shown to clients only as a generic message, so database details never leak.

404 Not Found "application/json"
422 Unprocessable Entity "application/json"
internal error: db locked
500 Internal Server Error "application/json"

options: Because 500 responses can't have a body.
To avoid leaking details like database errors to clients, while logging them in full on the server.
check.explain: Clients get a consistent JSON error; operators get the details in the logs. Leaking internals helps attackers and confuses users.

mistakes: **Putting the `Json` body extractor before others.** The body-consuming extractor must be the last argument.
**Holding a std Mutex guard across `.await` in a handler.** Lock, copy, unlock; or use an async-aware store.
**Testing only by running the server and curling.** Use `oneshot` for fast, deterministic tests.
keys: Routers map paths and methods to async handlers.
Extractors turn requests into typed, validated arguments.
Anything implementing `IntoResponse` can be returned, including your error type.
`oneshot` tests the whole stack without a network.

idea: **rusqlite** gives synchronous access to **SQLite**, a full SQL database stored in a single file (or in memory), which is perfect for CLIs, desktop apps and small services. With the `bundled` feature, SQLite is compiled into your program, so there's nothing to install. Open with `Connection::open("app.db")` or `open_in_memory()`, run schema statements with `execute_batch`, and insert with **`execute(sql, params![...])`**.

Always pass values as **parameters** (`?1`, `?2` or `:name` placeholders), never by formatting them into the SQL string. Parameters can't change the query's structure, which makes SQL injection impossible and handles quoting correctly. Query rows with `prepare` and **`query_map`**, mapping each row into a struct with `row.get(index or "name")`; `query_row` fetches exactly one. Use `Option<T>` for nullable columns.

**Transactions** group statements so they all succeed or none do: `let tx = conn.transaction()?; ... tx.commit()?;` (dropping without commit rolls back). They are also much faster for bulk inserts. For async services and other databases, **sqlx** offers async connection pools for PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite, and its `query!` macro checks SQL against a real database **at compile time**, catching typos and type mismatches before you run anything. **Diesel** and **SeaORM** are popular ORMs.
how: `Connection::open_in_memory()?` / `open(path)?`; `execute_batch` for schema.
`conn.execute("INSERT ... VALUES (?1, ?2)", params![a, b])?`; never `format!` SQL.
`prepare(...)?.query_map(params, |row| Ok(T { x: row.get(0)? }))?`.
`let tx = conn.transaction()?; ...; tx.commit()?;`
sqlx for async and compile-time-checked queries; Diesel/SeaORM for ORMs.

examples.title: Bugs in SQLite with rusqlite
examples.note: The inserts ran inside one transaction, so either all three rows were saved or none would have been. Query results mapped into structs, with the nullable `assignee` column as `Option<String>`. The `CHECK` constraint in the schema rejected an invalid severity, showing that the database enforces rules too.

check.q: Three bugs are inserted with severities 1, 4 and 2. The query selects `severity <= 2 ORDER BY severity`. Which bug is printed second?
options: `Bug { id: 3, title: "Slow search", severity: 2, assignee: Some("bo") }`
`Bug { id: 1, title: "Slow search", severity: 2, assignee: Some("bo") }`
`Bug { id: 2, title: "Typo in menu", severity: 4, assignee: None }`
check.explain: Only severities 1 and 2 pass the filter, sorted ascending, so "Slow search" (id 3) comes after "Crash on save".

examples.title: Why parameters, never format!
examples.note: Pasting user input into SQL let the `OR '1'='1'` fragment rewrite the query, so it matched every user. As a parameter, the same text was treated purely as a value and matched nobody. Parameters also handle quoting, so names like O'Brien need no escaping.

format!-built query matched 3 users (injection!)
parameterised query matched 0 users
apostrophes just work: O'Brien

check.q: Why did the query built with `format!` match every user?
options: The parameterised query had a bug.
SQLite ignores the WHERE clause in formatted queries.
The input's `' OR '1'='1` became part of the SQL and changed the query's logic.
check.explain: That's SQL injection. Parameters send the input as a value only, so it can never change the query's structure.

mistakes: **Building SQL with `format!`.** SQL injection and quoting bugs. Always use parameters.
**Bulk inserts without a transaction.** Each insert syncs to disk; a transaction is many times faster.
**Non-Option types for nullable columns.** `row.get` fails on NULL; use `Option<T>`.
keys: rusqlite with `bundled` embeds SQLite; no setup needed.
Parameters prevent injection and handle quoting.
`query_map` maps rows into structs; transactions make changes atomic.
sqlx adds async pools and compile-time-checked SQL.

idea: **`unsafe`** unlocks five abilities the compiler can't verify: dereferencing raw pointers, calling `unsafe` functions (including foreign ones), accessing mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits (`Send`, `Sync`), and accessing union fields. It does **not** turn off the borrow checker or type checking; it marks a place where **you** promise invariants the compiler can't check. Keep unsafe blocks tiny, document each with a `// SAFETY:` comment explaining why it's sound, and wrap them in **safe APIs** so callers can't misuse them.

The **foreign function interface** (FFI) is the main reason to write unsafe code. Declare C functions in an `unsafe extern "C" { fn strlen(s: *const c_char) -> usize; }` block (Rust 2024 requires the `unsafe` keyword there) and call them inside `unsafe { }`. Strings need conversion because C strings are NUL-terminated: **`CString::new("hi")`** creates an owned C string (failing if the text contains a NUL byte) and `.as_ptr()` lends it; **`CStr::from_ptr(p)`** borrows a C string returned to you.

The other direction exposes Rust to C: `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32` keeps the symbol name, and `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` builds a shared library. Tools help: **bindgen** generates Rust declarations from C headers, **cbindgen** generates headers from Rust, and the `cc` crate compiles C code in build scripts. For checking unsafe code, **Miri** (`cargo +nightly miri test`) detects undefined behaviour.
how: `unsafe extern "C" { fn name(args) -> ret; }`; call inside `unsafe { }`.
`CString::new(s)?.as_ptr()` to pass; `CStr::from_ptr(p).to_str()` to receive.
`extern "C" fn` callbacks for C APIs that take function pointers.
Expose: `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn ...`, `crate-type = ["cdylib"]`.
Wrap unsafe in safe functions with `// SAFETY:` comments; check with Miri.

Callers of `c_len`, `c_sort` and `env_var` can't trigger undefined behaviour.

strlen with an inner NUL: Err("nul byte found in provided data at position: 3")

getenv("DEFINITELY_UNSET_VAR") = None

To convert the text to ASCII.
C needs a NUL-terminated string, and `CString` guarantees one (rejecting text with an inner NUL).
check.explain: Rust `&str` isn't NUL-terminated. `CString::new` adds the terminator and fails if the text already contains a NUL byte, which C would treat as the end.

examples.note: Foreign functions are unsafe to call because the compiler can't check what C code does with the pointer, so calling `strlen` outside an `unsafe` block is error E0133. The fix is a small `unsafe { }` block with a SAFETY comment, ideally inside a safe wrapper like `c_len` above.

check.q: What is required to call a function declared in an `unsafe extern "C"` block?
options: Nothing: foreign functions are safe by default.
An `unsafe { }` block at the call site, ideally with a SAFETY comment.
check.explain: The compiler can't check what C code does with the arguments, so the caller must promise it's correct. Wrapping the call in a safe function contains that promise.

mistakes: **Large unsafe blocks.** Keep them minimal so the unchecked surface is small and reviewable.
**Passing a pointer from a temporary CString.** `CString::new(s).unwrap().as_ptr()` dangles immediately; keep the CString in a variable.
**Exposing raw-pointer APIs to Rust callers.** Wrap FFI in safe functions with documented invariants.
keys: `unsafe` marks promises the compiler can't verify; it disables no checks.
FFI: declare in `unsafe extern "C"`, convert with CString/CStr.
Safe wrappers and SAFETY comments contain the risk.
bindgen, cbindgen, cc and Miri support FFI work.

idea: **WebAssembly** (WASM) is a compact binary format that browsers (and runtimes like Wasmtime) execute at near-native speed in a sandbox. Rust compiles to it with the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target, and is one of the best languages for it: no garbage collector, small binaries and a mature toolchain. Typical uses are compute-heavy code in web apps (image and audio processing, parsers, simulations, games), sharing logic between server and browser, and plugin systems.

**wasm-bindgen** bridges Rust and JavaScript: mark functions or structs `#[wasm_bindgen]` and it generates the glue to pass **numbers, strings, arrays and objects** across the boundary (strings are copied, since Rust uses UTF-8 and JavaScript UTF-16). **wasm-pack** builds the crate (`crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]`), runs wasm-bindgen and produces a `pkg/` folder with the `.wasm` file, JavaScript bindings and TypeScript types, ready to import or publish to npm. The `web-sys` and `js-sys` crates expose browser APIs and JavaScript built-ins.

WASM **isn't** a replacement for JavaScript: DOM manipulation is still easier in JS, crossing the boundary has a cost, so pass data in large chunks, and download size matters (optimise with `opt-level = "s"`, `lto = true` and `wasm-opt`). For **desktop GUIs**, Tauri (a web front end with a Rust back end), egui (immediate-mode) and Iced (Elm-style) are popular choices.
how: `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown`; `cargo install wasm-pack`.
`[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]`; `#[wasm_bindgen] pub fn ...`.
`wasm-pack build --target web --release` → `pkg/` with .wasm, JS glue and .d.ts.
Keep logic in plain Rust (testable natively); a thin `#[wasm_bindgen]` layer on top.
Shrink: `opt-level = "s"`, `lto = true`, `wasm-opt`; pass data in chunks.

examples.title: The core logic, tested natively before it ever reaches a browser
examples.note: All the interesting behaviour lives in a plain Rust function, so it's tested with `cargo test` on your machine, quickly and with normal tooling. The WebAssembly part (next example) is only a thin wrapper that converts the result for JavaScript, which keeps the browser-specific code small.
examples.output:
running 3 tests
test tests::counts_words_and_headings ... ok
test tests::ignores_code_blocks_and_symbols ... ok
test tests::reading_time_rounds_up ... ok
test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
examples.label: cargo test output

check.q: Why keep the markdown statistics in a plain Rust function rather than behind `#[wasm_bindgen]`?
options: Plain functions run faster in the browser.
It can be tested natively with `cargo test`, and the wasm layer stays thin.
check.explain: The browser-specific code is just a wrapper. All the logic gets fast, ordinary tests.

examples.title: The wasm-bindgen layer and the JavaScript that calls it
examples.note: `#[wasm_bindgen]` generated the JavaScript glue, so the browser calls `word_stats` like a normal JS function and reads the struct's public fields as properties. The DOM work stays in JavaScript, where it's simplest, while Rust does the analysis. With size-oriented release settings the whole module is around 20 KB.

check.q: Which Cargo setting is needed for a crate built with wasm-pack?
check.explain: `cdylib` produces the `.wasm` module; `rlib` keeps the crate usable by native tests and other Rust crates.

mistakes: **Crossing the JS/WASM boundary in tight loops.** Each call and string copy costs; pass data in batches.
**Shipping debug builds.** They're many times larger; build with `--release` and size settings.
**Putting all logic behind `#[wasm_bindgen]`.** Keep a plain Rust core you can test natively.
keys: Rust compiles to WASM for fast, sandboxed code in browsers and runtimes.
wasm-bindgen generates JS glue; wasm-pack builds a ready-to-use package.
Keep logic in plain Rust; a thin binding layer on top.
Mind binary size and boundary costs; Tauri, egui and Iced cover desktop GUIs.

idea: Continuous integration (CI) runs the same checks on every push and pull request, so a mistake is caught minutes after it's made instead of weeks later. For Rust, employers expect a recognisable set: **cargo fmt --check** (layout), **cargo clippy -- -D warnings** (lints, with warnings treated as errors), and **cargo test** on each platform you support. A red check on a pull request is the cheapest bug report there is.

Speed matters, because a slow pipeline gets ignored. **Swatinem/rust-cache** keeps compiled dependencies between runs, a **matrix** runs the test job on Linux, macOS and Windows in parallel, and `needs:` lets the cheap checks fail fast before the expensive ones start. A **minimum supported Rust version** (MSRV) job proves the crate still builds on the oldest compiler you promise, and **cargo audit** or **cargo deny** flags dependencies with known security advisories.
A pipeline only protects the main branch if its checks are **required**: in the repository's branch protection settings, mark the jobs as required status checks so nothing merges red.
how: Steps: `actions/checkout`, `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable` (with `components: clippy, rustfmt`), `Swatinem/rust-cache@v2`.
Quality gate: `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`, `cargo test --all-features`.
`strategy.matrix.os` for platforms; `fail-fast: false` so every platform reports.
Extra jobs worth adding: MSRV (`rust-version` in Cargo.toml), `cargo audit`, coverage with `cargo llvm-cov`.
Make the jobs required in branch protection.

examples.title: Decide which checks a change needs
examples.note: Path filters like this (GitHub's `paths:` and `paths-ignore:` keys do the same declaratively) keep CI fast on documentation changes. Notice that any change to the workflow files themselves runs everything: a CI change must prove it still works.
examples.output:
["markdown links"]
["fmt", "clippy", "test (linux)", "test (macos)", "test (windows)"]
6

check.q: A pull request changes only README.md. Which line is printed for it?
check.explain: No code, Cargo files or workflow files changed, so only the documentation check runs. That's the point of path filters: fast CI for docs-only changes.

examples.title: A pre-push check that mirrors CI
examples.note: Save the real version as a Git pre-push hook or a `cargo xtask` command so your machine runs exactly what CI runs. Keeping the list in one place means the local check and the pipeline can't drift apart.
examples.output:
format  cargo fmt --all --check
lint    cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
test    cargo test --quiet
3 steps, stop at the first failure

check.q: Why keep the list of commands in one place for both the pre-push check and CI?
options: Because Git hooks can only run three commands.
Because cargo refuses to run clippy twice.
So the CI job doesn't need a cache.
So the local check and the pipeline can't drift apart and give different answers.
check.explain: If your machine runs the same gate as CI, a green local run predicts a green build, and you don't push code that fails formatting or lints.

mistakes: **Running `cargo clippy` without `-D warnings`.** Warnings print, the job still passes, and they pile up.
**Testing on one platform only.** Path separators, line endings and file locking differ on Windows.
**No cache.** Every run recompiles every dependency, and a 2-minute pipeline becomes 12.
**Checks that aren't required.** A red pipeline that can still be merged protects nothing.
keys: The Rust quality bar: fmt --check, clippy -D warnings, tests on each platform.
Cache dependencies; let cheap jobs fail first.
Add MSRV, audit and coverage jobs as the project grows.
Make the checks required before merging.

idea: Python is the language of most test automation, and Rust can make its slowest parts fast without asking anyone to leave Python. **PyO3** is the crate that connects the two: it converts Python values to Rust types and back, turns a Rust `Err` into a Python exception, and lets you mark functions with **`#[pyfunction]`** and group them in a **`#[pymodule]`**. **maturin** builds the result into a Python extension: `maturin develop` installs it into your virtual environment, and `maturin build --release` makes a wheel you can publish to PyPI.

The design rule that keeps this maintainable is a **thin wrapper**: put the real logic in ordinary Rust functions that know nothing about Python, test them with `cargo test`, and make each `#[pyfunction]` a few lines that convert types and errors. Then pytest only needs to check the boundary: names, argument types and exceptions.

Pick the right work to move. Rust pays off for CPU-heavy loops (parsing large logs, comparing thousands of names, hashing files) where Python spends its time in the interpreter. It doesn't help code that mostly waits on a browser, a network or a database.
how: Start with `maturin new --bindings pyo3 NAME`; `crate-type = ["cdylib"]` in Cargo.toml.
`#[pyfunction] fn f(x: Vec<bool>) -> PyResult<f64>`; register with `m.add_function(wrap_pyfunction!(f, m)?)?`.
Errors: `.map_err(PyValueError::new_err)` turns a `String` error into a `ValueError`.
Build: `maturin develop --release`; test with `cargo test` and `pytest`.
Measure before and after with the same input, in release builds.

examples.title: Keep the core free of PyO3
examples.note: The PyO3 wrapper for this would take `&str` and return a `BTreeMap<String, u32>`, which PyO3 turns into a Python dict. Returning `&str` keys borrowed from the input works in Rust but not across the boundary, so the wrapper converts them to owned Strings.
examples.output:
test_cart: 2 failure(s)
test_search: 1 failure(s)

check.q: The log has two FAIL lines for test_cart. Which line reports it?
check.explain: Each FAIL line adds one to that test's count, so test_cart reports 2. test_search failed once, and test_login never failed, so it isn't in the map at all.

examples.title: Errors that make sense on both sides
examples.note: With a Display implementation, the wrapper can raise `PyValueError::new_err(e.to_string())` and Python users see the same clear message Rust users do. A typed error enum keeps the Rust side testable: tests can match on `ParseError::BadLine { number: 2, .. }` instead of comparing strings.
examples.output:
Ok([1.5, 0.25])
error: line 2: can't read "slow"

check.q: The second call gets "1.5s" then "slow". What does the last line print?
check.explain: "slow" doesn't parse as a number, so collecting into a Result stops at line 2 with a BadLine error, and Display formats it.

mistakes: **Putting logic inside `#[pyfunction]`.** It can only be tested through Python; keep the wrapper thin.
**Measuring a debug build.** `maturin develop` without `--release` can be slower than Python.
**Moving I/O-bound code to Rust.** Waiting on a browser or network doesn't get faster.
**Panicking across the boundary.** Return `PyResult` so Python gets an exception, not a crash report.
keys: PyO3 converts types and errors; maturin builds and installs the extension.
Keep a plain Rust core and a thin wrapper.
Test the core with cargo test, the boundary with pytest.
Move CPU-heavy loops, and measure in release mode.

idea: `#[test]` with `assert_eq!` checks examples you thought of. The rest of the toolbox finds the cases you didn't. **Property-based testing** (the **proptest** crate) states a rule for every input, such as "decoding an encoding gives back the original", then generates hundreds of inputs and **shrinks** any failure to the smallest one. **Snapshot testing** (**insta**) stores a known-good output, such as a formatted report, and shows a readable diff when it changes. **Fuzzing** (**cargo-fuzz**) feeds random and mutated bytes into a parser for minutes or hours, looking for panics.

Two more tools measure the tests themselves. **Coverage** (**cargo llvm-cov**) shows which lines no test ran. **Mutation testing** (**cargo mutants**) changes your code (flips a `<`, replaces a return value) and reports every change that no test noticed: a stricter measure than coverage, because a line can be covered by a test that asserts nothing about it. **cargo nextest** runs tests faster, one process per test, with retries that expose flaky tests.
A QA engineer's value is knowing which question each tool answers, and picking the cheapest one that answers yours.
how: proptest: `proptest! { #[test] fn p(s in "[a-z]{0,20}") { prop_assert_eq!(...) } }`; regressions saved in `proptest-regressions/`.
insta: `insta::assert_snapshot!(report)`; review changes with `cargo insta review`.
cargo-fuzz: `cargo fuzz init`, `cargo fuzz run target` (nightly).
Coverage: `cargo llvm-cov --html`. Mutants: `cargo mutants`. Faster runs: `cargo nextest run`.
Good first properties: round trips, invariants, and agreement with a slow but obviously correct version.

examples.title: Compare a fast function with a simple oracle
examples.note: The oracle pattern is the easiest property to write when you're optimising: keep the slow version as the specification and check the fast one against it. Edge cases (0, all ones, the top bit) are listed explicitly, because random inputs rarely hit them.
examples.output:
10000 random values and 4 edge cases agree
popcount(0xFF) = 8

check.q: Why list 0, u32::MAX and 0x8000_0000 explicitly when 10,000 random values are already checked?
options: The oracle only works on those values.
To make the program run longer.
Random inputs rarely hit edge values, and edges are where bugs hide.
check.explain: Property tests and explicit edge cases complement each other: randomness explores broadly, and the listed values make sure the boundaries are always tried.

examples.title: What a surviving mutant looks like
examples.note: Both suites cover every line of `discount`, so coverage can't tell them apart. Only the strong suite tests the boundary value 5000, which is where `>=` and `>` disagree. That's the case mutation testing pushes you to add.
examples.output:
weak: pass on real code = true, mutant caught = false
strong: pass on real code = true, mutant caught = true

check.q: Which line is printed for the weak suite?
options: `weak: pass on real code = true, mutant caught = true`
`weak: pass on real code = false, mutant caught = false`
`weak: pass on real code = true, mutant caught = false`
check.explain: Neither 1000 nor 8000 sits at the 5000 boundary, where >= and > disagree, so the mutant survives even though every line is covered.

mistakes: **Treating coverage as the goal.** 100% coverage with weak assertions catches little; mutants show it.
**Random tests without a seed or shrinking.** A failure you can't reproduce is a failure you can't fix.
**Snapshots nobody reviews.** Accepting every change with `cargo insta accept` turns them into rubber stamps.
**Properties that restate the code.** Test a rule (round trip, invariant, oracle), not the same formula twice.
keys: proptest: rules for all inputs, with shrinking and saved regressions.
insta: readable diffs of known-good output; fuzzing: panics in parsers.
Coverage finds untested lines; mutation testing finds weak tests.
Choose the tool by the question you need answered.

idea: A **flaky test** passes and fails with the same code. It's worse than a missing test, because people learn to rerun and ignore red builds. Rust removes many causes (no data races in safe code), but `cargo test` runs tests **in parallel threads of one process**, which creates its own: two tests writing the same file, one test's `std::env::set_var` changing another's environment, or two tests binding the same port.

The other usual causes are the same as in any language: **real time** (a sleep that's long enough on a laptop and too short on a loaded CI machine, a date check around midnight), **randomness** without a fixed seed, **ordering** (iterating a `HashMap`, whose order changes between runs, then comparing with a list), and **external services** that are slow or down.

The fixes follow one principle: make the test control everything it depends on. Give each test its own temporary directory, pass configuration in instead of reading the environment, inject clocks and random generators, sort before comparing, and **wait for a condition** with a timeout instead of sleeping. To detect flakiness, rerun: `cargo nextest run --retries 2` reports tests that only passed on a retry.
how: Isolate: `tempfile::tempdir()` per test; bind to port 0 and read the chosen port back.
Inject: pass config maps, clocks and seeded RNGs as parameters.
Order: compare sorted Vecs or use BTreeMap when order matters.
Wait: poll a condition with a timeout instead of `thread::sleep`.
Detect: rerun loops, `cargo nextest run --retries N`, `-- --test-threads=1` as an experiment.

examples.title: HashMap order versus a stable comparison
examples.note: Rust deliberately randomises `HashMap` iteration order between runs to resist denial-of-service attacks, so a test that compares keys in their iteration order can pass for a week and then fail. Sorting, or collecting into a `BTreeMap`, makes the comparison deterministic.
examples.output:
sorted keys: ["#fast", "#rust", "#safe"]
as BTreeMap: {"#fast": 1, "#rust": 2, "#safe": 1}

check.q: Why is comparing a HashMap's keys in iteration order a flaky test?
options: Rust randomises HashMap iteration order between runs.
Keys are only sorted in release builds.
check.explain: The order is deliberately unpredictable. Sort the keys or use a BTreeMap when the test depends on order.

examples.title: Port 0 instead of a fixed port
examples.note: The test then passes the real address (from `local_addr`) to the client it's testing. The same idea, "let each test get its own resource", applies to temporary directories, database schemas and environment configuration.
examples.output: two servers, two different ports: true

check.q: What does binding to 127.0.0.1:0 do?
options: Asks the operating system for any free port, so parallel tests don't collide.
check.explain: Port 0 means "pick one for me". The test reads the real port back with local_addr and passes it to the client.

mistakes: **Fixing flakiness with `--test-threads=1` in CI.** It hides shared state and slows every run.
**Adding retries and moving on.** Retries are a detector, not a fix; track and remove the cause.
**Longer sleeps.** They make the suite slower and only move the failure to a busier machine.
**Comparing HashMap iteration order.** Sort first, or use BTreeMap.
keys: Parallel tests in one process share files, environment variables and ports.
Time, randomness, ordering and external services are the other usual causes.
Isolate and inject; wait on conditions; sort before comparing.
Rerun to detect, then fix the cause.

idea: Rust interviews, and QA-automation interviews where Rust is a plus, tend to test three things. First, **concepts in plain words**: ownership and moves, borrowing (any number of `&T` or exactly one `&mut T`), lifetimes as "how long a reference is valid", `Box`/`Rc`/`Arc`, `Send`/`Sync`, and `Result` versus `panic!`. A clear two-sentence answer with an example beats a long one.

Second, **reading the compiler**. You may be shown code that doesn't compile and asked why. Read the error aloud: its code (`E0502`), the two places it points to, and the rule behind it. Then offer more than one fix and say when you'd choose each.

Third, **live coding**. Before typing, restate the problem and list test cases, including edge cases (empty input, one element, duplicates, very large values). That's where a testing background shows. Then write the simplest correct version, run your cases by hand, and only then improve it. For behavioural questions, prepare **STAR** stories (situation, task, action, result) about quality work, with your actions and a measurable result.
how: Concepts: answer first, then one example, then the trade-off.
Compiler errors: code, the two spans, the rule, two fixes.
Live coding: restate, list test cases, simplest version, walk through, improve.
STAR: short situation and task, most time on action, end with a number.
Practise aloud; time yourself to about a minute per answer.

examples.title: Ownership in one screen
examples.note: This covers the three ways to pass a value: lend it (`&`), give it away (move), or copy it explicitly (`clone`). Saying "the compiler inserts the drop when the owner goes out of scope" answers the follow-up about memory without mentioning a garbage collector.
examples.output:
borrowed: 3, a still has 3 items
moved: 3
cloned: [4, 5] and [4, 5]

check.q: After `let m = take(a);`, what happens if the next line uses `a.len()`?
options: It doesn't compile: a was moved into take.
It prints 0, because take emptied the vector.
check.explain: Passing a Vec by value moves ownership; the compiler rejects any later use of a. Borrowing with &a would have kept it usable.

examples.title: A kata done the interview way
examples.note: Two passes over the string (count, then find) is O(n) and easy to explain; finding the first unique character by searching the rest of the string for each one is O(n²). The test cases written as a table at the top, including an accented character, are exactly what an interviewer hopes to hear before any code.
examples.output:
"" -> None ok
"a" -> Some('a') ok
"aabbc" -> Some('c') ok
"abab" -> None ok
"éaé" -> Some('a') ok

check.q: What does the line for the input "abab" print?
check.explain: Both characters appear twice, so no character is unique and find returns None, which matches the expected value.

mistakes: **Answering with definitions only.** Add an example and a trade-off.
**Coding before stating test cases.** Edge cases found late cost time and look careless.
**Fighting the borrow checker with `clone()` everywhere.** Explain the rule, then choose the right fix.
**STAR stories about the team.** Interviewers want your actions and your results.
keys: Plain-word answers: answer, example, trade-off.
Read compiler errors aloud: code, spans, rule, fixes.
Test cases first in live coding; simplest correct version, then improve.
STAR stories centred on your actions, ending with a measurable result.

idea: The first rule of cryptography in any language is **don't invent it**. Rust's ecosystem has two well-reviewed families of crates. **RustCrypto** is a set of small pure-Rust crates, one per algorithm: `sha2` for hashing, `hmac` for keyed signatures, `aes-gcm` and `chacha20poly1305` for authenticated encryption, `argon2` for password hashing. **ring** bundles a curated set of primitives in one audited crate with a deliberately small API. **sodiumoxide**, the libsodium binding listed on the roadmap, was archived by its maintainers; `dryoc` offers a libsodium-compatible API in pure Rust.

Knowing which primitive answers which question matters more than any API. A **hash** (SHA-256) detects accidental changes: anyone can recompute it. An **HMAC** proves a message came from someone with the shared key, which is how webhook signatures work. **Authenticated encryption** keeps data secret *and* detects tampering. **Password hashing** (argon2) is deliberately slow so stolen hashes are expensive to crack.
One habit applies everywhere secrets are compared: use a **constant-time** comparison, because `==` stops at the first different byte and the time it takes leaks information.
how: Hash: `Sha256::digest(data)`; incremental: `Sha256::new()`, `update`, `finalize`.
HMAC: `Hmac::<Sha256>::new_from_slice(key)`, `update`, `finalize`; verify with `verify_slice` (constant time).
Encrypt: `aes-gcm` or `chacha20poly1305` with a fresh random nonce per message.
Passwords: `argon2`, never a plain or salted SHA-256.
Compare secrets with constant-time functions (`subtle`, `ring::constant_time`, `verify_slice`).

examples.title: Why early-exit comparison leaks
examples.note: The early-exit version takes longer the more leading bytes are right, so an attacker who can time many requests learns the secret one byte at a time. The constant-time version always does the same work. Real code uses a vetted function rather than this hand-written loop, but this is the property to look for.
examples.output:
x3cr3t-token   early exit:  1 steps, constant time: 12 steps
s3cr9t-token   early exit:  5 steps, constant time: 12 steps
s3cr3t-tokex   early exit: 12 steps, constant time: 12 steps

check.q: The secret is "s3cr3t-token". Which guess takes the most steps with the early-exit comparison?
options: "s3cr9t-token", because it differs in the middle
"s3cr3t-tokex", because its first 11 bytes are right
All guesses take the same number of steps
check.explain: Early exit stops at the first wrong byte, so more correct leading bytes means more time. That timing difference is the leak; the constant-time version takes 12 steps for every guess.

mistakes: **Inventing a scheme** ("XOR with a key", "hash twice"). Use a standard construction from a vetted crate.
**Comparing tokens or HMAC tags with ==.** Use a constant-time comparison.
**Reusing a nonce** with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305: it breaks both secrecy and integrity.
**Hashing passwords with SHA-256.** Use argon2 (or bcrypt or scrypt), which are slow on purpose.
keys: RustCrypto (one crate per algorithm) and ring (one curated crate) are the standard choices.
Hash for accidents, HMAC for authenticity, AEAD for secrecy plus integrity, argon2 for passwords.
Compare secrets in constant time.
sodiumoxide is archived; dryoc is a pure-Rust alternative.

idea: **axum** is the course's main web framework, but job descriptions and existing codebases often name others. **actix-web** is one of the oldest and fastest Rust frameworks; it uses attribute macros (`#[get("/path")]`), an `App` builder and its own extractors, and runs on Tokio under its own actor-style system. **Rocket** is the most macro-driven: routes, guards and launch are declared with attributes, which makes small apps very short. **Loco** is a Rails-style framework built on axum: generators, migrations, background jobs and conventions out of the box.

The concepts transfer completely. Each framework maps a method and path to an async handler, uses **extractors** to turn parts of the request (path, query, JSON body, shared state) into typed arguments, and turns the return value into a response. Middleware, state sharing and testing utilities differ in name, not in idea.

Choose by context: axum when you want Tokio-native code and the tower middleware ecosystem, actix-web for a mature, high-performance option with a big user base, Rocket for quick, readable apps, Loco when a team wants Rails-style productivity.
how: actix-web: `#[get("/x")] async fn h() -> impl Responder`, `App::new().service(h)`, `web::Data` for state, `actix_web::test` for tests.
Rocket: `#[get("/x")] fn h() -> &'static str`, `#[launch] fn rocket() -> _ { rocket::build().mount("/", routes![h]) }`.
Loco: `cargo loco new`, generators for models and controllers, built on axum.
Compare frameworks by porting one route with its test.

examples.title: Extractors, without a framework
examples.note: In axum this is `Path(id): Path<u32>, Query(q): Query<Params>`; in actix-web `web::Path<u32>` and `web::Query<Params>`; in Rocket a `<id>` segment and a query guard. Seeing the plain version makes every framework's extractor look familiar.
examples.output: task 42 (full details)

check.q: The request is /tasks/42?verbose=true&page=1. What does the program print?
check.explain: The path extractor gives 42 and the query extractor finds verbose=true, so get_task gets both typed arguments, just as a framework's extractors would supply them.

mistakes: **Choosing by benchmark alone.** All of these are fast enough for most services; ecosystem and team fit matter more.
**Blocking inside a handler** (heavy CPU work or blocking I/O) in any async framework; use spawn_blocking.
**Testing only through a running server.** Each framework has an in-process test client.
keys: actix-web, Rocket and Loco solve the same problems as axum in different styles.
Handlers, extractors and responses are the shared concepts.
Choose by ecosystem, team and project, then test in-process.

idea: Good command-line tools feel consistent: helpful `--help`, clear errors, sensible exit codes, and output that works both for people and for scripts. **clap** is the standard argument parser. Its **derive API** builds the parser from a struct, with doc comments as help text; this idea came from **structopt**, which is now in maintenance mode and points to clap.

Colour helps people and hurts scripts, so the convention is to colour only when standard output is a terminal (`std::io::IsTerminal`) and to offer `--color auto|always|never`. For moving the cursor, raw keyboard input or clearing the screen, **termion** is a small Unix-only crate and **crossterm** works on Windows too. **ratatui** builds full terminal user interfaces (panels, lists, charts) on top of crossterm.
Test a CLI from the outside too: **assert_cmd** runs the compiled binary with arguments and checks its output and exit code, which catches mistakes unit tests can't see.
how: `#[derive(Parser)]` with `#[arg(short, long)]`, `ValueEnum` for fixed choices, `Args::parse()`.
Colour only when `stdout().is_terminal()`, overridable with a flag.
Exit codes: 0 success, 1 failure, 2 usage error (a common convention).
Terminal control: crossterm (cross-platform) or termion (Unix); TUIs: ratatui.
End-to-end tests: `assert_cmd::Command::cargo_bin("name")`.

examples.title: Exit codes and colour decided once
examples.note: When this runs with its output captured (as here), `is_terminal()` is false and no escape codes are printed, which is exactly what a log file or a test wants. grep uses the same exit-code convention: 0 found, 1 not found, 2 error.
examples.output:
exit 0: 3 matches
exit 1: no matches
exit 2: missing QUERY
colour on: false

check.q: The program's output is captured rather than shown in a terminal. Which line is printed last?
check.explain: is_terminal() is false when output is captured, so no escape codes are written and the last line reports colour off.

mistakes: **Always printing colour codes.** They corrupt logs and break text comparisons in tests.
**Exiting with 0 on failure.** Scripts and CI rely on the exit code.
**Writing errors to stdout.** Use stderr so piped output stays clean.
**Starting new code with structopt.** Use clap's derive API.
keys: clap derive is the standard; structopt led to it.
Colour only for terminals, with a --color override.
crossterm for cross-platform terminal control; ratatui for TUIs.
Test the binary end to end with assert_cmd.

idea: HTTP frameworks hide the network, but some tools need to work below or beside them. **UDP** (`std::net::UdpSocket`) sends independent datagrams: no connection, no guarantee of delivery or order, and very low overhead. It suits metrics (StatsD), discovery, games and DNS. **TCP** gives a reliable ordered byte stream, and HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 run on it.

**QUIC** combines the two ideas: it runs on UDP but provides reliable, encrypted (TLS 1.3) connections with many independent streams, so one lost packet doesn't stall unrelated requests. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, and **quinn** is the main Rust implementation, built on Tokio. **hyper** is the HTTP library inside axum and reqwest; you use it directly when building proxies or protocol-level tools.
For testing, the same rules as always apply: bind port 0 for a free port, set read timeouts so a lost packet can't hang a test, and never assume UDP delivery.
how: UDP: `UdpSocket::bind("127.0.0.1:0")`, `send_to`, `recv_from`, `set_read_timeout`.
TCP: `TcpListener` / `TcpStream` (std) or their Tokio versions.
QUIC: quinn `Endpoint`, `connect`, `open_bi` for a bidirectional stream; certificates via rustls (rcgen for tests).
hyper directly for proxies; reqwest and axum for everyday clients and servers.

examples.title: Datagrams keep their boundaries
examples.note: Each `recv_from` returns exactly one datagram, so message boundaries survive; with TCP the three writes could arrive as one read of "onetwothree", which is why TCP protocols need framing (a length prefix or a delimiter). On localhost these arrive in order, but across a real network UDP may drop or reorder them.
examples.output:
datagram of 3 bytes: one
datagram of 3 bytes: two
datagram of 5 bytes: three

check.q: Three datagrams "one", "two" and "three" are sent. Which line reports the second one?
check.explain: Each recv_from returns exactly one datagram, so message boundaries are kept. With TCP the bytes could arrive merged.

mistakes: **Assuming UDP delivery or order.** Add sequence numbers and retries, or use QUIC.
**No read timeout** on a UDP socket in tests: one lost packet hangs the suite.
**Treating TCP reads as messages.** A read can return part of a message or several messages.
keys: UDP: datagrams, no guarantees, low overhead.
QUIC (quinn): reliable encrypted streams over UDP; HTTP/3's transport.
hyper is the engine under axum and reqwest.
Port 0 and timeouts keep network tests reliable.

idea: `async fn` only describes work; a **runtime** runs it. At its core a runtime **polls** a future, and when the future returns `Pending`, it waits until the future's **waker** is called (because a socket became readable or a timer fired) before polling again. Around that core, a production runtime adds a scheduler for thousands of tasks, timers, and an I/O reactor built on the operating system's event APIs.

**Tokio** is the default choice and has the largest ecosystem. **smol** is a small runtime assembled from separate crates (async-executor, async-io, async-net), handy for libraries, tools and embedded Linux. **async-std** offered a std-like async API but was discontinued in 2025, and its authors recommend smol. Library authors often write runtime-agnostic code with the **futures** crate's traits and let the application choose.

A **WebAssembly runtime** is a different kind of runtime: **Wasmer** and **Wasmtime** load compiled `.wasm` modules and run them in a sandbox inside your program, which makes them a safe plugin system.
how: One runtime per application; don't mix Tokio-specific and smol-specific I/O types.
smol: `smol::block_on(async { ... })`, `smol::spawn`.
Runtime-agnostic libraries: depend on `futures` traits, not a runtime.
Wasm plugins: compile to `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, load with Wasmtime or Wasmer, call typed exports.

examples.title: A future that needs two polls
examples.note: This is the protocol every runtime speaks: Pending plus a wake-up, then another poll. A real reactor calls the waker when the operating system reports the socket is ready, so no CPU is wasted spinning; this loop just polls again immediately.
examples.output:
poll 1: pending
poll 2: ready with "data arrived"

check.q: What does the first line print?
check.explain: The first poll sets polled and returns Pending after asking to be woken; the second poll returns Ready.

mistakes: **Mixing runtimes**, such as Tokio sockets inside smol: they need their own reactor.
**Blocking in async code** (std::thread::sleep, heavy loops): it stalls every task on that thread.
**Starting new projects on async-std.** It's discontinued; choose Tokio or smol.
keys: A runtime polls futures and sleeps until wakers fire.
Tokio is the default; smol is the small alternative; async-std is discontinued.
Libraries can stay runtime-agnostic with the futures traits.
Wasmer and Wasmtime run WebAssembly plugins in a sandbox.

idea: Rust's game ecosystem has options at every level. **Bevy** is a data-driven engine built on an **entity-component-system** (ECS): entities are IDs, components are plain data structs, and systems are functions that query for components and run every frame, often in parallel. **macroquad** and **ggez** are simpler 2D frameworks with a classic game loop, great for small games and jams. **Fyrox** is a full engine with a scene editor. Underneath many of them, **wgpu** provides one GPU API over Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12 and WebGPU.

From a testing point of view, the key design choice is the same as everywhere: keep **rules** (movement, collisions, scoring) in plain functions or systems that don't need a window or a GPU, so they can be unit-tested, and keep rendering thin.
Bevy evolves quickly and renames APIs between releases, so tutorials and examples must match the version you depend on.
how: Bevy: `#[derive(Component)]`, systems take `Query<...>` and `Res<...>`, register with `add_systems(Update, ...)`.
macroquad: `#[macroquad::main("Title")] async fn main()` with a `loop { ...; next_frame().await }`.
Separate `update(state, input, dt)` from drawing; test update.
Use fixed time steps for deterministic simulation tests.

examples.title: A fixed-step simulation you can test
examples.note: Because the step is a pure function with a fixed `dt`, the same input always gives the same output, so a test can assert the exact number of bounces. Using the real frame time instead would make results vary with machine speed: a classic source of flaky game tests.
examples.output: after 5 simulated seconds: 2 bounces, height 4.59 m

check.q: Why does the simulation use a fixed dt of 1/60 instead of the real time since the last frame?
options: So the result is the same on every machine and tests can assert exact values.
To make the ball fall faster.
check.explain: With a fixed step, step() is a pure function of its input; variable frame times make results depend on machine speed, a common source of flaky tests.

mistakes: **Logic tangled with rendering**, so nothing can be tested without a window.
**Variable time steps in physics**, giving different results on fast and slow machines.
**Copying Bevy examples from another version** without checking renamed APIs.
keys: Bevy: ECS with components as data and systems as logic; wgpu underneath.
macroquad and ggez for simple 2D games; Fyrox for an editor-based engine.
Keep rules pure and use fixed time steps so they're testable.

idea: Embedded Rust runs on two very different kinds of hardware. On a **single-board computer** such as a Raspberry Pi, you have Linux and the standard library, so a crate like **rppal** simply gives you GPIO, I2C, SPI and PWM. On a **microcontroller** (an nRF52, an STM32, an RP2040) there is no operating system: the program starts with `#![no_std]`, keeping `core` (and optionally `alloc`), and its entry point never returns.

What makes embedded Rust scale is **embedded-hal**: a set of traits such as `OutputPin`, `I2c` and `SpiBus`. Chip support crates (HALs) such as **nrf-hal** implement those traits for their hardware, and driver crates for sensors and displays are written against the traits, so one driver works on any chip. The same design makes drivers testable on your laptop against mocks (embedded-hal-mock).
Tooling completes the picture: **probe-rs** flashes and debugs boards over a debug probe, defmt gives efficient logging, and simulators such as Wokwi let you experiment without hardware.
how: Linux boards: rppal (Raspberry Pi) with std.
Microcontrollers: `#![no_std]`, `#![no_main]`, a HAL crate, `cortex-m-rt` entry point, a panic handler.
Write drivers generic over embedded-hal traits; test with mocks.
Flash and debug: `probe-rs run`; try boards in Wokwi.

examples.title: A driver generic over a pin trait
examples.note: On real hardware, the only change is the pin type: an nrf-hal pin or an adapter around rppal's OutputPin. Everything the driver does can be checked in CI on a normal machine, and only a small hardware-in-the-loop suite needs a board.
examples.output: pulses: 3, edges recorded: 6

check.q: show_error_code(3) runs on the recording pin. What does the program print?
check.explain: Each pulse sets the pin high then low, so three pulses record six edges, three of them high.

mistakes: **Writing drivers against one chip's types**, so they can't be reused or tested.
**Assuming std on a microcontroller.** No heap, threads or files unless you add them.
**Testing only on hardware.** Mocks catch most logic bugs in seconds.
keys: Raspberry Pi: Linux, std, rppal. Microcontrollers: no_std, a HAL, no OS.
embedded-hal traits make drivers portable and testable.
probe-rs to flash and debug; simulators to start without hardware.

idea: Rust has several ways to build desktop apps, and they differ mostly in where the interface comes from. **Tauri** pairs a web front end (HTML, CSS, any JavaScript framework) with a Rust back end; it uses the operating system's web view, so apps are small, and the front end can only call the Rust **commands** you register. **gtk-rs** binds GTK for native Linux-first apps, and **relm4** adds an Elm-style structure (model, messages, update, view) on top. **gpui** is the GPU-accelerated framework built for the Zed editor. Pure-Rust toolkits include **egui** (immediate mode: describe the UI every frame) and **iced** (Elm-style).

Whichever you choose, the architecture advice is the same as for PyO3 wrappers and hardware adapters: keep the GUI a **thin layer** over a library crate that holds the logic and its tests. Return `Result` from commands so the interface can show errors instead of crashing.
how: Tauri: `#[tauri::command]` functions, `generate_handler!`, `invoke("name", args)` in the front end.
relm4: a model struct, a message enum, `update` and a view macro.
egui: implement `eframe::App` and draw widgets in `update` each frame.
Logic in a library crate; the GUI calls it; tests target the library and the command layer.

examples.title: An Elm-style update you can test without a window
examples.note: The view would just display `m.results` and `m.error`; every behaviour worth testing lives in `update`. Tauri apps get the same benefit by keeping commands thin and putting logic in a library the commands call.
examples.output:
Some("type something to search")
["tea", "teapot"] None

check.q: Search is sent first with an empty query. Which line is printed for it?
check.explain: The guarded Search arm catches the empty query and sets an error instead of searching. The later search for "tea" prints the results with no error.

mistakes: **Logic inside widget callbacks**, untestable without clicking through a window.
**Commands that panic** on bad input instead of returning `Result`.
**Exposing broad file or shell access** to a Tauri front end; register only the commands it needs.
keys: Tauri: web front end, Rust commands, small binaries.
gtk-rs and relm4 for native GTK; gpui for GPU-drawn apps; egui and iced in pure Rust.
Thin GUI over a tested library; Elm-style updates are easy to test.

idea: Every program is built from a handful of data structures, and choosing between them is choosing costs. **Big-O notation** describes how the work grows with the input: O(1) stays flat, O(log n) grows by one step each time the data doubles, O(n) doubles with it, and O(n²) quadruples. The most common performance bug in real code is a hidden O(n) inside a loop, such as `vec.contains(&x)` checked for every item, which quietly makes the whole loop O(n²).

Rust's standard collections each make a different trade. **Vec** is the default: contiguous memory, O(1) push and index, and the fastest iteration of anything. **VecDeque** adds O(1) at the front, so it is the queue. **HashMap** and **HashSet** give O(1) average lookups by key, in no order. **BTreeMap** and **BTreeSet** keep keys sorted with O(log n) operations, so ordered iteration and `range` queries are cheap. **BinaryHeap** always hands back the largest item in O(log n), which makes it the priority queue and the tool for "top k".

Algorithms come with the slice type: `sort` (stable) and `sort_unstable` are O(n log n), `binary_search` and `partition_point` are O(log n) on sorted data, `dedup` removes neighbouring duplicates and `select_nth_unstable` finds the k-th element in O(n) without a full sort. Writing merge, binary search and a bounded heap yourself once, as in this lesson's exercise, is how you learn their edge cases; in production code you call the standard versions, which are tuned and tested.
how: Default to `Vec`; switch only for a reason you can name.
Membership tests in a loop: build a `HashSet` once instead of calling `contains` on a Vec.
Ordered keys or ranges: `BTreeMap`. Largest first: `BinaryHeap` (use `Reverse` for smallest first).
Sort once, then `binary_search` many times.
Top k of n: a heap of size k is O(n log k); `select_nth_unstable` is O(n).

examples.title: An accidental O(n²) and its O(n) fix
examples.note: Both versions find the same 5,000 duplicates, but `Vec::contains` checks every item each time, so the first loop does roughly n²/2 comparisons while the HashSet version does n hash lookups. `HashSet::insert` returns false when the value was already there, which makes the duplicate count a one-liner.
examples.output:
duplicates: 5000 5000
HashSet version much faster: true

check.q: Both loops find 5,000 duplicates. Why is the Vec version so much slower?
options: `Vec::contains` scans the items one by one, so each check is O(n) and the loop is O(n²); `HashSet::insert` is O(1) on average.
The Vec version allocates a new Vec each time.
check.explain: A membership test on a Vec walks the Vec. Inside a loop over n items that becomes about n²/2 comparisons, while hashing jumps straight to the right bucket.

examples.title: BTreeMap ranges and a bounded heap for top-k
examples.note: `range(1005..1031)` walks only the matching keys because a BTreeMap is ordered. Wrapping values in `Reverse` turns the max-heap into a min-heap, so popping whenever it holds more than k removes the smallest and leaves the k largest. `partition_point` is binary search for the first item where a condition becomes false.
examples.output:
between 1005 and 1030: [(1005, 940), (1010, 85), (1020, 1210)]
three slowest: [1210, 940, 310]
first at least 300 ms is at index 3

check.q: Which three response times does the bounded heap keep?
check.explain: Each push of a fourth value pops the smallest (the heap holds Reverse values), so only the three largest survive: 1210, 940 and 310.

mistakes: **`contains` on a Vec inside a loop.** Build a HashSet once.
**Reaching for LinkedList or BTreeMap by habit.** Vec is faster for most workloads.
**Sorting everything to get the top few.** Use a bounded heap or `select_nth_unstable`.
**`binary_search` on unsorted data.** It returns a wrong answer, not an error.
keys: Big-O predicts growth: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
Vec by default; VecDeque, HashMap, BTreeMap and BinaryHeap each for a named reason.
Sorted data unlocks binary search and ranges.
A heap of size k finds the top k in one pass.

idea: Linked structures, lists and trees whose nodes point to other nodes, are the classic place where Rust feels different. In C a node holds a raw pointer that may be null; in Rust a node **owns** its children through `Option<Box<Node>>`. `Box` puts the child on the heap and gives the type a fixed size (a struct cannot contain itself directly), and `Option` stands for "there may be no child", with `None` playing the role of null, checked by the compiler.

Because every node has exactly one owner, moving nodes around means moving ownership. The key tool is `Option::take()`: it moves the value out of a field and leaves `None` behind, which is how you detach a node through a `&mut` reference without leaving a dangling pointer. `as_ref()` and `as_mut()` give you `Option<&T>` and `Option<&mut T>` for looking without taking. With those, a stack, a reversed list or a binary search tree needs no `unsafe` at all.

Structures where nodes are shared or point backwards (doubly linked lists, graphs) do not fit single ownership. The safe options are `Rc<RefCell<Node>>` with `Weak` for back edges, or, usually better, an **arena**: keep all nodes in a `Vec` and refer to them by index, as petgraph and many compilers do. Finally, remember that `Vec` and `VecDeque` beat linked lists for almost every real workload, because contiguous memory suits the CPU cache; linked structures earn their place when nodes must not move or when you split and join long sequences.
how: A child is `Option<Box<Node<T>>>`: None for no child, Box for an owned heap node.
`self.head.take()` moves the node out and leaves None; then relink.
`as_ref()` / `as_mut()` to look at or change a node without taking it.
Shared or backward links: an arena (`Vec<Node>` plus indices) or `Rc<RefCell<..>>` with `Weak`.
Long lists of boxes: write a loop-based `Drop` to avoid deep recursion.

examples.title: A queue made of two stacks, and why take() matters
examples.note: Without `take()`, `let next = *head;` would try to move out of a borrowed place and fail to compile: Rust will not leave the field empty behind your back. Two stacks make a queue with O(1) amortised cost because each item is moved between them at most once, a classic interview exercise that falls out naturally here.
examples.output: first served: Some(1), then: [2, 3, 4]

check.q: Jobs 1, 2 and 3 arrive, one is served, then job 4 arrives. What is printed?
check.explain: Moving the inbox stack onto the outbox reverses it, so items leave in arrival order. Job 4 waits in the inbox until the outbox is empty.

examples.title: An arena graph: nodes in a Vec, links as indices
examples.note: The cycle from mail back to api would be impossible with Box (two owners) and awkward with Rc (it leaks unless one side is Weak). Storing nodes in a Vec and links as indices sidesteps ownership entirely, keeps the nodes next to each other in memory, and makes the depth-first search a few lines.
examples.output:
api depends on: ["api", "cache", "db", "queue", "mail"]
cache depends on: ["cache", "db"]

check.q: Why store the graph as indices into a Vec instead of Box pointers between nodes?
options: Box gives each node one owner, and the cycle (mail points back to api) would need two; indices have no ownership at all.
Indices are always faster than pointers.
check.explain: Single ownership cannot express cycles or shared nodes. An arena owns every node and the links are plain numbers, which also keeps nodes together in memory.

mistakes: **Trying to move a field out through `&mut`.** Use `take()` or `std::mem::replace`.
**`Rc<RefCell<..>>` cycles without Weak.** The nodes are never freed.
**Using a linked list where a Vec or VecDeque would do.** It is usually slower.
**Recursive Drop on a very long list.** It can overflow the stack.
keys: `Option<Box<Node>>` is the safe nullable owning pointer.
`take()` moves a value out and leaves None.
Graphs and back links: arenas with indices, or Rc plus Weak.
Contiguous collections usually win on real hardware.

idea: Most services keep their data in a relational database, and Rust talks to it through a few well-known crates. **rusqlite** is a synchronous SQLite driver; **sqlx** is async and supports PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite, and its `query!` macros can check your SQL against the real schema at compile time; **Diesel** and **SeaORM** build queries from Rust types. Whichever you choose, the SQL ideas are the same: **JOIN** to combine tables (LEFT JOIN to keep rows without a match), **GROUP BY** with `COUNT` and `SUM` to summarise, **indexes** on the columns you filter and join on, and **constraints** (`NOT NULL`, `CHECK`, foreign keys) so the database rejects bad data itself.

Two rules matter most. First, values always travel as **bound parameters** (`?1`, `$1`), never inside the SQL text, which is what makes SQL injection impossible. Table and column names cannot be parameters, so if they come from users they must be checked against an allow-list. Second, related writes go in a **transaction** so they happen all together or not at all. Rust makes this pleasant: a `Transaction` rolls back when it is dropped without `commit()`, so an early return with `?` can never leave half the work behind.

Rows map naturally to structs: rusqlite's `query_map` takes a closure that reads columns into your type, sqlx's `query_as!` and `#[derive(FromRow)]` do it for you. The schema itself evolves through **migrations**, numbered SQL files applied in order (`sqlx migrate run`, refinery), so every environment has the same tables. A connection **pool** (built into sqlx, r2d2 or deadpool for others) shares a few connections between many requests.
how: Parameters for every value: `conn.execute("... WHERE id = ?1", params![id])`.
Identifiers from outside: check against an allow-list; never format them into SQL unchecked.
`let tx = conn.transaction()?; ...; tx.commit()?;` — dropped without commit means rollback.
Map rows to structs with `query_map` (rusqlite) or `query_as` / `FromRow` (sqlx).
Schema changes as migrations; a pool for concurrent access.

examples.title: Parameters keep data out of the SQL text
examples.note: With formatting, the second input turns the WHERE clause into a condition that is always true and the third ends the statement and starts a new one. With a parameter, the SQL text never changes and the input is only ever compared as a string. Database drivers send the two parts separately, so there is nothing to escape and nothing to get wrong.
examples.output:
input "Ada"
  formatted:    SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = 'Ada'
  parameterised: SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = ?1   params=["Ada"]
input "x' OR '1'='1"
  formatted:    SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'
  parameterised: SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = ?1   params=["x' OR '1'='1"]
input "x'; DROP TABLE staff;--"
  formatted:    SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = 'x'; DROP TABLE staff;--'
  parameterised: SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = ?1   params=["x'; DROP TABLE staff;--"]

check.q: Which query would return every row in the table?
options: `  formatted:    SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = 'Ada'`
`  formatted:    SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'`
`  parameterised: SELECT * FROM staff WHERE name = ?1   params=["x' OR '1'='1"]`
check.explain: Formatting let the input close the quote and add OR '1'='1', which is always true. With a parameter, the same text is only compared as a name, and no staff member is called that.

examples.title: A transaction that rolls back on drop
examples.note: This toy has the same shape as rusqlite's and sqlx's `Transaction`: changes go to a draft, `commit` consumes the transaction and makes them real, and `Drop` handles every other way out, including the early `return Err`. Because the rollback lives in `Drop`, no code path can forget it.
examples.output:
Ok(())
balances: [700, 350]
  (rolled back)
Err("account 1 would go negative")
balances: [700, 350]

check.q: The second transfer would make account 1 negative. What balances are printed after it?
check.explain: The early return drops the transaction without commit, so Drop discards the draft and the live balances stay as they were after the first transfer.

mistakes: **`format!` to put values into SQL.** That is SQL injection; bind parameters.
**Several related writes without a transaction.** A failure in the middle leaves the data half-changed.
**A new connection per request.** Use a pool.
**Changing the schema by hand on a server.** Use migrations so every environment matches.
keys: Values are parameters; identifiers need an allow-list.
Transactions are all-or-nothing; Rust's roll back on drop.
JOIN, GROUP BY, indexes and constraints work the same in every SQL database.
Migrations keep schemas in step; pools share connections.

idea: A service has to be configured and observed. **Configuration** (database address, port, log level, feature switches) comes from environment variables, so the same binary runs everywhere and secrets stay out of the repository. Read it once at start-up into a **typed struct** (a `u16` port, a `bool` flag), validate everything, and refuse to start with a clear list of problems. The envy, figment and config crates do this with serde; taking a map instead of calling `std::env::var` directly keeps the function testable.

**Logging** is how you see what a running program did. The **log** crate is a facade with macros (`error!`, `warn!`, `info!`, `debug!`, `trace!`) that libraries call; the application picks a backend such as env_logger. **tracing** is the modern choice for services: the same macros plus **fields** (`info!(user_id, hours, "shift saved")`) and **spans** that group every event of one request, written as text or JSON by tracing-subscriber. `RUST_LOG=info,my_app=debug` sets levels per module without recompiling.

Good logs answer the questions you will have at 3 a.m.: what happened, to which record, and why. Log identifiers and counts rather than whole payloads, never log secrets or personal data, use WARN for things someone should look at and ERROR for failures, and keep DEBUG for detail you switch on when needed. Beyond logs, **metrics** (counters and timings, via the metrics crate or OpenTelemetry) show trends, and a health endpoint tells the platform whether the service works.
how: Parse settings into a struct at start-up; collect every problem; exit non-zero with the list.
Libraries use `log` or `tracing` macros; the binary installs the subscriber once.
`tracing_subscriber::fmt().with_env_filter(EnvFilter::from_default_env()).init()`, then `RUST_LOG=debug`.
Add fields: `info!(order_id, total, "order placed")`; `#[instrument]` makes a span per call.
No secrets or personal data in logs; ids and counts instead.

examples.title: Settings parsed once, with every problem listed
examples.note: The first call fills in defaults and normalises the level; the second reports all three problems in one go, so an operator fixes them in one deploy instead of three. In a real binary `main` would build the map from `std::env::vars()` and call `std::process::exit(1)` after printing.
examples.output:
Ok(Settings { port: 9090, log_level: "debug", max_upload_mb: 10 })
refusing to start:
  - PORT must be 1-65535, got "http"
  - LOG_LEVEL must be error, warn, info, debug or trace, got "loud"
  - MAX_UPLOAD_MB must be a whole number

check.q: Why does parse collect problems in a Vec instead of returning at the first one?
options: Because ? cannot be used with HashMap.
Because Rust requires a Vec for errors.
So the operator sees every bad setting at once and fixes them all in one deploy.
check.explain: Stopping at the first error means one failed start per mistake. Listing them all turns three restarts into one.

examples.title: A span ties together every line of one request
examples.note: Every line carries the request it belongs to, and the inner lines also carry the user, without passing either value into `event` by hand. That is what tracing's spans and `#[instrument]` give you: when two requests interleave in a busy service, you can still pull out all the lines for r-102 and see exactly where it went wrong.
examples.output:
INFO  [request_id=r-101] request started
DEBUG [request_id=r-101 user_id=7] querying database
INFO  [request_id=r-101] loaded ada
INFO  [request_id=r-102] request started
DEBUG [request_id=r-102 user_id=9] querying database
WARN  [request_id=r-102] user not found

check.q: Which line shows the context of both spans at once?
check.explain: The DEBUG event happens inside load_user's span, which is inside the request's span, so both sets of fields are attached. Events after load_user returns only carry the request.

mistakes: **Reading environment variables all over the code.** Parse once into a typed struct.
**Failing on the first bad setting.** Report every problem together.
**`println!` instead of a logger.** No levels, no fields, no way to turn it down.
**Logging secrets, tokens or whole request bodies.** Log ids and counts.
keys: Config from the environment, validated at start-up into types.
log is the facade; tracing adds fields and spans.
RUST_LOG sets levels without recompiling.
Logs answer what, to which record, and why.

idea: Shipping a Rust service usually means a **container image**. A **multi-stage Dockerfile** builds in an image that has the full toolchain and copies only the finished binary into a small runtime image (debian-slim, distroless, or `scratch` for a static musl build), so what you ship is tens of megabytes with very little inside to attack. Cache the slow dependency build by copying `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock` first (cargo-chef automates this), run as a non-root user, and pass configuration in at run time.

**CI** checks every change before it merges: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, `cargo test`, and often `cargo deny` or `cargo audit` for dependency problems. A **release** is a tagged version: tools like release-plz or cargo-release bump the version from conventional commit messages, write the changelog and publish crates or images. **CD** then rolls the new image out gradually behind health checks and rolls back if they fail.

All of this runs through **pull requests**. Keep branches short-lived and changes small, write commit subjects in the imperative ("fix: reject empty shift names") with a body that says why, and describe in the PR what changed and how you tested it. Reviewers check correctness and tests first, then naming and structure, and label how serious each comment is; authors reply to every comment and keep the conversation about the code. Branch protection (required review, green CI) turns the habits into rules.
how: Multi-stage Dockerfile: build with `rust:<version>`, run from a slim or scratch image, as a non-root user.
Copy `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` and build dependencies before copying `src/` (or use cargo-chef).
CI: fmt, clippy with `-D warnings`, tests, and a dependency audit, on every pull request.
Versions follow SemVer; conventional commits let tools pick the next version and write the changelog.
Small pull requests; review comments labelled blocking, suggestion, question or nit.

examples.title: Picking the next version from commit messages
examples.note: This is the rule release-plz and semantic-release apply: fixes bump the patch, features the minor, and breaking changes the major. Cargo treats 0.x versions specially (0.9 to 0.10 is already a breaking change), which is why the breaking change bumps the minor version before 1.0. Consistent commit messages are what make the automation possible.

check.q: Which version does a breaking change produce from 0.9.3?
check.explain: Before 1.0, Cargo treats a minor bump (0.9 to 0.10) as incompatible, so tools bump the minor version for breaking changes. After 1.0, the major version goes up.
