examples.title: A tiny CI gate: run each check, report all failures
examples.note: CI runs every check and reports all failures, not just the first, so the author fixes everything in one round. With branch protection, "blocked" literally means the merge button is disabled until the checks are green, which is how teams keep main always releasable.
examples.output:
ok   cargo fmt --check
FAIL cargo clippy -- -D warnings
ok   cargo test
FAIL cargo deny check
blocked: 2 check(s) failed: cargo clippy -- -D warnings (needless_return in src/api.rs:41), cargo deny check (license GPL-3.0 not allowed for crate foo)

check.q: Why does the gate report both failures instead of stopping at clippy?
options: Because cargo deny must run after clippy.
So the author can fix everything in one round instead of pushing once per failure.
check.explain: Each CI round trip costs minutes of waiting. Running every independent check and listing all failures respects the author's time.

mistakes: **Shipping the build image.** It is over a gigabyte and full of tools; copy only the binary.
**Copying `src/` before building dependencies.** Every code change recompiles everything.
**Huge pull requests.** They get skimmed, and bugs get through.
**Ignoring clippy warnings in CI.** Use `-D warnings` so they block the merge.
keys: Multi-stage builds ship only the binary.
CI runs fmt, clippy, tests and audits on every pull request.
Conventional commits drive SemVer bumps and changelogs.
Small PRs and labelled review comments keep quality high.

idea: **System design** is reasoning about the pieces of a service and how they behave under load. A typical web system has a **load balancer** spreading requests over several **stateless application servers**, a **database** holding the truth, a **cache** for frequent reads, and a **queue** with **workers** for slow or unreliable jobs such as email. Stateless servers scale by adding more of them; the database is the hard part, scaled first with indexes, then read replicas, and only later by splitting data across machines.

Start every design with **rough numbers**. A day has about 86,400 seconds, so a million requests a day is about 12 a second on average; multiply by a peak factor (often 3 to 10) and compare with what one server handles in a load test. Estimate storage from row size times rows per day. These numbers decide everything else, and they are often smaller than people expect: one well-indexed database and a few Rust servers handle a lot.

Each component trades something. A **cache** trades freshness for speed, so decide how stale data may be (a TTL) and how entries are invalidated when data changes. A **queue** trades immediacy for reliability: requests return quickly and failed jobs are retried, so jobs must be **idempotent**, safe to run twice. **Rate limiting** protects the system from bursts, and **timeouts with retries and backoff** keep one slow dependency from taking everything down. In an interview, ask clarifying questions, estimate, draw the boxes, find the bottleneck, name the trade-off and say what you would measure.
how: Clarify requirements, then estimate peak requests per second, data size and latency targets.
Draw client, load balancer, stateless servers, database, cache, queue and workers.
Cache-aside: read cache, fall back to the database, delete the entry on write; set a TTL.
Queue slow work; make jobs idempotent; retry with backoff; cap retries.
Rate-limit at the edge; set timeouts on every outbound call.

examples.title: Back-of-the-envelope numbers for a service
examples.note: Fifteen million requests a day sounds big but is under 200 a second on average, and a Rust server measured at 800 per second covers the peak with two machines and a spare. The cache table shows why the last few percent of hit rate matter: going from 90% to 99% cuts database traffic tenfold again.
examples.output:
average 174 req/s, peak about 868 req/s
app servers needed: 3
hit rate   0%: average read  30.5 ms, database sees 100% of reads
hit rate  50%: average read  15.5 ms, database sees  50% of reads
hit rate  90%: average read   3.5 ms, database sees  10% of reads
hit rate  99%: average read   0.8 ms, database sees   1% of reads
storage: about 146 GB a year

check.q: Going from a 90% to a 99% cache hit rate does what to database reads?
options: Cuts them tenfold again, from 10% to 1% of all reads.
Nothing much: 90% is already nearly perfect.
Removes the need for a database.
check.explain: Only misses reach the database, so the share of reads it sees is 1 minus the hit rate. Small improvements near 100% make large differences.

examples.title: A token-bucket rate limiter
examples.note: The bucket holds up to five tokens and refills two per second: a burst of eight at once lets five through, then requests are allowed as tokens trickle back. By t=3.0 it has refilled to four tokens, so four of the five requests pass and the fifth is refused. This is the algorithm behind most API rate limits; tower and governor provide it as middleware for axum and other Rust services.
examples.output:
8 requests at t=0: 5 allowed
later requests:    [true, true, false, true, true, true, true, false]

check.q: Eight requests arrive at t=0 at a bucket with capacity 5. How many are allowed?
check.explain: The bucket starts full with five tokens and no time has passed to refill it, so the first five get a token and the rest are refused.

mistakes: **Designing before estimating.** The numbers decide which components you need.
**A cache without an invalidation rule.** Users see stale data with no obvious cause.
**Non-idempotent jobs on an at-least-once queue.** A retry charges twice.
**Calls to other services without timeouts.** One slow dependency stalls everything.
keys: Stateless servers scale out; the database is the bottleneck to plan for.
Estimate requests per second, data size and latency first.
Caches trade freshness for speed; queues trade immediacy for reliability.
Rate limits, timeouts and idempotent retries keep a system standing.

idea: Rust is installed and managed with **rustup**, the official toolchain installer. One command installs three things: `rustc`, the compiler that turns `.rs` source files into native programs; `cargo`, the build tool and package manager you will use every day; and the standard library with its documentation. rustup also keeps several **toolchains** side by side (stable, beta, nightly, or a pinned version for one project) and updates them with `rustup update`.

Rust releases a new stable version every six weeks. Updates are backwards compatible: code that compiled last year still compiles. Larger language changes are grouped into **editions** (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) that each crate opts into in its `Cargo.toml`, so the language can evolve without breaking old code. New projects use the latest edition.

Two more pieces complete the setup. **rust-analyzer**, the language server, gives your editor completion, inline types and instant errors; install it as your editor's Rust extension. And `rustup doc` opens the standard library documentation and the Rust Book **offline**, which is handy when you are on a train or the website is slow.
how: Install: the command from rustup.rs (macOS/Linux) or rustup-init.exe (Windows).
Check: `rustc --version`, `cargo --version`, `rustup show`.
Update: `rustup update`; pin a project with a `rust-toolchain.toml` file.
Add tools: `rustup component add clippy rustfmt`.
Offline docs: `rustup doc` (or `rustup doc --book`, `rustup doc --std`).
Editor: install the rust-analyzer extension.

examples.title: Checking an installation
examples.code:
$ rustc --version && cargo --version && rustup --version
rustc 1.97.0 (2d8144b78 2026-07-07)
cargo 1.97.0 (c980f4866 2026-06-30)
rustup 1.28.2 (e4f3ad6f8 2025-04-28)
$ rustup show active-toolchain
stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu (default)
$ rustup update
info: syncing channel updates for 'stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu'
  stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu unchanged - rustc 1.97.0 (2d8144b78 2026-07-07)
examples.note: Each tool reports its version and release date; rustc and cargo are released together. The active toolchain is "stable" for this machine's platform, and `rustup update` keeps it current. These lines were recorded on a real machine; your versions will be the same or newer.

check.q: Which command brings your installed Rust toolchain up to the latest stable release?
check.explain: rustup manages toolchains, so `rustup update` upgrades rustc, cargo and the docs together. `cargo update` only refreshes a project's dependencies in Cargo.lock.

examples.title: Asking the compiler about itself
examples.note: `cfg!` and `std::env::consts` reveal how and for which platform the program was built. A `usize`, the type used for sizes and indexes, is 8 bytes on 64-bit systems. Building the same file with `--release` (or `-O`) would print "release build".
examples.output:
This program was compiled as a debug build.
Target OS: linux, architecture: x86_64
A usize here is 8 bytes

check.q: This program was built normally, without `--release`. What does its first line say?
options: `This program was compiled as a debug build.`
`This program was compiled as a test build.`
`This program was compiled as a release build.`
check.explain: `cfg!(debug_assertions)` is true in a default (debug) build. Building with `--release` or `-O` turns debug assertions off, so the same file would report a release build.

mistakes: **Installing Rust from an old system package.** It is often months out of date. Use rustup.
**Forgetting rust-analyzer.** Coding Rust without inline errors and types is much harder than it needs to be.
**Mixing toolchains by accident.** If a project needs a specific version, pin it with `rust-toolchain.toml`.
keys: rustup installs and updates rustc, cargo and the standard library.
Stable releases every six weeks; editions bundle larger changes.
rust-analyzer gives your editor completion and instant errors.
`rustup doc` opens the docs and the Book offline.

idea: Every Rust program starts at a function called `main`. `fn main() { ... }` declares it: `fn` introduces a function, the parentheses hold parameters (none here), and the body sits in curly braces. Inside, `println!("Hello, world!");` prints a line. The `!` means `println!` is a **macro**, not a function: macros generate code at compile time, which lets `println!` check its format string and arguments before the program ever runs. Statements end with a semicolon.

Rust is a **compiled** language. `rustc main.rs` reads the source, checks it thoroughly (types, ownership, borrowing) and produces a native executable, `main` (or `main.exe` on Windows), that runs without Rust installed. Compiling and running are separate steps: you can give the executable to someone else and they run it directly. The compiler's checks are strict, and its error messages are famously helpful: they point at the exact spot, explain the problem and often suggest the fix.

Formatting with `println!` uses placeholders: `{}` for a value's user-facing form, `{:?}` for its debug form, and you can put variable names directly inside the braces: `println!("{name} is {age}")`. Code style is standardised by `rustfmt`: four spaces of indentation and braces on the same line.
how: `fn main() { ... }` is the entry point.
`println!` prints with a newline; `print!` without; `eprintln!` to standard error.
Placeholders: `{}`, `{:?}`, `{name}`, `{:.2}` for two decimals, `{:>8}` to right-align.
Compile with `rustc main.rs`; run `./main` (Windows: `.\main.exe`).
Format with `rustfmt main.rs` (or `cargo fmt` in projects).

examples.title: Formatting with println!
examples.note: Names can go straight inside the braces, or values can follow the format string. Format specs control decimals, alignment and zero-padding, and `{:?}` shows the debug form, with quotes for strings. The last line went to standard error, which is where error messages belong.
examples.output:
Hello, Ferris!
Ferris is 9 years old
height: 0.29 m, padded: [   9] [9   ] [0009]
debug form of a string: "Ferris"
this line goes to standard error

check.q: What does the line with the padding specs print?
check.explain: Numbers are right-aligned by default (`{:4}`), `{:<4}` left-aligns, and `{:04}` pads with zeros. `{:.2}` keeps two decimals.

examples.title: The compiler checks format strings before running
examples.note: The format string asks for two values but only one was given, and the program does not compile at all: `println!` is a macro, so this is checked at compile time and the error points at the exact placeholders. In many languages this mistake would only appear, or silently print garbage, at run time.
examples.output:
error: 2 positional arguments in format string, but there is 1 argument
 --> main.rs:3:15
  |
3 |     println!("{} has {} people", city);
  |               ^^     ^^          ----
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: Why is this mistake caught before the program ever runs?
options: Cargo runs the program once in the background to look for errors.
Rust converts the missing argument to an empty string and warns.
`println!` is a macro, so the compiler checks the format string against the arguments at compile time.
The operating system checks every string before running a program.
check.explain: Macros expand at compile time, so the number of `{}` placeholders and arguments is checked during compilation. Many languages only discover this when the line runs.

mistakes: **Forgetting the `!`.** `println("hi")` looks for a function that does not exist.
**Expecting to run the `.rs` file directly.** Compile it first, then run the executable.
**Ignoring the compiler's suggestions.** Its "help:" lines usually contain the fix.
keys: `fn main` is where a program starts; `println!` is a macro that prints.
Format placeholders: `{}`, `{:?}`, `{name}`, with width and precision specs.
`rustc` compiles to a native executable that runs on its own.
Mistakes in format strings are caught at compile time.

idea: Real projects use **Cargo**, Rust's build system and package manager. `cargo new hello_cargo` creates a folder with a `Cargo.toml` manifest (the package's name, version, edition and dependencies), a `src/main.rs` with a hello-world program, and a fresh git repository with a `.gitignore`. From then on, Cargo builds the right files with the right flags, and downloads and compiles any **crates** (libraries) you depend on.

Four commands cover daily work. `cargo build` compiles into `target/debug/`. `cargo run` builds if needed and runs the program. `cargo check` only checks that the code compiles, without producing an executable, which is much faster and ideal while writing code. `cargo build --release` compiles with optimisations into `target/release/`; it takes longer to build but the program runs much faster, so it is what you measure and ship.

Cargo also creates `Cargo.lock`, which records the exact versions of every dependency, so builds are reproducible. The `target/` folder holds build output and is ignored by git. Other everyday commands: `cargo fmt` formats the code, `cargo clippy` runs the linter, `cargo test` runs tests and `cargo doc --open` builds documentation for your project and its dependencies.
how: `cargo new name` (binary) or `cargo new --lib name` (library).
`cargo check` while coding; `cargo run` to try it; `cargo build --release` to ship or benchmark.
Pass arguments to your program after `--`: `cargo run -- input.txt`.
`Cargo.toml` is yours to edit; `Cargo.lock` is managed by Cargo (commit it for programs).
`cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo test`, `cargo doc --open`.

examples.title: A Cargo project from start to finish
examples.code:
$ cargo new hello_cargo
    Creating binary (application) `hello_cargo` package
$ cd hello_cargo && find . -not -path './.git*' -type f | sort
./Cargo.toml
./src/main.rs
$ cat Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "hello_cargo"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
$ cargo run
   Compiling hello_cargo v0.1.0 (~/hello_cargo)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.76s
     Running `target/debug/hello_cargo`
Hello, world!
$ cargo check
    Checking hello_cargo v0.1.0 (~/hello_cargo)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.03s
$ cargo build --release && ls target/release/hello_cargo
   Compiling hello_cargo v0.1.0 (~/hello_cargo)
    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 0.15s
target/release/hello_cargo
examples.note: `cargo new` produced a manifest and a ready-to-run program. `cargo run` compiled and ran it in one step, `cargo check` verified the code without building an executable (notice how much faster), and the release build landed in its own folder. Recorded on a real machine.

check.q: You only want to know whether your code compiles, as fast as possible. Which command fits best?
check.explain: `cargo check` type-checks without producing an executable, which is much faster than a full build. A release build is the slowest option, because it optimises.

examples.title: Reading arguments passed with cargo run --
examples.note: Run without arguments, as here, the program sees only its own name and prints a usage line. With `cargo run -- Ada`, everything after `--` is passed to the program instead of to Cargo, so it would greet Ada. `args.get(1)` returns an Option instead of panicking when the argument is missing.
examples.output:
program: prog
0 extra argument(s): []
usage: cargo run -- NAME

check.q: How would you pass the name Ada to this program through Cargo?
check.explain: Everything after `--` goes to your program instead of to Cargo. Without the `--`, Cargo would try to interpret `Ada` itself.

mistakes: **Using `cargo build` while writing code.** `cargo check` is much faster for "does it compile?".
**Benchmarking a debug build.** Debug builds can be ten times slower. Measure with `--release`.
**Committing `target/`.** It is build output; Cargo's `.gitignore` already excludes it.
keys: `cargo new` sets up a package: Cargo.toml, src/main.rs and git.
`check` to verify, `run` to try, `build --release` to ship.
Cargo.lock pins exact dependency versions.
`cargo fmt`, `clippy`, `test` and `doc` are part of the daily toolkit.

idea: The guessing game starts by reading what the player types. Input comes from **standard input**, reached through `std::io::stdin()`. Its `read_line` method appends the typed line, including the newline, to a `String` you provide. That string must be **mutable** (`let mut guess = String::new();`), because variables in Rust are immutable by default and `read_line` needs to change it.

The string is passed as `&mut guess`: a **mutable reference**. `read_line` borrows the string to write into it, without taking ownership, so you can still use `guess` afterwards. The `&mut` makes it explicit at the call site that the function will modify your variable, a theme you will see throughout Rust.

Reading can fail (the input might not be valid UTF-8, or the stream might be closed), so `read_line` returns a **`Result`**: either `Ok` with the number of bytes read, or `Err` with an error. Rust will not let you silently ignore it; the compiler warns about an unused `Result`. For now, `.expect("Failed to read line")` says "crash with this message if it failed"; later lessons handle errors gracefully. `use std::io;` at the top brings the module into scope so you can write `io::stdin()`.
how: `use std::io;` then `let mut guess = String::new();`.
`io::stdin().read_line(&mut guess).expect("Failed to read line");`
`read_line` appends, including the newline; `guess.trim()` removes it.
Returns `Result<usize>`: the byte count on success.
`let` is immutable; add `mut` only when the value must change.

examples.title: Reading a line and seeing what you got
examples.note: The input was "  42" plus a newline, and `read_line` kept all of it: the debug form shows the spaces and the `\n`, which is why the first `println!` printed an extra blank line. `trim()` gives the clean text. The byte count includes the newline.
examples.output:
Guess the number! Please input your guess.
You guessed:   42

read 5 bytes; debug form "  42\n"; trimmed "42"

check.q: The user typed `  42` and pressed Enter. What does `guess` contain after `read_line`?
check.explain: `read_line` keeps everything typed, including the newline from Enter. That is why the program calls `trim()` before parsing.

examples.title: Forgetting mut
examples.note: Without `mut`, the compiler refuses to hand out a mutable reference to `guess`, and its help line suggests exactly the fix: make the binding mutable. Immutability by default means every variable that changes is clearly marked.
examples.output:
error[E0596]: cannot borrow `guess` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable
 --> main.rs:5:27
  |
5 |     io::stdin().read_line(&mut guess).expect("Failed to read line");
  |                           ^^^^^^^^^^ cannot borrow as mutable
  |
help: consider changing this to be mutable
  |
4 |     let mut guess = String::new();
  |         +++
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: What single change makes this program compile?
options: Declare the variable with `let mut guess`.
check.explain: `read_line` needs a mutable reference to fill the string, and a mutable reference requires a mutable binding. The compiler's help line shows the missing `mut`.

mistakes: **Forgetting that the newline is included.** Comparing `guess == "42"` fails. Trim first.
**Declaring the String without `mut`.** `read_line` needs to modify it.
**Ignoring the `Result`.** At least call `expect` with a clear message; later, handle the error.
keys: `io::stdin().read_line(&mut s)` appends a line, newline included.
Variables are immutable unless declared `mut`.
`&mut` lends a value to be modified without giving it away.
Fallible operations return `Result`; `expect` crashes with a message on error.

idea: The standard library has no random-number generator, so the game uses a **crate**: a package of Rust code published on crates.io. Adding one is a single line in the `[dependencies]` section of `Cargo.toml` (`rand = "0.9"`), or `cargo add rand`. The next build downloads it and everything it depends on, compiles them, and links them in.

The version requirement `"0.9"` is a **semantic versioning** range: any version compatible with 0.9 (0.9.0 up to, but not including, 0.10.0). On the first build, Cargo picks the newest matching versions and writes them to **`Cargo.lock`**. Later builds, on any machine, use exactly those versions until you run `cargo update`, which is what makes builds reproducible: a new release of a crate never changes your program by surprise.

To use the crate, bring what you need into scope and call it: `rand::random_range(1..=100)` returns a random integer from 1 to 100 inclusive (`..=` is an inclusive range; `1..100` would stop at 99). Each crate's documentation is on docs.rs, and `cargo doc --open` builds the docs for exactly the versions in your lock file.
how: `cargo add rand` or add `rand = "0.9"` under `[dependencies]`.
Build once: Cargo downloads, compiles and records versions in `Cargo.lock`.
`cargo update` moves to the newest compatible versions on purpose.
`1..=100` includes 100; `1..100` excludes it.
Read a crate's API on docs.rs or with `cargo doc --open`.

examples.title: A secret number from the rand crate
examples.note: The numbers differ on every run, so the example prints facts that are always true: the secret is in range, and a thousand dice rolls cover 1 through 6 because the range is inclusive. `rand::random()` produces any type that supports it, here booleans for coin flips. The crate was declared in Cargo.toml as `rand = "0.9"`.
examples.output:
secret is between 1 and 100: true
1000 dice rolls: lowest 1, highest 6
100 coin flips include both sides: true

check.q: Why does this example print facts like "between 1 and 100: true" rather than the actual numbers?
options: Printing random numbers would leak the secret to the compiler.
The numbers change on every run, but the facts are always true, so the printed output stays the same.
The numbers are only generated in release builds.
check.explain: Random values differ on each run. Printing properties that always hold keeps the output repeatable while still showing what the code does.

examples.title: Cargo.toml and what Cargo.lock records
examples.code:
# Cargo.toml: what you asked for (a compatible range)
[package]
name = "guessing_game"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
rand = "0.9"          # means >= 0.9.0 and < 0.10.0

# Cargo.lock: what you got (written by Cargo, exact versions)
# [[package]]
# name = "rand"
# version = "0.9.2"
# dependencies = ["rand_chacha", "rand_core"]
#
# [[package]]
# name = "rand_core"
# version = "0.9.3"
examples.note: `Cargo.toml` states the range you accept; `Cargo.lock` records the exact versions chosen, including crates you never named (rand's own dependencies). Commit the lock file for applications so every build uses the same code.

check.q: Which file records the exact versions of every crate used, including rand's own dependencies?
check.explain: Cargo.toml states the version range you accept. Cargo.lock records exactly what was chosen, so every build of an application uses the same code.

mistakes: **Using `1..100` when you mean up to 100.** That range stops at 99. Use `1..=100`.
**Editing Cargo.lock by hand.** Let Cargo manage it; use `cargo update`.
**Copying API examples from an old blog post.** Crate APIs change between versions. Check docs.rs for your version.
keys: Crates from crates.io add functionality; declare them in Cargo.toml.
Version requirements are SemVer ranges; Cargo.lock pins exact versions.
`..=` is inclusive, `..` exclusive.
docs.rs and `cargo doc --open` document the versions you use.

idea: To compare the guess with the secret, the text must become a number. `guess.trim().parse::<u32>()` (or `let guess: u32 = guess.trim().parse()...`) converts it, and returns a `Result`, because "abc" is not a number. The type annotation tells `parse` what to produce; Rust infers types almost everywhere, but here there is nothing else to infer from.

`guess.cmp(&secret)` compares two values and returns an `Ordering`, an enum with three variants: `Less`, `Greater` and `Equal`. A **`match`** expression handles each one in its own **arm**, and the compiler checks that every variant is covered, so you cannot forget a case.

The game repeats with **`loop`**, an infinite loop that you leave with **`break`** when the guess is right. Bad input should not crash the game: instead of `expect`, match on the `Result` from `parse`. `Ok(num) => num` uses the number; `Err(_) => continue` skips to the next round (the underscore is a catch-all that ignores the error's details). This shift, from crashing on errors to handling them, is the heart of idiomatic Rust.
how: `let guess: u32 = match guess.trim().parse() { Ok(n) => n, Err(_) => continue };`
`use std::cmp::Ordering;` then `match guess.cmp(&secret) { Ordering::Less => ..., ... }`.
`loop { ... }` repeats; `break` leaves; `continue` starts the next pass.
`match` must cover every case; `_` matches anything.
Shadowing: reuse the name `guess` for the number.

examples.title: The finished game, with scripted guesses
examples.note: Each line of input is parsed; "twenty" fails, gets a friendly message and `continue` moves on without counting a try. `cmp` returns an Ordering and `match` handles all three outcomes; the winning arm `break`s out, so the final 99 is never read. A fixed secret makes the run repeatable here.
examples.output:
50: too big!
"twenty" is not a number, try again
25: too small!
40: too small!
42: you win after 4 tries!

check.q: The scripted guesses are 50, twenty, 25, 40, 42 and 99, and the secret is 42. What is the last line printed?
check.explain: "twenty" fails to parse, and `continue` skips it without counting a try, so 42 is the fourth counted guess. The winning arm breaks out of the loop, so 99 is never read.

examples.title: match must cover every case
examples.note: The compiler refuses the program because `Ordering::Equal` is not handled, and it names the missing pattern. This exhaustiveness check is why a `match` in Rust can be trusted: adding a new variant to an enum later makes the compiler point at every match that must deal with it.
examples.output:
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `std::cmp::Ordering::Equal` not covered
 --> main.rs:6:11
  |
6 |     match guess.cmp(&secret) {
  |           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ pattern `std::cmp::Ordering::Equal` not covered
  |
  = note: not covered
  = note: the matched value is of type `std::cmp::Ordering`
help: ensure that all possible cases are being handled by adding a match arm with a wildcard pattern or an explicit pattern as shown
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: Why is it useful that the compiler rejects a `match` that forgets `Ordering::Equal`?
options: It makes the program run faster.
It stops you from using `match` with numbers.
It automatically adds a default arm for you.
If a case is ever missed, including a variant added later, the compiler points at every `match` that must handle it.
check.explain: Exhaustiveness checking means a `match` can be trusted to handle every case. Adding a variant to an enum later turns every incomplete match into a compile error.

mistakes: **Parsing without trimming.** The newline makes `"42\n".parse()` fail. Trim first.
**Using `expect` on user input.** One typo crashes the game. Match on the Result.
**Forgetting `break`.** The game never ends after a correct guess.
keys: `parse` converts text to numbers and returns a Result; annotate the target type.
`cmp` gives an `Ordering`; `match` handles each variant, checked for completeness.
`loop`, `break` and `continue` control repetition.
Handle bad input with `match` instead of crashing.

idea: In Rust, variables are **immutable by default**: `let x = 5;` binds a value that cannot change. Trying to assign `x = 6;` is a compile error. This is deliberate: when values cannot change unexpectedly, code is easier to reason about, especially with threads. When a value must change, say so with `mut`: `let mut count = 0;`. Reading `mut` in code tells you exactly which values move.

**Constants** (`const MAX_POINTS: u32 = 100_000;`) are always immutable, must have a type annotation, can be declared in any scope including globally, and must be set to a value computable at compile time. They are named in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Underscores in numbers are only for readability.

**Shadowing** declares a new variable with the same name as an old one: `let spaces = "   "; let spaces = spaces.len();`. The second `let` creates a new binding (even of a different type) and the old one is hidden. That is different from `mut`: shadowing makes a new variable each time and the result is still immutable, which is handy for transforming a value step by step (trim, then parse) without inventing names like `spaces_str` and `spaces_num`. Shadowing inside an inner block ends when the block ends.
how: `let x = 5;` immutable; `let mut x = 5;` mutable.
`const NAME: Type = value;` for compile-time constants, any scope.
`static` for a single global location (rarely needed; mutable statics need `unsafe`).
Shadow with another `let` to transform a value or change its type.
Shadowing in a block lasts until the block's closing brace.

examples.title: mut, const and shadowing side by side
examples.note: `total` changes, so it is `mut`; the constant is computed at compile time. Shadowing turned `input` from padded text into trimmed text into a number without new names. The inner `x` existed only inside its block, so the outer `x` is still 5 afterwards.
examples.output:
total seconds: 21600
input doubled: 84
inner x: 50
outer x: 5

check.q: After the inner block ends, what does the last line print?
check.explain: The inner `let x` shadowed the outer one only inside its block. When the block ends, the outer `x` is visible again, unchanged at 5.

examples.title: Assigning twice to an immutable variable
examples.note: The compiler rejects the second assignment and points at both the first binding and the attempted change, suggesting `let mut speed`. Mistakes where a value changes unexpectedly simply cannot happen to immutable variables.
examples.output:
error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable `speed`
 --> main.rs:4:5
  |
2 |     let speed = 50;
  |         ----- first assignment to `speed`
3 |     println!("speed: {speed}");
4 |     speed = 80;
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable
  |
help: consider making this binding mutable
  |
  ...
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: Which fix does the compiler suggest for assigning to `speed` twice?
check.explain: Variables are immutable by default, so a value that changes must be declared `mut`. Shadowing with a new `let` would also work if you want a new variable rather than a changed one.

mistakes: **Adding `mut` everywhere by habit.** Then nothing tells readers what changes. Use it only when needed (the compiler warns about unnecessary `mut`).
**Confusing shadowing with mutation.** Shadowing creates a new variable; the old value is not changed.
**Constants without a type.** `const` always needs an explicit type.
keys: Variables are immutable by default; `mut` marks the ones that change.
`const` values are computed at compile time, typed and named in capitals.
Shadowing reuses a name for a new value, possibly of a new type.
Shadowing in a block ends with the block.

idea: Rust's **scalar types** are single values: integers, floating-point numbers, booleans and characters. Integers come in signed (`i8`, `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `i128`, `isize`) and unsigned (`u8` … `u128`, `usize`) sizes; the number is the width in bits, and `isize`/`usize` match the machine's pointer size (used for indexes and lengths). Without other information, integers default to `i32` and floats to `f64`.

Every integer type has a fixed range, so arithmetic can **overflow**: `255u8 + 1` does not fit. In debug builds Rust panics on overflow; in release builds it wraps around silently. When overflow is possible and you care, say what you want explicitly: `checked_add` returns `None` on overflow, `saturating_add` clamps to the maximum, `wrapping_add` wraps, and `overflowing_add` returns the result and a flag.

Floats (`f32`, `f64`) follow IEEE 754, with the usual surprises (`0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`). Integer division truncates towards zero (`-7 / 2 == -3`) and `%` gives the remainder. Rust **never converts numbers implicitly**: adding an `i32` to an `f64` is a compile error, and you convert with `as` (which can truncate) or the safer `From`/`TryFrom`. A `bool` is `true` or `false`. A `char` is a single Unicode scalar value, 4 bytes, written in single quotes: `'a'`, `'é'`, `'🦀'`.
how: Integers default to `i32`, floats to `f64`; suffixes like `10u8` or `2.5f32` pick a type.
Overflow: debug panics, release wraps; use `checked_`, `saturating_`, `wrapping_` methods to choose.
Integer `/` truncates towards zero; `%` is the remainder.
No implicit conversion: `x as f64`, `u8::try_from(n)`, `i64::from(x)`.
`char` is a Unicode scalar value (4 bytes); `'a'` is a char, `"a"` a string.

examples.title: Ranges, overflow handling and conversions
examples.note: The checked, saturating, wrapping and overflowing methods make overflow behaviour explicit instead of depending on the build mode. `as` silently truncated 300 to 44, while `try_from` reported the problem as an error. A char always takes 4 bytes in memory, but the crab needs 4 bytes in UTF-8 text while an ASCII letter needs 1.
examples.output:
u8: 0..=255, i32: -2147483648..=2147483647
checked:    Some(255) and None
saturating: 255
wrapping:   4
overflowing:(4, true)
-7 / 2 = -3, -7 % 2 = -1, 7.0 / 2.0 = 3.5
0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
300 as u8 = 44 (truncated), try_from: Err(TryFromIntError(PosOverflow))
🦀 is a char of 4 bytes in memory, 4 bytes in UTF-8

check.q: What do `300 as u8` and `u8::try_from(300)` do?
options: Both panic, because 300 does not fit in a u8.
`as` silently truncates to 44, while `try_from` returns an error.
`as` returns an error and `try_from` truncates to 44.
check.explain: `as` keeps only the low 8 bits (300 − 256 = 44) without complaint. `try_from` checks the range and reports `Err` when the value does not fit.

examples.title: No implicit conversions between number types
examples.note: Multiplying an `i32` by an `f64` does not compile: Rust never guesses how to convert, because every implicit conversion is a chance to lose precision silently. The fix is explicit, such as `items as f64 * price` or `f64::from(items) * price`.

error[E0277]: cannot multiply `i32` by `f64`
 --> main.rs:4:23
  |
4 |     let total = items * price;
  |                       ^ no implementation for `i32 * f64`

help: the following other types implement trait `Mul<Rhs>`
  = note: `i32` implements `Mul`
  |
  = note: in this macro invocation
  ...

check.q: How do you fix multiplying `items: i32` by `price: f64`?
options: Nothing: Rust converts the i32 to f64 automatically.
Convert explicitly, for example `items as f64 * price` or `f64::from(items) * price`.
check.explain: Rust never converts between number types implicitly, because every implicit conversion could silently lose precision. You choose the conversion and write it out.

mistakes: **Assuming overflow panics in release builds.** It wraps silently. Use checked or saturating arithmetic when it matters.
**Converting with `as` without thinking.** It truncates and wraps. Prefer `try_from` when values may not fit.
**Comparing floats with `==`.** Compare within a tolerance.
keys: Fixed-width integers (`i8`…`u128`, `isize`/`usize`) and floats (`f32`, `f64`).
Overflow: panic in debug, wrap in release; choose behaviour with checked/saturating/wrapping methods.
No implicit numeric conversion; use `as`, `From` or `TryFrom`.
`char` is a 4-byte Unicode scalar value.

idea: **Compound types** group several values. A **tuple** holds a fixed number of values of possibly different types: `let point: (i32, f64, char) = (3, 1.5, 'x');`. Read the parts by **destructuring** (`let (x, y, z) = point;`) or by position with `.0`, `.1`, `.2`. The empty tuple `()` is called **unit**: it is the value of expressions that return nothing, such as a function with no return value. Functions often return tuples to give back several results at once.

An **array** holds a fixed number of values of the **same** type, stored next to each other: `let days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];` has type `[&str; 3]`; the length is part of the type. `[0; 5]` creates five zeros. Arrays live on the stack and are ideal when the size is known and fixed (the months of the year, a 3×3 grid). When the size changes at run time, use a `Vec` (chapter 8).

Indexing an array is **bounds-checked**: `days[10]` does not read random memory, as it might in C; it panics with a clear message. When an index may be out of range, `days.get(10)` returns an `Option` (`None` instead of a panic). Iterate with `for day in days` or `for (i, day) in days.iter().enumerate()`.
how: Tuples: `(a, b, c)`; `let (x, y, _) = t;`; `t.0`; `()` is unit.
Arrays: `[1, 2, 3]` of type `[i32; 3]`; `[value; n]` repeats.
`arr.len()`, `arr[i]` (panics if out of range), `arr.get(i)` (returns Option).
Iterate with `for x in arr` or `.iter().enumerate()`.
Use `Vec` when the length is not fixed.

examples.title: Tuples, arrays and safe indexing
examples.note: The tuple mixes a string, a float and a char, read both by destructuring and with `.1`. The function returns two values as a tuple. `[[0u8; 3]; 2]` builds a 2×3 grid, and `get` returns `Some` or `None` instead of panicking for index 9.

Montréal: -7.5°C (also -7.5 via .1)
lowest -7, highest 4, 5 readings
grid: [[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
get(1) = Some(-3), get(9) = None
day 2 was above zero
day 4 was above zero

check.q: The readings array holds 3, -3, 4, -7 and 0. What does the `get` line print?
check.explain: Indexes start at 0, so index 1 is the second reading, -3. `get` returns an Option, so an index past the end gives `None` instead of panicking.

examples.title: Out-of-bounds indexing panics instead of reading garbage
examples.note: The program panicked at the indexing line with a message naming the index and the length, and stopped before reading memory it does not own. In C the same mistake could silently read whatever happens to follow the array; Rust's bounds check turns it into a clear, immediate failure.
examples.output:
asking for month #7

thread 'main' panicked at main.rs:5:17:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 7
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

check.q: What does Rust do when you index an array past its end, like `months[7]` on a 3-element array?
options: It panics with "index out of bounds" and stops before touching memory it does not own.
It returns whatever value is stored in memory after the array.
check.explain: Every index is bounds-checked. A clear panic is far better than silently reading garbage, which is what the same mistake can do in C. Use `get` when an index might be out of range.

mistakes: **Using an array when the size changes.** Arrays have a fixed length. Use `Vec`.
**Indexing with user-provided numbers.** Use `.get()` and handle `None`.
**Long tuples.** `(String, i32, f64, bool, u8)` is unreadable. Use a struct with named fields.
keys: Tuples group fixed values of different types; `()` is unit.
Arrays hold a fixed number of same-typed values; the length is part of the type.
Indexing is bounds-checked: a panic instead of undefined behaviour.
`.get()` returns an Option for safe access.

idea: Functions are declared with `fn`, take **typed parameters** and declare a return type after an arrow: `fn area(width: f64, height: f64) -> f64`. Parameter types are always required (Rust does not infer them across function boundaries), which makes every function signature a precise contract. Names use snake_case.

Rust distinguishes **statements** from **expressions**. A statement performs an action and returns nothing: `let x = 5;` is a statement. An expression evaluates to a value: `5 + 1`, a function call, a block `{ ... }`, an `if`, a `match`. The key rule: a block's value is its **last expression**, written **without a semicolon**. Adding a semicolon turns it into a statement whose value is `()`.

So a function returns the value of its final expression: `fn square(x: i32) -> i32 { x * x }`. The `return` keyword exists for leaving early (`if n < 0 { return 0; }`), but the idiomatic style ends with a bare expression. This expression-oriented design is why `let y = if x > 0 { 1 } else { -1 };` and `let total = { let a = 2; a * 3 };` work: blocks and `if` produce values.
how: `fn name(p: Type, q: Type) -> Ret { ... }`; parameters always typed.
The last expression without `;` is the return value.
`return value;` for early exits.
Blocks are expressions: `let v = { ...; expr };`.
No return type means the function returns `()`.

examples.title: Expressions everywhere
examples.note: `celsius_to_f` returns its final expression. `grade` leaves early with `return` for invalid scores, otherwise its value is the `match`. The block assigned to `area` evaluates to its last line, and `if` produces a value directly. `.map(grade)` applies the function to every array element.

check.q: `grade` maps 95, 85, 72, 40 and 120 to letters, and anything above 100 is invalid. What is printed?
check.explain: The early `return '?'` handles invalid scores before the `match`, so 120 becomes '?'. The other scores fall into their ranges.

examples.title: One semicolon too many
examples.note: With the semicolon, `x * x;` is a statement and the function body evaluates to `()`, which does not match the promised `i32`. The compiler explains the mismatch and points at the semicolon, suggesting you remove it: one of the most common first-week errors.

error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> main.rs:1:22

1 | fn square(x: i32) -> i32 {
  |    ------            ^^^ expected `i32`, found `()`
  |    |
  |    implicitly returns `()` as its body has no tail or `return` expression
2 |     x * x;
  |          - help: remove this semicolon to return this value

check.q: Why does `fn square(x: i32) -> i32 { x * x; }` fail to compile?
options: `x * x` can overflow, so the compiler rejects it.
Parameters cannot be used in arithmetic without `mut`.
The semicolon makes `x * x;` a statement, so the body evaluates to `()`, not an `i32`.
Functions must always use the `return` keyword.
check.explain: A block's value is its final expression. Adding a semicolon turns that expression into a statement, leaving the unit value `()`. Removing the semicolon fixes it.

mistakes: **A semicolon after the final expression.** The function then returns `()`.
**Leaving out parameter types.** They are always required.
**Using `return` at the end of every function.** It works, but idiomatic Rust ends with a bare expression.
keys: Functions have typed parameters and an explicit return type.
Statements do things; expressions produce values.
A block's value is its last expression without a semicolon.
`return` is for early exits; blocks, `if` and `match` are expressions.

idea: Rust's control flow is built from expressions. **`if`/`else`** takes a condition that must be a `bool` (no truthiness: `if count` is an error; write `if count != 0`). Because `if` is an expression, both branches must produce the same type when its value is used: `let parity = if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" };`.

There are three loops. **`loop`** repeats forever until `break`, and `break value` makes the loop itself evaluate to that value, which is handy for retrying until something succeeds. **`while`** repeats while a condition holds. **`for`** iterates over anything iterable: arrays, ranges (`for i in 1..=10`), and later vectors, maps and iterator chains; it is the safest and most common loop, because it cannot go out of bounds. `.rev()` iterates backwards.

Nested loops can be **labelled**: `'outer: for ...` lets an inner `break 'outer;` or `continue 'outer;` jump out of or continue the outer loop directly, instead of juggling flag variables. Prefer `for` over `while` with an index counter: `while i < arr.len()` with manual indexing is slower (bounds checks on each access) and easier to get wrong.
how: `if cond { } else if other { } else { }`; conditions must be `bool`.
`let x = if c { a } else { b };` both branches the same type.
`loop { ... break value; }`; `while cond { }`; `for x in iterable { }`.
Ranges: `0..n` exclusive, `1..=n` inclusive, `.rev()` backwards, `.step_by(2)`.
Labels: `'outer: for ... { for ... { break 'outer; } }`.

examples.title: loop with a value, labels, ranges
examples.note: `break` with a value made the `loop` an expression that produced the answer. The labelled `break 'search` left both loops at once when the first even number was found. Ranges compose with `.rev()` and `.step_by()`, and `while` suits the Collatz sequence, where the number of steps is not known in advance.

first even number 8 at row 1, column 1

check.q: The countdown is `(1..=10).rev().step_by(3)`. What does the countdown line print?
check.explain: `rev()` starts at 10 and `step_by(3)` keeps every third value: 10, 7, 4, 1. The range is inclusive, so 1 is reached.

examples.title: Conditions must be bool
examples.note: Rust has no "truthiness": an integer is not a condition, and the compiler says it expected `bool` and found an integer. Writing `if unread > 0` states the intent exactly, and removes a whole class of bugs from languages where 0, empty strings and null are silently false.

error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> main.rs:3:8
  |
3 |     if unread {
  |        ^^^^^^ expected `bool`, found integer

check.q: What is the idiomatic way to write `if unread { ... }` when `unread` is a number?
check.explain: Rust has no truthiness: conditions must be `bool`. A comparison states the intent exactly. Casting an integer to bool with `as` is not allowed either.

mistakes: **Using a number or Option as a condition.** Compare explicitly (`> 0`, `.is_some()`).
**`while i < len` with manual indexing.** Use `for` over the collection.
**Flag variables to escape nested loops.** Use a loop label.
keys: `if` is an expression; conditions must be `bool`.
`loop` can return a value with `break value`.
`for` over ranges and collections is the safest loop; `while` for unknown counts.
Labels let `break` and `continue` target an outer loop.

idea: **Ownership** is how Rust manages memory without a garbage collector and without manual `free`. Three rules: every value has exactly one **owner** (a variable); there is only one owner at a time; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is **dropped** and its memory freed. The compiler checks these rules at compile time, so they cost nothing at run time.

The rules matter most for data on the **heap**. A `String` is three words on the stack (a pointer, a length and a capacity) pointing at text stored on the heap. If `let s2 = s1;` copied only those three words, both variables would point at the same heap memory and both would try to free it. Rust's answer is the **move**: after `let s2 = s1;`, `s1` is no longer valid, ownership has moved to `s2`, and using `s1` is a compile error. Nothing is copied on the heap; only the three stack words move.

When you really want two independent copies, ask for one with **`.clone()`**, which duplicates the heap data (and is visibly a potentially costly operation). Simple values that live entirely on the stack, like integers, floats, booleans, chars and tuples of them, implement the **`Copy`** trait: assignment copies them and both variables stay usable, because copying a few bytes is cheap and there is nothing to free twice.
how: One owner per value; the value is dropped when its owner's scope ends.
`let b = a;` moves heap-owning types (`String`, `Vec`, `Box`): `a` becomes unusable.
`.clone()` makes a deep copy explicitly.
`Copy` types (integers, floats, bool, char, tuples/arrays of Copy) are copied, not moved.
String literals (`&str`) are references to fixed text, not owned heap strings.

examples.title: Moves, clones, copies and drops
examples.note: After the move, only `s2` owns the text; the clone has its own heap buffer, which is why the pointers differ. Integers are simply copied. The `Drop` messages show exactly when values are freed: the inner value at the closing brace of its block, and main's value after "end of main".
examples.output:
s2 = hello, s3 = hello, same heap data? false
x = 5, y = 5
inside the block
  dropping inner value
after the block
end of main
  dropping main's value

check.q: The inner value is created inside a block, and main's value at the top of `main`. Which line is printed last?
check.explain: Values are dropped at the end of their scope, in reverse order of creation. Main's value lives until the closing brace of `main`, after "end of main" is printed.

examples.title: Using a value after it moved
examples.note: The compiler rejects the use of `greeting` after the move and explains why: `String` does not implement `Copy`, so assignment moved it. It even points at the line where the move happened and suggests `.clone()` if a copy is really needed. This is the compile-time check that makes double frees impossible.
examples.output:
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `greeting`
 --> main.rs:4:16
  |
2 |     let greeting = String::from("bonjour");
  |         -------- move occurs because `greeting` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
3 |     let moved = greeting;
  |                 -------- value moved here
4 |     println!("{greeting}, {moved}");
  |                ^^^^^^^^ value borrowed here after move
  |
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  ...

check.q: Why can't you use `greeting` after `let other = greeting;`?
options: Strings can only be read once.
`String` is not `Copy`, so the assignment moved ownership to `other`.
The compiler needs a type annotation on `other`.
check.explain: Assigning a String moves it: only one variable owns the heap data at a time. That rule is how Rust frees memory exactly once. Use `.clone()` if you really need two copies.

mistakes: **Cloning everything to silence the compiler.** It works but hides design problems and costs time. Borrow instead (lesson 4.3).
**Thinking a move copies data.** Only the small stack part moves; the heap data stays where it is.
**Expecting `String` to behave like an integer.** Heap-owning types move; `Copy` types copy.
keys: Every value has one owner and is dropped when the owner goes out of scope.
Assigning a heap-owning value moves it; the old variable becomes invalid.
`.clone()` copies deeply and explicitly.
`Copy` types (simple stack values) are copied instead of moved.

idea: Function calls follow the same ownership rules as assignment. Passing a `String` to a function **moves** it into the parameter: the function now owns it, and when the function ends the value is dropped, so the caller can no longer use it. Passing an integer **copies** it, and the caller keeps using its own.

Return values move ownership back out. A function that creates a `String` and returns it hands ownership to the caller; a function can also take ownership, use the value and give it back. That works, but threading every value in and out of functions (`let (s, len) = calculate_length(s);`) quickly becomes clumsy.

The usual solution is **borrowing**, the next lesson: pass a reference so the function can use the value without owning it. Taking ownership is still the right choice when the function genuinely needs to keep the value (storing it in a struct, sending it to another thread) or consume it (turning it into something else). A good guideline when designing functions: borrow (`&T`) to read, borrow mutably (`&mut T`) to modify in place, take by value (`T`) only to keep or consume.
how: Passing a non-Copy value moves it into the function.
Returning a value moves ownership to the caller.
`Copy` arguments are copied; the caller keeps its value.
Take ownership only to keep or consume; otherwise borrow.
The compiler tells you where a value moved if you use it afterwards.

examples.title: Values moving into and out of functions
examples.note: `take_and_shout` consumed its argument, so `original` cannot be used afterwards. `make_greeting` created a String and gave it to the caller. The integer was copied. `store` took ownership of each entry to keep it in the vector, a legitimate reason to take a value by ownership.

Hello, Ada! (11 bytes)
42 and n is still 21

check.q: `double(n)` is called with `n = 21`, an `i32`. What does that line print?
check.explain: Integers are `Copy`, so passing `n` to a function copies it. The function returns 42, and the caller's `n` is unchanged.

examples.title: The caller lost the value
examples.note: `word_count` only needed to read the text, yet its `String` parameter took ownership, so `essay` was moved and is unusable afterwards. The compiler even suggests changing the parameter to borrow. The fix is `fn word_count(text: &str)` and calling `word_count(&essay)`, exactly the next lesson.

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `essay`
 --> main.rs:8:34
  |
6 |     let essay = String::from("Rust moves values into functions");
  |         ----- move occurs because `essay` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
7 |     let words = word_count(essay);
  |                            ----- value moved here
8 |     println!("{words} words in: {essay}");
  |                                  ^^^^^ value borrowed here after move
  |
 --> main.rs:1:21
