check.q: `word_count` only reads the text. What is the best fix for the moved `essay`?
options: Change the parameter to `text: &str` and call `word_count(&essay)`.
Return the String from `word_count` along with the count.
check.explain: A function that only reads should borrow. A `&str` parameter accepts a borrowed String and leaves ownership with the caller. Cloning works but copies the text for no reason.

mistakes: **Taking `String` parameters for read-only functions.** Callers lose their values. Take `&str`.
**Returning tuples just to give values back.** Borrow instead.
**Forgetting that `store(v)` gives `v` away.** If you need it later, pass a reference or a clone.
keys: Passing a value to a function moves or copies it, like assignment.
Returning a value moves ownership to the caller.
Take ownership only when the function keeps or consumes the value.
Prefer borrowing for functions that just read or modify.

idea: A **reference** lets you use a value without owning it. `&s` creates a shared reference (a **borrow**); a function parameter `text: &String` (or better `&str`) receives it, and the caller keeps ownership: nothing is moved and nothing is dropped when the function returns. To modify a borrowed value, use a **mutable reference**, `&mut s`, which requires the variable itself to be `mut`.

The **borrowing rules**, checked at compile time, are what make Rust memory-safe and free of data races: at any moment you can have **either** any number of shared references (`&T`) **or** exactly one mutable reference (`&mut T`), never both; and references must always be **valid**, never outliving the value they point to. "Many readers or one writer" means no part of the program can change data while another part is reading it.

The rules apply to where references are actually used, not to where they are written (this is called non-lexical lifetimes): a shared reference's borrow ends after its last use, so you can create a mutable reference afterwards in the same scope. And because a reference can never outlive its value, **dangling references** are impossible: returning a reference to a local variable is a compile error.
how: `&value` borrows immutably; `&mut value` borrows mutably (the variable must be `mut`).
Many `&T` at once, or one `&mut T`, never both at the same time.
A borrow lasts until the reference's last use.
Use `*r` to read or write through a reference when needed (`*count += 1`).
Functions that only read take `&T`; functions that modify take `&mut T`.

examples.title: Shared and mutable borrows in practice
examples.note: Two shared references read the string at the same time. Once their last use had passed, the mutable borrows for `add_exclamation` were allowed, and the caller still owns `message` throughout. `*counter += 1` writes through the mutable reference to change the caller's variable.
examples.output:
borrowing is cheap / borrowing is cheap / longest word: 9
borrowing is cheap!!
visits: 3

check.q: `visit(&mut count)` is called three times, and each call runs `*counter += 1`. What does the last line print?
check.explain: The mutable reference lets the function write to the caller's variable through `*counter`, so each call adds one to `count`.

examples.title: Reading and writing at the same time
examples.note: `first` borrows into the vector, then `push` needs a mutable borrow while `first` is still used afterwards. The compiler refuses, and for a real reason: pushing may reallocate the vector's buffer, which would leave `first` pointing at freed memory. Moving the `println!` above the `push` makes it compile.
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: Why does the compiler refuse `scores.push(...)` while `first` still borrows an element?
options: `push` is only allowed on empty vectors.
`push` may reallocate the vector's buffer, which would leave `first` pointing at freed memory.
`first` is a copy, and copies block changes.
Vectors cannot grow after an element has been read.
check.explain: A shared borrow promises that the data won't change or move. A push that reallocates would break that promise, so the compiler rejects it. Moving the last use of `first` above the push fixes it.

mistakes: **Holding a reference while modifying the collection.** Finish using the reference first, or copy the value out.
**Trying to return a reference to a local variable.** The value dies at the end of the function. Return the owned value.
**Adding `&mut` everywhere.** Use shared references unless you need to modify.
keys: References borrow without taking ownership.
Either many shared references or one mutable reference at a time.
Borrows end at their last use.
References can never dangle; the compiler guarantees it.

idea: A **slice** is a reference to a contiguous part of a collection: a view, not a copy. A **string slice**, `&str`, points into some UTF-8 text: `&s[0..5]` refers to the first five bytes of `s`. It is a pointer plus a length, so creating one is free, and because it is a reference, the borrowing rules keep it valid: you cannot clear a `String` while a slice into it is still in use.

String **literals** are slices too: `"hello"` has type `&'static str`, a slice pointing into text baked into the program binary. That is why idiomatic functions take `&str` rather than `&String`: a `&str` parameter accepts literals, whole Strings (via `&s`, thanks to automatic deref coercion) and parts of Strings, while `&String` accepts only the second.

Range syntax mirrors the rest of the language: `&s[..3]`, `&s[2..]`, `&s[..]`. Slice ranges are in **bytes**, and must fall on character boundaries: slicing `"café"` at byte 4 splits the `é` (two bytes) and panics. For text, prefer methods that work in characters or words (`split_whitespace`, `chars`, `find`). Other collections have slices too: `&v[1..3]` on a `Vec<i32>` or an array is a `&[i32]`, and functions that take `&[T]` accept arrays, vectors and parts of them alike.
how: `&s[a..b]` slices bytes a to b-1; `&s[..b]`, `&s[a..]`, `&s[..]`.
Take `&str` parameters, not `&String`; take `&[T]`, not `&Vec<T>`.
Literals are `&'static str`.
Byte ranges must be on char boundaries; prefer `split_whitespace`, `find`, `chars` for text.
A slice keeps its source borrowed until its last use.

examples.title: first_word and friends with slices
examples.note: Because `first_word` takes `&str`, it accepted a whole String, a literal and a part of a String. `sum(&[i32])` likewise works on arrays, vectors and sub-slices. "café" has 5 bytes but 4 characters; byte 4 falls inside the two-byte é, so slicing there would panic.
examples.output:
"hello" "literal" "wonderful"
"hello" "world" "wonderful"
15 60 5
5 bytes, 4 chars, last char Some('é')
is byte 4 a char boundary? false

check.q: For the text "café", what does the byte-and-char line print?
check.explain: Strings are UTF-8: "é" takes two bytes, so "café" has 5 bytes but 4 characters. `.chars().last()` returns an Option of the final character.

examples.title: A slice keeps its source borrowed
examples.note: `word` is a slice pointing into `text`. Clearing the string while `word` is still used would leave it pointing at nothing, so the compiler rejects the program. In languages that return an index instead of a slice, this bug compiles and silently produces wrong results.
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: Why is `text.clear()` rejected while the slice `word` is still used?
options: Slices make the original string read-only forever.
Strings cannot be cleared once sliced.
`word` borrows part of `text`, and clearing it would leave the slice pointing at nothing.
check.explain: A slice is a borrow into its source. While it is in use, the source cannot be changed. Once the slice's last use is over, clearing is allowed again.

mistakes: **`&String` and `&Vec<T>` parameters.** They reject literals, arrays and sub-slices. Use `&str` and `&[T]`.
**Slicing text at arbitrary byte positions.** Non-ASCII characters make it panic. Use char-aware methods.
**Returning indexes into a string instead of slices.** The indexes go stale silently; slices are checked.
keys: Slices are views (pointer + length) into part of a collection.
String literals are `&'static str`; `&str` parameters accept every kind of string.
String slice ranges are in bytes and must respect char boundaries.
Borrowing rules keep slices valid as long as they are used.

idea: A **struct** groups related values under one name, with a **named field** for each: `struct User { name: String, email: String, active: bool, logins: u64 }`. Create an instance by giving every field a value, in any order, and read or (if the binding is `mut`) change fields with dot notation. Mutability applies to the whole instance; Rust has no per-field `mut`.

Two shortcuts reduce repetition. **Field init shorthand**: when a variable has the same name as a field, write `User { name, email, active: true, logins: 0 }`. **Struct update syntax**: `User { email: new_email, ..other }` takes the remaining fields from another instance; note that this moves any non-Copy fields (like `String`s) out of `other`.

Two other shapes exist. **Tuple structs** have a name but unnamed fields (`struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);`), useful to give a distinct type to a plain tuple: an `Rgb` and a `Point3(u8, u8, u8)` cannot be mixed up even though their contents match. **Unit-like structs** have no fields at all (`struct AlwaysEqual;`) and are used to implement traits on a type that holds no data. Structs usually **own** their data (`String` rather than `&str`), so an instance is valid for as long as it exists; holding references requires lifetimes (chapter 10).
how: `struct Name { field: Type, ... }`; create with `Name { field: value, ... }`.
Field init shorthand: `Name { field }` when a variable has the same name.
Update syntax: `Name { changed: v, ..old }` (moves non-Copy fields from `old`).
Tuple structs: `struct Meters(f64);` read with `.0`.
Unit-like structs: `struct Marker;`.
Own the data (`String`, `Vec`) unless you need references and lifetimes.

examples.title: Structs in every shape
examples.note: `new_user` used field init shorthand. Ben's instance took `active` and `logins` from Ada through update syntax; those are Copy, so Ada keeps them, and her name and email were not used by the update, so they stay hers too. Tuple structs give names to tuples, and `#[derive(Debug)]` makes every shape printable with `{:?}`.

check.q: Ben was created with `..ada`, but only `active` and `logins` were copied from Ada. Why can Ada still be used in full afterwards?
options: The fields taken from Ada are `Copy` types, so nothing of hers was moved.
Ada was declared `mut`, which prevents moves.
Struct update syntax always clones every field.
check.explain: Update syntax moves or copies the fields it uses. Ben supplied his own `name` and `email`, so only the `bool` and `u32` came from Ada, and those are copied.

examples.title: Update syntax moves Strings
examples.note: `..base` moved `host`, a String, out of `base`, so `base` can no longer be used as a whole. The compiler explains that a partial move occurred. Cloning the field (`host: base.host.clone()`) or using `..base.clone()` keeps `base` intact.
examples.output:
error[E0382]: borrow of partially moved value: `base`
  --> main.rs:10:30
   |
 9 |     let other = Config { port: 9090, ..base };
   |                 ----------------------------- value partially moved here
10 |     println!("{other:?} and {base:?}");
   |                              ^^^^ value borrowed here after partial move
   |
   = note: partial move occurs because `base.host` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: After `let b = Config { port: 9000, ..base };`, where `host` is a String, how can you keep `base` usable?
options: Write `..base.clone()`, or clone the `host` field explicitly.
Put the `..base` line before the `port` field.
Use `&base` instead of `base` after the update.
check.explain: `..base` moved the String field out of `base`, leaving it partly moved. Cloning gives the new struct its own copy so `base` stays whole.

mistakes: **Forgetting that update syntax moves non-Copy fields.** The source becomes partially unusable.
**Using `&str` fields to avoid allocating.** You then need lifetimes. Own the data with `String` at first.
**Plain tuples for meaningful data.** `(f64, f64)` could be anything; a named struct or tuple struct documents itself.
keys: Structs group named fields; the whole instance is mutable or not.
Field init shorthand and update syntax cut repetition (update moves non-Copy fields).
Tuple structs give distinct types to tuples; unit structs have no fields.
Structs normally own their data.

idea: The Book's rectangle program shows why structs matter by refactoring the same calculation three times. Version one passes `width` and `height` as two loose parameters: nothing says they belong together. Version two uses a tuple `(u32, u32)`: grouped, but `dims.0` and `dims.1` hide which is which, so swapping them is an easy, silent bug. Version three defines `struct Rectangle { width: u32, height: u32 }` and passes `&Rectangle`: grouped and labelled, and the function signature now reads like the problem.

Printing a struct needs a format. `{}` uses the `Display` trait, which you write by hand when there is a sensible user-facing form. For developers, add `#[derive(Debug)]` and print with `{:?}`, or `{:#?}` for a pretty, multi-line layout.

The **`dbg!`** macro is the debugging companion: `dbg!(expression)` prints the file, line, the expression's source text and its value to standard error, then **returns** the value, so it can wrap part of a larger expression without changing the program (`let area = dbg!(width * 2) * height;`). Pass a reference (`dbg!(&rect)`) when you do not want it to take ownership. Remove `dbg!` calls before committing; that is what `println!` and logging are for.
how: Group related values in a struct; pass `&Struct` to functions that read them.
`#[derive(Debug)]` then `{:?}` or `{:#?}`.
Implement `Display` for user-facing output (lesson 10.2 covers traits).
`dbg!(expr)` prints file:line, the expression and its value to stderr, and returns the value.
`dbg!(&value)` to avoid moving it.

examples.title: Three versions of the same program
examples.note: All three versions compute 1500, but only the struct version says what the numbers mean, and `area(&rect)` borrows rather than taking the rectangle. `{:?}` prints the debug form on one line; `{:#?}` spreads it over several lines with indentation, easier to read for nested data.

check.q: What is the difference between `{:?}` and `{:#?}`?
options: `{:?}` prints the debug form on one line; `{:#?}` spreads it over several indented lines.
check.explain: Both use the `Debug` trait. The `#` flag asks for "pretty" output, which is easier to read for nested structs.

examples.title: dbg! returns its value
examples.note: `dbg!` printed the expression `30 * scale` with its value and returned 60 into the struct field, so the program's behaviour did not change. Debug output goes to standard error with the file and line number, which is why it appears with `[main.rs:...]` prefixes. Passing `&rect` kept ownership in `main`.

check.q: What does `let w = dbg!(30 * scale);` assign to `w`, with `scale = 2`?
options: 60, the value of the expression, after printing it to standard error
check.explain: `dbg!` prints the file, line, expression and value, then returns the value, so it can be dropped into the middle of code without changing behaviour.

mistakes: **Loose parameters or tuples for related data.** Order mix-ups compile silently. Use a struct.
**`dbg!(value)` on a value you still need.** It moves non-Copy values. Use `dbg!(&value)`.
**Leaving `dbg!` calls in committed code.** Clippy can warn about them (`clippy::dbg_macro`).
keys: Structs make related data grouped and labelled; signatures document themselves.
`#[derive(Debug)]` with `{:?}` and `{:#?}` prints structs for developers.
`dbg!` shows file, line, expression and value, and returns the value.
Borrow with `&` when passing structs to functions that only read them.

idea: **Methods** are functions defined inside an `impl` block for a type, whose first parameter is `self`. They are called with dot syntax (`rect.area()`), and the type of `self` says what the method does with the instance: `&self` borrows it to read (most common), `&mut self` borrows it to modify, and plain `self` takes ownership, consuming the instance (useful when transforming it into something else). Rust automatically adds `&`, `&mut` or `*` at the call site to match, so you always write `rect.area()`.

Methods can take extra parameters after `self`: `rect.can_hold(&other)`. Grouping behaviour with the data in `impl` blocks also organises code: everything you can do with a `Rectangle` is in one place, and other code finds it by typing `rect.` in an editor.

Functions in an `impl` block that do **not** take `self` are **associated functions**, called with `::` on the type: `Rectangle::square(10)`. They are most often **constructors**; by convention `new` is the standard constructor, but descriptive names (`square`, `from_config`, `with_capacity`) are common and clearer. Inside an `impl`, `Self` is an alias for the type. A type can have several `impl` blocks.
how: `impl Type { fn method(&self) ... }`; call `value.method()`.
`&self` to read, `&mut self` to modify, `self` to consume.
Extra parameters follow `self`: `fn can_hold(&self, other: &Rectangle) -> bool`.
Associated functions (no `self`): `fn new(...) -> Self`, called `Type::new(...)`.
`Self` refers to the type inside its `impl`.

examples.title: Rectangle with methods and constructors
examples.note: `new` and `square` are associated functions called with `::`. `area` and `can_hold` borrow with `&self`, `scale` needs `&mut self` (so `big` is declared `mut`), and `into_square` takes `self` by value, consuming `small`, which cannot be used afterwards. Every call site uses the same dot syntax.

check.q: Why can't `small` be used after `small.into_square()`?
options: `into_square` takes `self` by value, so it consumed `small`.
Methods that start with `into` delete their struct.
check.explain: A method's receiver decides what happens to the value: `&self` borrows, `&mut self` borrows mutably, and `self` takes ownership. By convention, `into_*` methods consume.

examples.title: Calling a &mut self method on an immutable binding
examples.note: `increment` takes `&mut self`, which requires a mutable binding, and `counter` was declared without `mut`. The compiler suggests `let mut counter`. The method's signature makes its side effect visible, and the compiler enforces it.
examples.output:
error[E0596]: cannot borrow `counter` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable
  --> main.rs:13:5
   |
13 |     counter.increment();
   |     ^^^^^^^ cannot borrow as mutable
   |
help: consider changing this to be mutable
   |
12 |     let mut counter = Counter { count: 0 };
   |         +++
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: `increment` is declared with `&mut self`. What must the caller do?
options: Nothing: methods can always change their struct.
Declare the value with `let mut counter`.
check.explain: A `&mut self` method needs a mutable borrow, and mutable borrows require a mutable binding. The signature makes the side effect visible at every call site.

mistakes: **Taking `self` by value when `&self` would do.** Callers lose the instance after one call.
**Using `&mut self` for read-only methods.** It needlessly blocks other borrows.
**Constructors that leave fields invalid.** Validate in `new` (or return a `Result`) so instances are always usable.
keys: Methods live in `impl` blocks and take `self`, `&self` or `&mut self`.
Choose `&self` to read, `&mut self` to modify, `self` to consume.
Associated functions (no `self`) such as `new` are called with `Type::`.
`Self` names the type inside its `impl`.

idea: An **enum** defines a type by listing its possible **variants**: a value is exactly one of them. `enum IpAddr { V4(u8, u8, u8, u8), V6(String) }` says an address is either a version 4 address holding four bytes or a version 6 address holding a string. Unlike enums in many languages, each Rust variant can carry **its own data**, of different shapes: none, a tuple, or named fields. That makes enums perfect for modelling "one of several kinds of thing", such as messages, commands, events or states.
Enums can have methods in `impl` blocks, just like structs, and they are usually handled with `match` (next lesson), which forces you to deal with every variant.

The most important enum in the standard library is **`Option<T>`**: `Some(value)` or `None`. Rust has **no null**: a value that might be missing has type `Option<T>`, which is a different type from `T`, so the compiler stops you from using it as if it were always present. To get at the inner value you must handle the `None` case, with `match`, `if let`, or methods like `unwrap_or`, `map` and `?`. The billion-dollar mistake of null-pointer errors becomes a compile-time check.
how: `enum Name { A, B(i32), C { x: i32, y: i32 } }`; create with `Name::B(5)`.
Put methods on enums in `impl` blocks.
`Option<T>` = `Some(T)` or `None`; no null in safe Rust.
Get the value out by handling `None`: `match`, `if let`, `unwrap_or`, `map`.
`Option<T>` and `T` are different types; the compiler keeps them apart.

examples.title: Variants with different data, and Option instead of null
examples.note: Each variant holds different data, yet all are one type, so they fit in one array and one method handles them all. `find_user` returns `Option` instead of a null; the caller decides what a missing user means, here with `unwrap_or`.
examples.output:
write "hi"
move to (3, -1)
colour #0080ff
quit
user 1: Ada (raw: Some("Ada"))
user 7: unknown (raw: None)

check.q: `find_user(7)` finds nobody, and the caller uses `unwrap_or("unknown")`. What does that line print?
check.explain: `find_user` returns `None` for missing users, and `unwrap_or` supplies the fallback. The raw value is still printed as `None`.

examples.title: An Option is not the value inside it
examples.note: You cannot multiply an `Option<u32>` as if it were a number, because it might be `None`. The compiler refuses until you handle the missing case, for example `price.map(|p| p * 115 / 100)` or `price.unwrap_or(0) * 115 / 100`. This is the check that eliminates null-pointer crashes.
examples.output:
error[E0369]: cannot multiply `Option<u32>` by `{integer}`
 --> main.rs:3:26
  |
3 |     let with_tax = price * 115 / 100;
  |                    ----- ^ --- {integer}
  |                    |
  |                    Option<u32>
  |
  = note: `Option<u32>` is defined in another crate
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: `price` is an `Option<u32>`. Which expression adds 15% when there is a price and keeps `None` otherwise?
check.explain: `map` applies the closure only to a value inside `Some` and leaves `None` untouched. `unwrap` would panic on `None`, and an Option can't be multiplied directly.

mistakes: **Separate structs plus a "kind" field.** An enum with data per variant models it directly and safely.
**Sentinel values like -1 or "" for "missing".** Use `Option`.
**Calling `.unwrap()` everywhere.** It panics on `None`; handle the case or use `unwrap_or`, `?`, `if let`.
keys: Enums list variants; each variant can carry different data.
Enums get methods like structs and are handled with `match`.
`Option<T>` replaces null: `Some(value)` or `None`.
The compiler forces you to handle `None` before using the value.

idea: **`match`** compares a value against a series of **patterns** and runs the code of the first arm that matches. Each arm is `pattern => expression`, and the whole `match` is an expression, so it can produce a value. Patterns can be literal values, variable names, wildcards and, most powerfully, enum variants that **bind** the data inside them: `Coin::Quarter(state) => ...` gives you the `state` stored in that variant.

Matching is **exhaustive**: the compiler checks that every possible value is covered and refuses the program otherwise. For enums like `Option` this means you cannot forget the `None` case; for integers or strings, where listing every value is impossible, finish with a **catch-all**: a variable name (`other => ...`) if you need the value, or `_` if you do not. Arms are checked in order, so put specific patterns before general ones (a catch-all first would make the rest unreachable, and the compiler warns).

Arms can have multiple patterns with `|` (`1 | 2 => ...`), ranges (`1..=9`), and **guards**: extra conditions after `if` (`Some(n) if n < 0 => ...`). An arm's expression can be a block `{ ... }` for several lines. Matching on a reference (`match &value`) binds references, leaving the value usable afterwards.
how: `match value { pattern => expr, ... }`; first matching arm wins.
Bind variant data: `Some(x) => ...`, `Shape::Circle { radius } => ...`.
Exhaustive: cover every case, or end with `other =>` / `_ =>`.
`|` for alternatives, `a..=b` for ranges, `if cond` guards.
`match` is an expression: `let label = match n { ... };`.

examples.title: Binding data, guards and catch-alls
examples.note: The quarter arm bound the province stored in the variant and used a block for two lines. In `describe`, a guard handled extreme cold, `t @ -20..=0` matched a range while binding the value, `1 | 2 | 3` listed alternatives, and the final `Some(t)` caught everything else. Order matters: the guard arm must come before the general one.
examples.output:
a commemorative quarter from Quebec!
  a commemorative quarter from Ontario!
total: 61 cents
no reading
-31°: dangerously cold
-5°: freezing
barely above zero
18°

check.q: `describe(Some(-5))` meets these arms in order: a guard `t < -20`, then `t @ -20..=0`, then `1 | 2 | 3`, then `Some(t)`. What does it print?
check.explain: -5 is not below -20, so the guard arm is skipped. It falls into the `-20..=0` range, and `t @` binds it so the message can show the value.

examples.title: Forgetting None
examples.note: The compiler lists the missing pattern, `None`, and refuses to compile. Every `match` on an Option, Result or your own enum is checked like this, which is why adding a new variant to an enum safely flags every place in the code that must handle it.
examples.output:
error[E0004]: non-exhaustive patterns: `None` not covered
 --> main.rs:2:11
  |
2 |     match n {
  |           ^ pattern `None` not covered
  |
  = note: not covered
  = note: the matched value is of type `Option<u32>`

mistakes: **A catch-all arm first.** Every later arm becomes unreachable. Put specific patterns first.
**Using `_` when you will later add variants.** A wildcard silences the compiler's helpful "not covered" errors. Prefer listing variants for your own enums.
**Matching an owned value you still need.** Match on a reference (`match &value`).
keys: `match` tries patterns in order and is an expression.
Patterns bind data from enum variants.
Matching is exhaustive: cover every case or use a catch-all.
`|`, ranges, `@` bindings and `if` guards refine patterns.

idea: Sometimes you care about just one pattern. Writing a full `match` with a `_ => ()` arm is noisy, so Rust offers **`if let`**: `if let Some(max) = config_max { println!("max is {max}"); }` runs the block only when the pattern matches, binding the value. An `else` branch handles everything else. It is the same pattern matching as `match`, minus the exhaustiveness check, a trade of thoroughness for brevity that suits "do something if present" cases.

**`let ... else`** (let-else) handles the opposite situation: you need a value to continue, and otherwise you want to leave. `let Some(user) = find_user(id) else { return Err("no such user"); };` binds `user` for the **rest of the function** (not just a block, unlike `if let`), and the `else` block must **diverge**: `return`, `break`, `continue` or panic. This keeps the "happy path" un-indented instead of nesting it inside `if let` blocks.

**`while let`** loops as long as a pattern matches, for example popping from a stack until it is empty: `while let Some(top) = stack.pop() { ... }`. Together with `match`, these four forms cover every situation: all cases (`match`), one case (`if let`), required value or leave (`let else`), and repeat while matching (`while let`).
how: `if let Pattern = value { ... } else { ... }` for one interesting case.
`let Pattern = value else { return ...; };` to require a value; the binding lives on after it.
The `else` of let-else must diverge: `return`, `break`, `continue`, `panic!`.
`while let Some(x) = stack.pop() { ... }` loops until the pattern fails.
Use `match` when several cases matter; the compiler checks it exhaustively.

mistakes: **`if let` where several cases matter.** You lose exhaustiveness checking. Use `match`.
**Deeply nested `if let` blocks.** Use let-else to keep the happy path flat.
**Forgetting that `if let` bindings only live inside the block.** Use let-else when you need the value afterwards.
keys: `if let` handles one pattern, with an optional `else`.
`let ... else` requires a value or diverges; the binding lasts for the rest of the scope.
`while let` repeats while a pattern matches.
`match` remains the tool when every case matters.

idea: Rust code is organised in three layers. A **crate** is the smallest unit the compiler builds: either a **binary crate** (a program with a `main` function) or a **library crate** (code for other crates to use, with no `main`). Each crate has a **crate root**, the source file the compiler starts from: `src/main.rs` for the binary and `src/lib.rs` for the library. A **package** is what `cargo new` creates: a folder with a `Cargo.toml` that describes how to build one or more crates.

The rules are simple. A package can contain at most **one library** crate and any number of **binary** crates. Cargo finds them by convention, no configuration needed: `src/lib.rs` makes the library (named after the package), `src/main.rs` makes a binary with the package's name, and every file in `src/bin/` becomes an additional binary named after the file.

The common professional layout is a **library plus a thin binary**: almost all the logic lives in `src/lib.rs` (and its modules), and `src/main.rs` only parses arguments and calls the library. The library is then easy to test, reuse and document, and the binary refers to it by the package name (`use my_package::run;`) exactly as an outside crate would.
how: Binary crate root: `src/main.rs`; library crate root: `src/lib.rs`.
Extra binaries: `src/bin/name.rs`, run with `cargo run --bin name`.
One library, many binaries per package.
The binary uses the library by the package name: `use package_name::item;`.
Keep logic in the library; keep `main.rs` thin.

examples.title: One package, a library and two binaries

check.q: How did Cargo know there are two binaries in this package?
options: From the file layout: `src/main.rs` is the default binary and every file in `src/bin/` is another.
Each binary must be listed in `Cargo.lock`.
Binaries are detected by searching for `fn main` in every file.
The library declares them with `pub bin`.
check.explain: Cargo follows conventions: `lib.rs` is the library, `main.rs` the default binary, and `src/bin/*.rs` extra binaries. No configuration is needed.

examples.title: A library function and a thin main in one file

check.q: Why is `analyse` written to return data instead of printing?
options: Printing is not allowed inside modules.
Logic that returns values can be tested and reused; `main` only handles input and output.
Returning data is faster than printing.
check.explain: Keeping logic pure and pushing input and output to the edges is the professional shape: tests call `analyse` directly, and other binaries can reuse it.

mistakes: **All the logic in `main.rs`.** It cannot be unit-tested from integration tests or reused. Move it to `lib.rs`.
**Expecting two libraries in one package.** A package has at most one; use a workspace for more (lesson 14.3).
**Referring to the library as `crate::` from main.rs.** In the binary, the library is an external crate: use its package name.
keys: Crates are compiled units: binaries have `main`, libraries do not.
Crate roots: `src/main.rs`, `src/lib.rs`; extra binaries in `src/bin/`.
A package has at most one library and any number of binaries.
Put logic in the library and keep the binary thin.

idea: **Modules** organise code inside a crate into a tree of named scopes. `mod front_of_house { ... }` declares a module; modules can nest, and the crate root is the implicit top of the tree, called `crate`. Modules group related code and, just as importantly, control **privacy**.

Everything in Rust is **private by default**: an item (function, struct, enum, module, constant) is visible only inside the module where it is defined and its children. `pub` makes an item visible to the parent module and beyond. That default lets you hide implementation details and change them freely, exposing only a small, deliberate public interface.

Privacy has two details worth remembering. For **structs**, `pub struct` makes the type public but its **fields stay private** unless each is marked `pub`; a struct with private fields can only be created through a public constructor, which is how you guarantee its fields are always valid. For **enums**, `pub enum` makes **all variants** public, because an enum with hidden variants would be unusable. Child modules can see everything in their ancestors (private items included); parents cannot see into children's private items.
how: `mod name { ... }` declares a module; nest freely.
Items are private by default; `pub` exposes them to the parent and beyond.
`pub struct` with private fields + a `pub fn new` keeps invariants.
`pub enum` exposes all variants.
Children see their ancestors' private items; parents don't see children's.

examples.title: A restaurant module tree with privacy
examples.note: The private helper `seat_estimate` is used inside its module but invisible outside. `Breakfast` is public with one public and one private field, so outside code can change the toast but cannot create a breakfast directly or pick the fruit; it must use `Breakfast::summer`. The enum's variants are public automatically.

check.q: Why can't outside code write `Breakfast { toast: ..., fruit: ... }` directly?
options: `fruit` is a private field, so only code inside the module can build a Breakfast.
Structs can never be built outside their module.
check.explain: A struct literal needs every field, and private fields can't be named outside the module. A public constructor like `Breakfast::summer` becomes the only way in, which lets the module enforce its rules.

Private fields are encrypted at run time.
The only way to change a balance is through methods that enforce the rules, and the compiler guarantees it.

mistakes: **Making everything `pub`.** You lose the ability to change internals. Expose the minimum.
**`pub struct` and expecting public fields.** Fields need their own `pub`.
**Public fields on types with invariants.** Keep them private and provide methods.
keys: Modules form a tree rooted at `crate`.
Items are private by default; `pub` opens them up.
Struct fields have their own privacy; enum variants follow the enum.
Private fields plus constructors guarantee valid instances.

idea: A **path** names an item in the module tree. An **absolute path** starts from the crate root with `crate::` (or from an external crate's name, like `std::`); a **relative path** starts from the current module, using `self::` (optional) or **`super::`** to go up to the parent. Choose absolute paths when code might move independently of what it uses, relative ones for tightly related modules; both are common.

Writing long paths everywhere is tiring, so **`use`** creates a shortcut in the current scope: `use std::collections::HashMap;`. The idiom is to bring **functions** in by their parent module (`use crate::util::files;` then `files::read(...)`), so a call shows where the function comes from, and to bring **structs, enums and traits** in by their full path (`use std::collections::HashMap;`). Rename on import with **`as`** when two names clash (`use std::fmt::Result as FmtResult;`). Group imports with braces and `self`: `use std::io::{self, Write};`.

**`pub use`** re-exports a name: it brings an item into scope and makes it public at the new location. Libraries use this to offer a simple, flat public API (`mylib::Config`) while keeping a deeper internal structure (`mylib::config::loader::Config`). External crates from Cargo.toml are available by name; `std` is always available.
how: `crate::a::b::f()` absolute; `super::f()` parent; `self::f()` current module.
`use path::Item;` creates a shortcut for the current scope only.
Functions: import the parent module; types and traits: import the item.
`as` renames; `{self, A, B}` groups; `*` glob (mostly for preludes and tests).
`pub use` re-exports to build a clean public API.

examples.title: use, as, super and pub use
examples.note: `super::tax::amount` reached a private sibling module from inside `pricing`. `pub use self::model::Item` re-exported the struct so users write `shop::Item` instead of `shop::model::Item`. `as` renamed `fmt::Result` to avoid confusing it with the ordinary `Result`, and `pricing::with_tax` shows where the function lives at the call site.

check.explain: `pub use` re-exports an item at a shorter, more convenient path, so the public API doesn't have to mirror the internal folder structure.

options: A `use` only creates a shortcut in its own scope, and `printing` is a separate scope.
`use` statements only apply to the next line.
Child modules can't call functions from their parent.

mistakes: **Expecting `use` to apply inside child modules.** Each module has its own scope.
**Importing functions directly.** `read()` alone hides its origin; import the module and call `files::read()`.
**Exposing a deep internal structure.** Re-export the important types with `pub use`.
keys: Absolute paths start at `crate::`; relative ones use `self::` and `super::`.
`use` creates scope-local shortcuts; `as` renames.
Import modules for functions, items for types and traits.
`pub use` re-exports to give a library a clean API.

idea: As a crate grows, modules move out of one big file into their own files. The rule is short: **`mod name;`** (with a semicolon instead of a body) tells the compiler "the contents of this module are in a file". For a module declared in the crate root, the compiler looks for **`src/name.rs`** (or the older style `src/name/mod.rs`). For a nested module `mod hosting;` declared inside `src/front_of_house.rs`, it looks in **`src/front_of_house/hosting.rs`**: the folder is named after the parent module.

Each file is declared **exactly once**, with `mod`, in its parent. `mod` is not an import: it defines where a module sits in the tree. After that, other code refers to it by path and `use`, as before. Forgetting the `mod` line is the classic mistake: the file exists, but the compiler never reads it, and `use crate::name` fails with "unresolved import".

Moving code between files never changes paths: `crate::front_of_house::hosting::add_to_waitlist` is the same whether `hosting` is inline or in a file. So you can start with everything in one file and split it later without touching any calling code. Organise modules by **feature** (orders, billing, users) rather than by kind of thing (models, utils), so a change usually touches one module.
how: `mod name;` in the parent; contents in `name.rs` next to it.
Nested: `src/parent.rs` contains `mod child;`, contents in `src/parent/child.rs`.
Declare each module once; use paths and `use` everywhere else.
Paths stay the same whether a module is inline or in a file.
Organise by feature; keep `lib.rs`/`main.rs` mostly as a list of modules.

src
├── front_of_house
│   └── hosting.rs
├── front_of_house.rs
└── lib.rs
$ cat src/lib.rs

pub use crate::front_of_house::hosting;

pub fn eat_at_restaurant() -> String {
    hosting::add_to_waitlist("Ada")

$ cat src/front_of_house.rs
pub mod hosting;                    // contents in src/front_of_house/hosting.rs
$ cat src/front_of_house/hosting.rs

$ cargo test --quiet --doc 2>/dev/null; cargo build --quiet && echo "builds"

The path `crate::front_of_house::hosting::add_to_waitlist` is identical to the version with everything in one file, so no calling code changed.

check.explain: A child module's file lives in a folder named after its parent. The path in code, `crate::front_of_house::hosting`, matches the folders.

options: Nothing: the module path stays exactly the same.

mistakes: **Creating `name.rs` but forgetting `mod name;`.** The compiler never reads the file.
**Declaring the same file with `mod` in two places.** Declare it once; use paths elsewhere.
**Thinking `mod` imports like `use`.** `mod` places a module in the tree; `use` creates shortcuts.
keys: `mod name;` loads a module's body from `name.rs` (or `name/mod.rs`).
Nested modules live in a folder named after their parent.
Each module is declared once; paths are unaffected by file layout.
Split files when it helps reading; organise by feature.

idea: **`Vec<T>`** is a growable list of values of one type, stored next to each other on the heap. Create one with `Vec::new()` (an annotation like `Vec<i32>` is needed if nothing is pushed yet) or with the `vec![1, 2, 3]` macro. `push` adds to the end and `pop` removes from the end, returning an `Option` (`None` when empty). The vector must be `mut` to change.

Two ways to read an element: indexing `v[2]` returns the value and **panics** if the index is out of range, while `v.get(2)` returns `Option<&T>`, `None` when out of range. Use indexing when an out-of-range index is a bug, `get` when it can legitimately happen (user input).

Iterate with `for x in &v` (shared references), `for x in &mut v` (mutable references, change each element with `*x += 1`) or `for x in v` (takes ownership, consuming the vector). The borrowing rules apply to vectors as a whole: holding a reference to an element while pushing is refused, because `push` may move the whole buffer to a bigger allocation. To store different types in one vector, wrap them in an **enum** (or use trait objects, chapter 18). When a vector is dropped, all its elements are dropped too.
how: `Vec::new()`, `vec![...]`, `Vec::with_capacity(n)` if you know the size.
`push`, `pop` (returns Option), `insert`, `remove`, `len`, `is_empty`, `contains`, `sort`.
`v[i]` panics if out of range; `v.get(i)` returns Option.
Iterate: `&v` read, `&mut v` modify (`*x`), `v` consume.
An enum lets one Vec hold several kinds of value.

options: When the index comes from user input.
Always: `get` is slower and should be avoided.
When you want the program to keep running after a bad index.
When an out-of-range index would mean a bug, so stopping with a panic is the right reaction.

**Indexing with untrusted numbers.** Use `get` and handle `None`.
**`for x in v` when you still need `v`.** That consumes it; iterate over `&v`.
keys: `Vec<T>` is a growable, heap-allocated list of one type.
`push`/`pop`, indexing (panics) versus `get` (Option).
Iterate with `&v`, `&mut v` or `v` depending on what you need.
Use an enum to store different kinds of value in one vector.

idea: Rust has two main string types. **`String`** is an owned, growable, heap-allocated UTF-8 buffer: you can push to it and change it. **`&str`** (a string slice) is a borrowed view into UTF-8 text owned by someone else: a `String`, or text baked into the binary for literals. Functions usually take `&str` and return `String`; `&String` converts to `&str` automatically.

Build strings with `push_str` (append a `&str`), `push` (append a `char`), `format!` (like `println!` but returning a `String`, the most readable way to combine values), or `+`, which takes ownership of its left side: `s1 + &s2` moves `s1` and reuses its buffer. `to_string()`, `String::from` and `.to_owned()` turn a `&str` into a `String`.

A Rust string is a sequence of **UTF-8 bytes**, and characters take 1 to 4 bytes each. That is why **strings cannot be indexed** with `s[0]`: a byte position does not identify a character, and returning one byte of "é" would be wrong. Instead, choose the unit you mean: `.bytes()` for raw bytes, `.chars()` for Unicode scalar values, and for user-perceived characters ("grapheme clusters", like a flag emoji or an accented letter built from two code points) the `unicode-segmentation` crate. `len()` returns the number of **bytes**.
how: `String::new()`, `String::from("x")`, `"x".to_string()`, `format!(...)`.
`push_str(&str)`, `push(char)`, `s1 + &s2` (moves s1), `insert_str`, `replace`, `trim`.
`len()` is bytes; `chars().count()` is characters.
No `s[i]`; iterate `.chars()` or `.bytes()`; slice with byte ranges on char boundaries.
Take `&str` parameters; return `String`.

Character-aware methods (`chars`, `to_uppercase`, `replace`) handle UTF-8 correctly.

check.q: How do you get the first character of a String as a `char`?
check.explain: `chars()` iterates over characters and `next()` returns the first one as an `Option<char>` (None for an empty string). Strings can't be indexed by an integer.

**Using `+` in loops.** Use `push_str` or collect into a String; `format!` for combinations.

idea: **`HashMap<K, V>`** stores values by key, with fast lookup, insertion and removal (average constant time). Create one with `HashMap::new()` (it is not in the prelude: `use std::collections::HashMap;`), add with `insert`, and read with `get`, which returns `Option<&V>` because the key might be missing. Iterating gives `(key, value)` pairs in an **arbitrary order** that can differ between runs; sort the keys (or use a `BTreeMap`) when order matters.
Ownership applies: inserting a `String` key or value **moves** it into the map, while `Copy` values are copied. `insert` on an existing key **overwrites** the old value and returns it.

The **entry API** handles the common "update or insert" pattern in one lookup. `map.entry(key).or_insert(default)` returns a mutable reference to the value, inserting the default first if the key was missing. Word counting becomes `*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;`. Variants: `or_insert_with(|| expensive())` computes the default only when needed, `or_default()` uses the type's default, and `and_modify(|v| ...)` changes an existing value. Keys must implement `Eq` and `Hash`: strings, integers, tuples of them, and your own types with `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]`.
how: `use std::collections::HashMap;` `let mut m = HashMap::new();`.
`insert(k, v)` (returns the old value), `get(&k)` → Option, `contains_key`, `remove`.
Iterate `for (k, v) in &m`: order is arbitrary; sort for stable output.
Entry API: `*m.entry(k).or_insert(0) += 1`, `.or_default()`, `.and_modify(...)`.
Keys need `Eq + Hash`; inserted Strings are moved in.

Results were collected and sorted before printing, because HashMap iteration order is arbitrary. `insert` on an existing key returned the old value; `and_modify` changed tea, while cake did not exist so `or_insert` added it. `or_default` created an empty Vec for each new initial.

check.q: Cake is not in the map yet, so `stock.entry("cake").and_modify(|n| *n += 1).or_insert(5)` runs on a missing key. Which line shows the final stock, printed sorted?
check.explain: `and_modify` only runs for an existing key, so `or_insert` adds cake with 5. The output is sorted before printing, which is why cake comes first: HashMap iteration order is arbitrary.

**`if map.contains_key(k) { ... } else { insert }`.** Two lookups and clumsy code. Use the entry API.
**Expecting to use a String after inserting it.** The map took ownership.

idea: Rust divides errors into two kinds. **Recoverable** errors, like a missing file or bad input, are expected possibilities and are returned as values with `Result` (next lesson). **Unrecoverable** errors are bugs: a condition that should be impossible, such as an index past the end or a broken invariant. For those, the program **panics**.

A panic happens when you call `panic!("message")` or when code you call panics: indexing out of bounds, `unwrap()` on `None` or `Err`, integer overflow in debug builds, division by zero. By default the panicking thread **unwinds**: it walks back up the stack, running destructors (`Drop`) so resources are released, prints the message with the file and line, and ends. A panic in `main`'s thread ends the program with a non-zero exit code.

To see how the program got there, run with **`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`**: the backtrace lists the chain of function calls, most recent first; look for the first lines that are in your own code. For smaller binaries, a release profile can switch to `panic = "abort"` in `Cargo.toml`, which ends the process immediately without unwinding. Panics are not exceptions to be caught for control flow; they signal bugs to fix.
how: `panic!("msg {x}")` for impossible states; `unreachable!()`, `todo!()`, `unimplemented!()` are variants.
Common hidden panics: `v[i]`, `unwrap`, `expect`, overflow in debug, divide by zero.
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1 cargo run` shows the call chain; read from the top for your own frames.
Unwinding runs `Drop` code; `panic = "abort"` in `[profile.release]` skips it.
Use `Result` for expected failures; panic for bugs.

idea: **`Result<T, E>`** is the enum for operations that can fail: `Ok(value)` on success, `Err(error)` on failure. Functions like `File::open` and `str::parse` return it, and because it is a type, the compiler makes sure callers deal with it; you cannot accidentally use a `Result` as if it were the value inside.

Handle it with `match`, matching `Ok` and `Err`, and even different **kinds** of error (`ErrorKind::NotFound` versus permission problems). Shortcuts: `unwrap()` returns the value or panics; `expect("message")` does the same with your message (prefer it); `unwrap_or(default)` and `unwrap_or_else(|e| ...)` substitute a value; `map` and `map_err` transform the success or error value.

The **`?` operator** is the workhorse for **propagating** errors. Placed after an expression returning `Result`, it gives the `Ok` value, or immediately returns the `Err` from the current function. That function must itself return a `Result` (or `Option`, for `?` on Options) with a compatible error type: `?` converts the error with `From` if needed. A chain of fallible steps then reads as a straight line: `let text = fs::read_to_string(path)?; let n: u32 = text.trim().parse()?;`. `main` can return `Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>` so `?` works there too.
how: `match result { Ok(v) => ..., Err(e) => ... }`; inspect `e.kind()` for io errors.
`expect("why")` over `unwrap()`; `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_else`, `map`, `map_err`.
`value?` returns early with the error; the function must return `Result`/`Option`.
`?` converts error types via `From`; `Box<dyn Error>` accepts any error.
`fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>` to use `?` in main.

idea: When should code panic and when should it return a `Result`? The default for a function that can fail is **`Result`**: it lets the caller decide, and callers know their situation better than you do. Panicking is appropriate when continuing would be wrong or dangerous: a **bug** in the program (a broken invariant, an impossible state), a violated **contract** that the caller was told about (like indexing past the end), or bad state that code cannot recover from.

`unwrap` and `expect` are acceptable in a few places: examples and prototypes, tests (a panic is a test failure), and when you have information the compiler lacks, such as parsing a hard-coded valid IP address. In that last case, `expect` should explain why it cannot fail: `"127.0.0.1".parse::<IpAddr>().expect("hard-coded address is valid")`.

The best tool is often to **encode rules in types**. Instead of checking "is this a number from 1 to 100?" in every function, create a `Guess` type whose constructor validates once (returning a `Result`, or panicking if out-of-range values are a programming error), with a private field so no other code can create an invalid one. Every function that takes a `Guess` then knows the value is valid, and the check is never forgotten or duplicated. This "parse, don't validate" approach is one of the most powerful habits in Rust.
how: Return `Result` for failures the caller can expect or handle.
Panic for bugs, broken invariants and violated documented contracts.
`expect("reason it can't fail")` for values you know are valid.
Validate once in a constructor; keep the field private; pass the type around.
Document panics in a `# Panics` section of the doc comment.

idea: **Generics** let one piece of code work with many types. Instead of writing `largest_i32`, `largest_f64` and `largest_char`, write `fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T` once. `<T>` declares a **type parameter**, and the **bound** `T: PartialOrd` says what the code needs from it: here, the ability to compare with `>`. Without the bound, the compiler refuses, because it cannot assume an arbitrary `T` supports comparison.

Structs, enums and methods can be generic too: `struct Point<T> { x: T, y: T }` holds two values of the same type, and `Point<T, U>` allows different ones. `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` are generic enums you already use. In an `impl<T> Point<T>` block, methods work for every `T`; an `impl Point<f64>` block adds methods only for one concrete type (`distance_from_origin` makes sense for floats, not for strings).

Generics cost **nothing at run time**. The compiler performs **monomorphisation**: for each concrete type you actually use, it generates a specialised copy of the code, as if you had written `largest_i32` and `largest_char` by hand. You get the convenience of writing code once with the speed of hand-written specialised code; the price is slightly longer compile times and larger binaries.
how: `fn name<T: Bound>(x: T) -> T`; several parameters: `<T, U>`.
`struct S<T> { field: T }`, `enum E<T> { A(T), B }`.
`impl<T> S<T> { ... }` for all T; `impl S<f64> { ... }` for one type.
Add bounds for every capability you use: `PartialOrd`, `Clone`, `Display`, `Copy`.
Monomorphisation: zero run-time cost, specialised code per type.

idea: A **trait** defines behaviour that types can share: a set of method signatures, like an interface. `trait Summary { fn summarize(&self) -> String; }` says "anything that implements Summary can produce a summary". Each type provides its own implementation in an `impl Summary for Article` block. Traits can also provide **default methods** with a body, which implementors get for free and may override; a default method can call other methods of the trait, so implementing one small required method can unlock several.

Traits become powerful as **bounds**. A function parameter `item: &impl Summary` accepts any type that implements the trait; the longer form `fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T)` means the same and is needed when two parameters must be the same type. Combine traits with `+` (`T: Summary + Display`), and move long bounds into a **`where` clause** for readability. Returning `impl Trait` hides the concrete type behind the trait, which is essential for closures and iterators.

One rule keeps the ecosystem coherent, the **orphan rule**: you can implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate. You can implement `Display` for your `Article`, or your `Summary` for `Vec<T>`, but not the standard `Display` for the standard `Vec`. Many useful traits can be **derived** automatically: `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default)]`.
how: `trait Name { fn required(&self) -> T; fn provided(&self) -> T { ... } }`.
`impl Name for Type { ... }`; default methods may be overridden.
Parameters: `&impl Trait` or `<T: Trait>`; combine with `+`; use `where` for long bounds.
Return `impl Trait` to hide a concrete type.
Orphan rule: your trait or your type. Derive common traits when possible.

idea: Every reference has a **lifetime**: the part of the program during which it is valid. Usually the compiler infers lifetimes and you never see them. The **borrow checker** compares lifetimes to guarantee that no reference outlives the data it points to, which is how Rust rules out dangling references entirely.

Sometimes the compiler needs help. In `fn longest(x: &str, y: &str) -> &str`, the returned reference comes from either `x` or `y`, and the compiler cannot know which, so it cannot check callers. **Lifetime annotations** describe the relationship: `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str` says "the result lives at least as long as the shorter of the two inputs". Annotations do not change how long anything lives; they **describe** constraints so the compiler can check them at every call site. A caller that uses the result after one of the inputs has been dropped is rejected.

Structs that **hold references** need annotations too: `struct Excerpt<'a> { part: &'a str }` means an Excerpt cannot outlive the text it borrows from. Three **elision rules** let you omit annotations in the common cases (one input reference, or a method with `&self`), which is why most functions never show them. The special lifetime `'static` means "valid for the whole program", the lifetime of string literals.
how: Annotate when a returned reference could come from several inputs: `fn f<'a>(x: &'a T, y: &'a T) -> &'a T`.
Annotations describe relationships; they never extend a value's life.
Structs holding references: `struct S<'a> { field: &'a str }`.
Elision covers one-input functions and `&self` methods.
`'static`: valid for the entire program (literals); don't add it to silence errors.

idea: Real signatures often combine all three tools: type parameters, trait bounds and lifetimes. Reading them is a skill: take each part in turn. In `fn longest_with_note<'a, T>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str, note: T) -> &'a str where T: Display`, the angle brackets declare a lifetime `'a` and a type `T`; the parameters say `x` and `y` are borrowed for `'a` and `note` is any displayable value; the return borrows for `'a`; the `where` clause states the bound. Lifetimes come first in the list, by convention.

The combination shines in data structures that **borrow** and work with **any type**. A `struct Labelled<'a, T> { label: &'a str, value: T }` can wrap anything while borrowing its label; an `impl<'a, T: Display> Labelled<'a, T>` gives it methods for displayable values. Generic functions over slices of references, such as "find the longest item that matches a predicate", naturally carry all three.

The compiler checks each part independently: bounds say what operations `T` supports, lifetimes say how long references remain valid, and the types make sure everything fits. When a signature gets hard to read, a `where` clause, descriptive type parameter names (`Item` instead of `T`) and a short doc comment help more than clever tricks.
how: Order: lifetimes, then types: `<'a, 'b, T, U>`.
Put long bounds in `where`; name parameters meaningfully when it helps.
Structs can be generic and borrow: `struct S<'a, T> { r: &'a str, v: T }`.
`impl<'a, T: Bound> S<'a, T>` adds methods under conditions.
Read signatures part by part: generics, parameters, return, bounds.

idea: A **test** in Rust is a function annotated with `#[test]`. `cargo test` compiles your code in test mode, runs every test function (in parallel by default), and reports which passed and failed. A test fails when it panics, so checks are macros that panic on failure: `assert!(condition)`, `assert_eq!(left, right)` and `assert_ne!(left, right)`. The `_eq` forms print both values when they differ, which makes failures easy to diagnose; add a custom message after the values: `assert_eq!(total, 30, "total for {items:?}")`.

Tests usually live in a module annotated `#[cfg(test)]` at the bottom of the file, with `use super::*;` to see the code under test. The `cfg(test)` attribute means the module is only compiled for `cargo test`, so tests add nothing to the release binary.

To check that code panics when it should, add `#[should_panic]`, ideally with `expected = "part of the message"` so the test fails if it panics for the wrong reason. Tests can also return `Result<(), E>`: returning `Err` fails the test, and the `?` operator works inside, which is convenient for tests that call fallible functions.

`assert!`, `assert_eq!(left, right)`, `assert_ne!`, each with optional format arguments.

idea: `cargo test` accepts options for itself and, after `--`, for the **test binary**. The most useful ones change what runs and what you see. Tests run in **parallel** threads by default, which is fast but means tests must not share state such as a file or environment variable; `cargo test -- --test-threads=1` runs them one at a time when they must.

Output from passing tests is **captured** (hidden) so the report stays readable; only failing tests show what they printed. `cargo test -- --show-output` (or `--nocapture`) shows everything, useful when debugging. To run a **subset**, pass a filter: `cargo test split` runs every test whose name contains "split", and `cargo test tests::exact_name -- --exact` runs one.

Slow tests (network, large data) can be marked **`#[ignore]`** (optionally with a reason): they are skipped by default and listed as ignored, and `cargo test -- --ignored` runs only them, `--include-ignored` runs everything. `cargo test --release` tests optimised code, and `cargo test --doc` runs only documentation examples. Exit codes follow convention: 0 when all tests pass, non-zero otherwise, which is what CI relies on.

idea: Rust projects use two kinds of tests. **Unit tests** sit next to the code they test, inside a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in the same file. Because a child module can see its parent's private items, unit tests can test **private functions** too, which is handy for tricky internal helpers.

**Integration tests** live in the `tests/` folder at the top of the package, one crate per file. They use your library exactly as an outside user would: only its **public API**, imported by the package name (`use mylib::parse;`). No `#[cfg(test)]` is needed; Cargo compiles them only for `cargo test`. They catch problems unit tests miss: a function you forgot to make public, or modules that work alone but not together.

Shared setup code for integration tests goes in **`tests/common/mod.rs`** (not `tests/common.rs`, which Cargo would treat as a test file of its own) and is pulled in with `mod common;`. Binary crates cannot be tested this way, because a binary exposes no API, which is another reason to keep logic in `src/lib.rs` with a thin `src/main.rs`. `cargo test --test name` runs one integration test file.
how: Unit tests: `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; }` in each source file; may test private items.
Integration tests: `tests/*.rs`, each a separate crate using only the public API.
Shared helpers: `tests/common/mod.rs`, included with `mod common;`.

idea: The chapter's project is **minigrep**, a small version of the classic `grep` tool: `minigrep QUERY FILE` prints every line of the file that contains the query. It brings together much of the first half of the book: command-line arguments, files, strings, error handling, modules and tests.

Arguments come from **`std::env::args()`**, an iterator over the program's arguments as `String`s; the first is the program's own path. `let args: Vec<String> = env::args().collect();` gathers them; `collect` needs the type annotation to know what collection to build. (`env::args` panics if an argument is not valid Unicode; `env::args_os` returns `OsString`s for programs that must handle any file name.)

Reading the whole file is one call: **`fs::read_to_string(path)`** returns `Result<String, io::Error>`. The first version keeps everything in `main`, uses indexing for the arguments and `expect` for the file, and simply prints what it read. It works for the happy path, and it is deliberately naive: missing arguments panic with an index-out-of-bounds message and errors are reported crudely. The next lessons fix that step by step, which is how real programs grow.

idea: The refactoring separates **concerns**. Argument parsing moves into a `Config` struct with a `build` function: `Config::build(&args) -> Result<Config, &'static str>`. It checks there are enough arguments and returns `Err("not enough arguments")` instead of panicking. Grouping `query` and `file_path` in a struct also documents that they belong together.

The program logic moves into **`run(config) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>`**: read the file with `?`, search, print. `Box<dyn Error>` means "any kind of error", so `run` can propagate I/O errors (and later others) with `?` without defining an error type yet.

`main` becomes a thin shell: build the config, call `run`, and turn any error into a message on standard error and a non-zero exit code with **`process::exit(1)`**. `unwrap_or_else(|err| { ...; process::exit(1) })` handles the config error in one expression, and `if let Err(e) = run(config)` handles the run error. Finally, `Config` and `run` move into **`src/lib.rs`**, so they can be tested, while `src/main.rs` keeps only the wiring. This structure (parse, run, report) suits almost every command-line program.

`fn run(config: Config) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>` with `?` inside.
`main`: `Config::build(&args).unwrap_or_else(|e| { eprintln!(...); process::exit(1) })`.
`if let Err(e) = run(config) { eprintln!(...); process::exit(1); }`.

idea: The search logic is developed **test first**. Write a test describing the behaviour (given this query and these contents, the result is exactly these lines), watch it fail, then write just enough code to make it pass. The test pins down details before you write them: does "duct" match "productive"? (Yes: it is a substring search.)

The function signature needs an explicit **lifetime**: `pub fn search<'a>(query: &str, contents: &'a str) -> Vec<&'a str>`. The returned lines are slices of `contents`, not of `query`, and the annotation tells the compiler exactly that: the results live as long as `contents`. Without it, the compiler cannot tell which input the returned references borrow from and asks for the annotation. Returning slices instead of new Strings avoids copying every matching line.

The implementation is a loop: for each line in `contents.lines()`, if `line.contains(query)`, push it onto a result vector. Once the test passes, `run` calls `search` and prints each result. Because `search` takes text, not a file name, it is easy to test with string literals, a design that falls out naturally when tests come first.

idea: The last feature is an option: **case-insensitive** search, controlled by an **environment variable**. The value is read once in `Config::build` and stored in an `ignore_case: bool` field, so `run` does not depend on the environment.

`search_case_insensitive` lowercases the query and each line before comparing (`to_lowercase` returns a new String, which handles Unicode correctly, unlike ASCII-only tricks). It gets its own test first, like `search`.

The program also separates its two output streams properly. Results go to **standard output** with `println!`, and error messages to **standard error** with **`eprintln!`**. That way `minigrep body poem.txt > results.txt` writes only results to the file while errors still appear on the screen, and a pipeline does not silently pass error text to the next program. This is a convention every command-line tool should follow.

idea: A **closure** is an anonymous function you can store in a variable or pass to another function, and unlike a regular `fn`, it can **capture** values from the scope where it is defined: `let limit = 10; let small = |n: i32| n < limit;`. Closures are written with pipes around the parameters, and types are usually **inferred**, though you can annotate them. Once inferred for a closure, the types are fixed: calling it first with an `i32` and then with a `String` is an error.

A closure captures each variable in the least demanding way its body allows: by **shared reference** if it only reads, by **mutable reference** if it changes the variable, and by **value** (moving it in) if it consumes it. The `move` keyword forces capture by value, which is required when the closure must outlive the current scope, such as a closure passed to a new thread.

How a closure captures determines which **`Fn` traits** it implements, and functions that take closures state which they need. **`FnOnce`**: can be called at least once (every closure; one that moves a captured value out can only be called once). **`FnMut`**: can be called repeatedly and may mutate captured state. **`Fn`**: can be called repeatedly without mutating anything. `unwrap_or_else` takes an `FnOnce`, `sort_by_key` an `FnMut`, and a function you call from several threads would need `Fn`.
how: `let add = |a: i32, b: i32| a + b;` or with inferred types `|x| x + 1`.
Captures by reference, mutable reference or value, as the body needs.
`move |x| ...` forces capture by value (threads, returned closures).
Accept closures with `impl Fn(T) -> U`, `impl FnMut(...)`, `impl FnOnce(...)`.
`FnOnce` ⊇ `FnMut` ⊇ `Fn`: ask for the least restrictive trait you can.

examples.title: The three ways of capturing
examples.note: Each closure captured as little as it needed: `add_bonus` only read `bonus`, the click counter mutated `clicks` (an FnMut), and `greet` took ownership of `name` with `move`. `make_adder` returns a closure that carries its own copy of `amount`. `sort_by_key` accepts an FnMut, so the closure could count how often it was called.

**Forgetting `move` for threads or returned closures.** The borrow would outlive the data.

idea: An **iterator** produces a sequence of values one at a time. The `Iterator` trait requires one method, `next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>`, returning `Some(item)` until the sequence is exhausted and then `None`. `for` loops call `next` for you. Collections offer three ways to iterate: `iter()` yields shared references, `iter_mut()` mutable references, and `into_iter()` owned values, consuming the collection.

Iterator methods come in two kinds. **Iterator adaptors** (`map`, `filter`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `skip`, `take`, `rev`, `chain`, `flat_map`...) wrap an iterator in a new one and are **lazy**: nothing happens until something consumes them, and the compiler warns about an unused adaptor chain. **Consuming adaptors** (`sum`, `count`, `collect`, `max`, `min_by_key`, `fold`, `any`, `all`, `find`, `position`...) call `next` until done and produce a result. `collect` can build a `Vec`, `String`, `HashMap` and more; tell it which with a type annotation or the turbofish (`collect::<Vec<_>>()`).

Chains of adaptors read like a description of the computation (`filter` the valid ones, `map` to prices, `sum`), and because of laziness and inlining they compile to code as fast as a hand-written loop. Your own types become iterators by implementing `next`, and then get every adaptor for free.
how: `iter()` → `&T`, `iter_mut()` → `&mut T`, `into_iter()` → `T`.
Adaptors are lazy: `map`, `filter`, `enumerate`, `zip`, `take`, `skip`, `rev`, `chain`, `flat_map`.
Consumers: `sum`, `count`, `collect`, `fold`, `any`, `all`, `find`, `max_by_key`, `position`.
`collect::<Vec<_>>()` or annotate the target type.
Implement `Iterator` with `type Item` and `fn next` to get all adaptors.

examples.title: Iterator chains, lazily evaluated
examples.note: Each chain reads like its description: filter paid orders, map to amounts, sum. The last part shows laziness: creating the `map` ran nothing, and `take(2)` pulled exactly two items through it, so the closure ran only twice even though there are four orders.

["1:tea", "2:cake", "3:scone", "4:tea"]

check.explain: Iterators are lazy: creating `map` ran nothing, and `take(2)` pulled exactly two items through it, so the closure ran twice.

examples.title: Your own iterator gets every adaptor for free

idea: With closures and iterators, minigrep gets cleaner. `Config::build` used to take `&[String]` and **clone** the query and file path, because it could not take ownership of strings inside a borrowed slice. Instead, it can take the **argument iterator itself**: `fn build(mut args: impl Iterator<Item = String>) -> Result<Config, &'static str>`. Calling `args.next()` hands over owned Strings directly, skipping the program name and returning a clear error when an argument is missing (`match args.next() { Some(arg) => arg, None => return Err(...) }`). No clones, and `main` passes `env::args()` straight in.

`search` becomes a single expression: `contents.lines().filter(|line| line.contains(query)).collect()`. It says what it does, has no mutable state, and is easier to change (adding `.map(str::trim)` or making it lazy is one step).

Is the iterator version slower? The Book benchmarks it, and the answer is no: iterators are a **zero-cost abstraction**. The compiler inlines the closures and adaptors and often produces exactly the machine code of the hand-written loop, sometimes better, because it can drop bounds checks and unroll loops. Write the clear version, and measure if performance matters.
how: `fn build(mut args: impl Iterator<Item = String>)`; call `args.next()` for each argument.
`args.next();` first to skip the program name.
Return `Err` when `next()` is `None`; no indexing, no cloning.
`search` as `lines().filter(...).collect()`.
Benchmark in release mode before assuming loops are faster.

**Benchmarking debug builds.** Optimisations change everything; use `--release`.
keys: Taking `impl Iterator<Item = String>` lets `build` own arguments without cloning.
`next()` with `ok_or` and `?` gives clear errors for missing arguments.

Iterators are zero-cost: as fast as hand-written loops.

idea: Cargo builds with **profiles**: predefined sets of compiler settings. `dev` (used by `cargo build` and `cargo run`) compiles fast with no optimisation (`opt-level = 0`) and full debug info, ideal while writing code. `release` (`cargo build --release`) optimises heavily (`opt-level = 3`), takes longer to compile and produces much faster programs, so it is what you ship and benchmark. Override settings in `Cargo.toml` under `[profile.dev]` or `[profile.release]`: for example `opt-level = 1` in dev for faster tests, or `lto = true` and `codegen-units = 1` in release for a little more speed.

Rust has special comments for **documentation**. `///` documents the item that follows (function, struct, method) using **Markdown**, and `//!` documents the enclosing item, usually the crate or module at the top of `lib.rs`. `cargo doc --open` turns them into an HTML site like the standard library's, including your dependencies' docs.

By convention, doc comments use **sections**: `# Examples` (the most important), `# Panics` (when the function panics), `# Errors` (what errors a `Result` can contain and why), and `# Safety` (for `unsafe` functions). Code blocks inside doc comments are **doc tests**: `cargo test` compiles and runs them, so examples in documentation are guaranteed to stay correct.
how: Profiles: `dev` (fast compile) and `release` (fast program); customise in `[profile.*]`.
`///` for the next item, `//!` for the enclosing crate or module; Markdown inside.
Sections: `# Examples`, `# Panics`, `# Errors`, `# Safety`.
Code blocks in docs are compiled and run by `cargo test` (doc tests).
`cargo doc --open` builds and opens the HTML docs.

examples.title: Customising profiles
examples.code:
[package]
name = "minigrep"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[profile.dev]
opt-level = 1          # a little optimisation: faster tests, still quick to build

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3          # the default for release
lto = true             # link-time optimisation across crates
codegen-units = 1      # slower build, slightly faster binary
panic = "abort"        # smaller binary; no unwinding on panic
strip = true           # remove debug symbols from the shipped binary
examples.note: Only the settings you list change; everything else keeps the profile's defaults. The dev tweak speeds up test runs that do heavy computation, while the release settings trade build time for a smaller, faster binary. `panic = "abort"` means destructors do not run on panic, which is fine for many command-line tools.

The program can no longer panic.

check.explain: Abort skips unwinding, which gives a slightly smaller, faster binary. That's fine for many tools, but cleanup code in `Drop` won't run on a panic.

idea: Publishing a library to **crates.io** shares it with every Rust user through `cargo add`. Before publishing, shape the **public API**. Your internal module structure may be deep (`art::kinds::PrimaryColor`, `art::utils::mix`), which is awkward for users. **`pub use`** re-exports the important items at the crate root, so users write `use art::{PrimaryColor, mix};`, and the docs list them on the front page, while you keep organising internals however you like.

crates.io requires **metadata** in `Cargo.toml`: a unique `name`, a `version`, a `description`, a `license` (an SPDX identifier such as `"MIT OR Apache-2.0"`, the Rust ecosystem's common dual licence), and usually `repository`, `readme`, `keywords` and `categories`. `cargo publish --dry-run` checks everything without uploading, and `cargo package --list` shows exactly which files will be included.

Publishing is **permanent**: a version can never be overwritten or deleted, so that crates depending on it never break. Publish fixes as a new version, following semantic versioning (a breaking change in a 1.x crate means 2.0.0). If a release is broken, **`cargo yank --vers 1.0.1`** stops new projects from selecting it, while existing projects with that version in their `Cargo.lock` keep working. Log in once with an API token from crates.io (`cargo login`).
how: Re-export with `pub use` at the crate root for a flat, convenient API.
Required metadata: `description`, `license` (SPDX), plus `repository`, `readme`, `keywords`, `categories`.
`cargo publish --dry-run` and `cargo package --list` before publishing.
Versions are permanent; publish fixes as new SemVer versions.
`cargo yank --vers X` hides a broken version from new resolutions; `--undo` reverses.

examples.title: A deep module tree with a flat public API
examples.note: Internally, the types live in `kinds` and the function in `utils`, but the `pub use` lines make them available directly at the crate root. Users get a short, flat import path, the documentation front page lists them, and the internal structure can change later without breaking anyone.

check.explain: Re-exports decouple the public API from the internal module layout, so users write `art::mix` and internal moves don't break them.

examples.title: Metadata for crates.io

[package]
name = "billsplit"
version = "0.2.1"
edition = "2024"
description = "Split restaurant bills to the cent, fairly."
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"
repository = "https://github.com/you/billsplit"
readme = "README.md"
keywords = ["money", "bill", "split", "restaurant"]
categories = ["finance", "command-line-utilities"]

#   cargo publish --dry-run      # build and check without uploading

check.explain: Publishing fails without a description and a license (or license-file). The other fields are optional but help people find and trust the crate.

**Publishing without a dry run.** Mistakes are permanent; versions cannot be replaced.
**Breaking changes in a minor version.** SemVer tells Cargo it is safe to upgrade; users' builds break.
