idea: **Macros** are code that writes code at compile time. You have used them since `println!`: they take a variable number of arguments, can introduce new syntax, and expand into ordinary Rust before type checking. Functions can't do either: a function has a fixed signature and runs at run time. The cost is that macros are harder to write, read and debug, so reach for them only when a function or generic will not do.

**Declarative macros** (`macro_rules!`) work by pattern matching on code. Each rule has a matcher and a transcriber: `($x:expr) => { ... }`. **Fragment specifiers** say what each piece may be: `expr` (an expression), `ident` (a name), `ty` (a type), `tt` (any single token tree), `literal`, `block`, `pat`. **Repetition** `$( ... ),*` matches zero or more comma-separated items (`+` for one or more), and the transcriber repeats code for each. Macros are **hygienic**: variables they introduce cannot clash with the caller's.

**Procedural macros** are Rust functions that receive a token stream and return one, compiled in a separate crate. They come in three kinds: **custom derive** (`#[derive(Serialize)]`), **attribute-like** (`#[route(GET, "/")]`) and **function-like** (`sql!(SELECT ...)`). Most programmers use them far more than they write them; Track 2's macro module covers writing one.
how: `macro_rules! name { (pattern) => { expansion }; ... }`.
Fragments: `$e:expr`, `$i:ident`, `$t:ty`, `$x:tt`, `$l:literal`, `$b:block`, `$p:pat`.
Repetition: `$( $x:expr ),*` in the matcher, `$( ... )*` in the transcriber; add `$(,)?` for a trailing comma.
Hygiene keeps macro-internal names separate from the caller's.
Procedural macros: derive, attribute and function-like, in a `proc-macro` crate.

examples.title: A vec-like macro, a hashmap literal and a generated function
examples.note: `my_vec!` has two rules: one for no arguments and one for a comma-separated list (with an optional trailing comma), whose `$( v.push($x); )+` repeats once per expression. `map!` uses the custom `=>` syntax a function could never accept, and `getter!` generates whole methods from an identifier and a type.

check.q: In `$( v.push($x); )+`, how many times does `v.push` appear in the expansion of `my_vec![1, 5, 16]`?
options: Three: once per expression matched by the repetition.
check.explain: A repetition in the expansion repeats once per item captured by the matching repetition in the pattern.

examples.title: Hygiene: a macro's variables don't leak
examples.note: The macro's internal `tmp` did not clash with the caller's `tmp`, and the argument `tmp + 1` used the caller's variable: that is hygiene. The expression was also evaluated as a unit because `$x:expr` captures it whole. `count!` is a recursive macro that peels off one token tree per step.
examples.output:
(3 + 1)^4 = 256, and the caller's tmp is still 3
count!(a b c d) = 4

check.q: A macro uses its own `tmp` internally and is called with the caller's `tmp = 3` as `power4!(tmp + 1)`. What is printed?
options: `(3 + 1)^4 = 256, and the caller's tmp is still 3`
`(3 + 1)^4 = 256, and the caller's tmp is still 4`
`(3 + 1)^4 = 13, and the caller's tmp is still 3`
check.explain: Hygiene keeps the macro's `tmp` separate from the caller's, and `$x:expr` captures `tmp + 1` as one whole expression, so it is 4 to the fourth power.

mistakes: **Writing a macro when a function or generic would do.** Macros are harder to read and debug.
**Forgetting repetition separators.** `$( $x:expr ),*` needs commas between items; add `$(,)?` to allow a trailing one.
**Expecting macros to see types.** They work on tokens before type checking.
keys: Macros generate code at compile time and accept flexible syntax.
`macro_rules!` matches patterns of fragments and repeats with `$(...)*`.
Hygiene prevents name clashes between macro and caller.
Procedural macros (derive, attribute, function-like) transform token streams.

idea: The final project builds a web server from scratch with only the standard library, which shows what frameworks do underneath. HTTP runs over **TCP**: a client opens a connection, sends a text **request**, and the server sends back a text **response**. `TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:7878")` claims a port, and `listener.incoming()` yields a `TcpStream` for each connection.

An HTTP request starts with a **request line**, `GET /index.html HTTP/1.1`, followed by headers and a blank line. Wrapping the stream in a `BufReader` and reading lines until the empty one gives you the request; often only the first line matters for routing. A response starts with a **status line**, `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, then headers such as `Content-Length` (how many bytes of body follow), a blank line, and the body. Every line ends with `\r\n`.

The first version serves `hello.html` for `GET /` and a 404 page for everything else, choosing the status line and file with a `match` on the request line. It handles one connection at a time, and binding can fail (for example when the port is already in use, or a port below 1024 needs administrator rights), so real code handles that error instead of unwrapping.
how: `let listener = TcpListener::bind(addr)?;` `for stream in listener.incoming()`.
Read the request line: `BufReader::new(&stream).lines().next()`.
Response: status line, `Content-Length: N`, blank line, body; lines end with `\r\n`.
Route with `match request_line.as_str() { "GET / HTTP/1.1" => ..., _ => 404 }`.
Write with `stream.write_all(response.as_bytes())`.

examples.title: A server and a client in one program
examples.note: The server read only the request line and matched on it to pick a status and body, then wrote a response with a correct `Content-Length`. A client in the same program sent two raw HTTP requests, so the whole exchange is visible: 200 for `/` and 404 for anything else. Binding to port 0 lets the operating system choose a free port.
examples.output:
GET / -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK | body:

Hello!

Hi from Rust

GET /missing -> HTTP/1.1 404 NOT FOUND | body:

Oops!

Sorry, I don't know what you asked for.

check.q: Why does the test server bind to port 0?
options: The operating system then picks a free port, so the example never clashes with another program.
Port 0 is the standard HTTP port.
Port 0 accepts connections from any machine.
check.explain: Asking for port 0 means "any free port". The program then reads the real port with `local_addr()` and connects to it.

examples.title: Binding can fail, so handle it
examples.note: Binding the same address twice fails with `AddrInUse`, the same error you get when another program already uses your port. A real server reports this clearly (and exits with an error) instead of crashing on `unwrap`.
examples.output:
first listener bound to a port chosen by the OS: true
second bind failed: Address already in use (os error 98) (AddrInUse)

check.q: What error do you get when binding to a port another program already uses?
check.explain: A port can have only one listener. A real server should report this clearly instead of crashing on `unwrap`.

mistakes: **Forgetting `Content-Length` or the blank line.** Browsers wait or show garbage. Follow the format exactly, with `\r\n`.
**Reading the whole request before responding.** Read up to the blank line; the body comes after.
**Unwrapping `bind`.** Ports may be in use or need privileges; report the error.
keys: `TcpListener::bind` and `incoming()` accept TCP connections.
An HTTP request starts with a request line; read it with a BufReader.
A response is a status line, headers, a blank line and a body.
Route by matching on the request line; handle bind errors.

idea: A single-threaded server handles one request at a time, so one slow request blocks everyone. Adding a `/sleep` route that waits five seconds shows it: while it sleeps, even `/` has to wait. Spawning a new thread per connection fixes that but has no limit: a flood of requests would create thousands of threads and exhaust the machine.

A **thread pool** keeps a fixed number of worker threads waiting for jobs. The Book designs the API first, the way you'd want to use it: `let pool = ThreadPool::new(4); pool.execute(|| handle(stream));`, mirroring `thread::spawn`. Then it builds the implementation to fit. `ThreadPool::new(size)` creates a **channel** and `size` **Workers**; each Worker owns a thread that loops, receiving jobs from the channel and running them. A job is a boxed closure: `type Job = Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>;`. `execute` boxes the closure and sends it down the channel.

Since every worker receives from the same channel and the receiver can't be cloned, it is shared as **`Arc<Mutex<Receiver<Job>>>`**: a worker locks the mutex, takes the next job, and **releases the lock before running the job** (by letting the guard drop at the end of the `let` statement), so other workers can pick up jobs concurrently. This is the producer-consumer pattern from chapter 16, applied.
how: Design the API first: `ThreadPool::new(n)`, `pool.execute(closure)`.
`type Job = Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>;`
Workers share `Arc<Mutex<mpsc::Receiver<Job>>>`.
Worker loop: `let job = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv();` then run the job outside the lock.
Validate `size > 0` in `new` (or return a Result from `build`).

examples.title: The ThreadPool, and why the lock must be released before running a job
examples.note: Eight 100 ms jobs on four workers finished in about two rounds, so four ran at once. That only works because each worker drops the lock before running its job: the `let` statement ends the guard's life, so the next worker can receive immediately. Holding the lock while running (for example `while let Ok(job) = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv()`) would serialise the pool.
examples.output: finished [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] in about 2 rounds of 100 ms (4 workers, 8 jobs)

check.q: Why must each worker receive the job in a separate `let` statement?
options: The lock guard is dropped at the end of that statement, so the next worker can take a job while this one runs.
Jobs can only be received once per worker.
check.explain: Releasing the lock before running the job lets all workers run in parallel; that's how eight jobs finish in two rounds on four workers.

examples.title: The mistake that serialises the pool
examples.note: In a `while let`, the temporary lock guard lives until the end of the loop body, so each worker held the mutex while running its job, and the other workers waited. Four jobs on four workers took four rounds instead of one. The fix is to receive in a separate `let` statement, as in the previous example.
examples.output: 4 jobs on 4 workers took about 4 rounds: one at a time

check.q: In `while let Ok(job) = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv() { job(); }`, why do the jobs run one at a time?
options: `recv` only returns one job per second.
`while let` loops can't run in threads.
The temporary lock guard lives until the end of the loop body, so each worker holds the mutex while running its job.
The channel only holds one job.
check.explain: Temporaries in a `while let` condition live for the whole body. Receiving with a separate `let` drops the guard first.

mistakes: **One thread per connection without a limit.** A burst of requests exhausts the machine. Use a pool.
**Holding the mutex while running the job.** The pool becomes single-threaded. Receive in its own statement.
**Designing the implementation before the API.** Write how you want to call it first.
keys: A thread pool runs jobs on a fixed set of workers.
Jobs are `Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>` sent through a channel.
Workers share the receiver as `Arc<Mutex<Receiver<Job>>>`.
Release the lock before running each job.

idea: A server should shut down **gracefully**: stop accepting new work, let in-flight requests finish, and then stop the worker threads cleanly, instead of having the process killed mid-request. In the thread pool, that logic belongs in **`impl Drop for ThreadPool`**, so it happens automatically whenever the pool goes out of scope.

Shutdown has two steps. First, **close the channel** by dropping the sender: each worker's `recv()` then returns `Err` once the queue is empty, which tells it to leave its loop. Second, **join every worker** so the program waits for them to finish their current job. Ownership makes both steps slightly tricky, because `drop` only receives `&mut self`, and you cannot move a field out of a borrowed struct. The Book's solution stores the sender as **`Option<Sender<Job>>`** and each worker's thread as `Option<JoinHandle<()>>` (or drains the vector), so `take()` can move them out, leaving `None` behind.

The demo server then stops after two requests with `listener.incoming().take(2)`, and the logs show the shutdown sequence: the pool is dropped at the end of `main`, the channel closes, each worker reports that it is disconnecting, and the joins complete. The same pattern (signal, drain, join) applies to any service with background workers.
how: `sender: Option<mpsc::Sender<Job>>`; `execute` uses `self.sender.as_ref().unwrap()`.
In `Drop`: `drop(self.sender.take());` closes the channel.
Then `for worker in self.workers.drain(..) { worker.thread.join().unwrap(); }`.
Workers exit their loop when `recv()` returns `Err`.
Demo: `incoming().take(2)` to stop after two requests.

examples.title: Drop for ThreadPool shuts everything down cleanly
examples.note: When the pool went out of scope, `Drop` took the sender out of its `Option` and dropped it, so each worker's `recv` returned an error once the queue was empty and its loop ended; then every worker was joined. All four requests, including the slow `/sleep`, completed before the program moved on: a graceful shutdown.
examples.output:
all jobs submitted; leaving the scope drops the pool
channel closed; waiting for 3 workers
joined workers [0, 1, 2]
every in-flight request finished before shutdown: ["/", "/", "/about", "/sleep"]

check.q: What makes each worker's loop end when the pool is dropped?
options: `Drop` drops the sender, so `recv` returns an error once the queue is empty.
The pool sends a "stop" closure to each worker.
Each worker is killed with a signal.
Workers count jobs and stop after eight.
check.explain: When every sender is gone, the channel closes. Workers finish their current jobs, see the error, exit their loops and are joined.

examples.title: You can't move a field out of &mut self
examples.note: `drop` gets `&mut self`, and moving `self.sender` out of a borrowed struct is not allowed: the compiler explains that the value is behind a mutable reference. Wrapping the field in an `Option` and calling `self.sender.take()` moves it out and leaves `None` in its place, which is exactly what the pool does.
examples.output:
error[E0507]: cannot move out of `self.sender` which is behind a mutable reference
 --> main.rs:9:14
  |
9 |         drop(self.sender);
  |              ^^^^^^^^^^^ move occurs because `self.sender` has type `std::sync::mpsc::Sender<String>`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
  |
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  |
9 |         drop(self.sender.clone());
  |                         ++++++++
examples.label: Compiler output

check.q: How does the pool drop its sender inside `fn drop(&mut self)`?
options: It stores the sender in an `Option` and calls `self.sender.take()`.
It clones the sender and drops the clone.
It sets the sender to null.
check.explain: You can't move a field out of a borrowed struct. `Option::take` moves the value out and leaves `None` behind.

mistakes: **Letting the process exit with workers mid-job.** Join them in `Drop`.
**Joining before closing the channel.** Workers wait for jobs forever and the join never returns.
**Moving fields out of `&mut self`.** Store them in `Option` and use `take()`.
keys: Graceful shutdown: stop accepting work, finish in-flight jobs, join workers.
Put shutdown logic in `Drop` so it happens automatically.
Close the channel first, then join.
`Option` + `take()` moves owned fields out inside `drop`.

idea: A load tester answers one question: **how does a service behave under a given amount of concurrent traffic?** Before writing code, decide what to measure. **Throughput** is completed requests per second. **Latency** is how long each request took, and it must be reported as **percentiles** (p50, p95, p99), not an average: the average hides the slow tail, and the tail is what users feel and what service-level objectives are written against. Also count **status codes** (a fast stream of 500s is not success) and **errors** (timeouts, refused connections), kept separate from HTTP responses.

Then design the interface the way users will type it: `loadtest http://localhost:3000/health -n 1000 -c 50 --timeout 5s --json`. The number of requests, the concurrency, a timeout and an output format cover most needs; extras (custom headers, a request body, a duration-based mode) can wait for later versions.

The key design decision is **separating the statistics and the scheduling from the network**. A `Target` trait with one method, "perform one request and report the outcome", lets the real app use reqwest while tests use a fake target that returns scripted outcomes instantly. The percentile code, the concurrency limiter and the report can then be tested exhaustively without a server, which is exactly how professional tools stay trustworthy.
how: Measure throughput, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), status counts and errors.
Model outcomes as an enum: a response with status and latency, or an error with a kind.
Validate the plan up front: positive counts, concurrency ≤ requests, sane timeout.
Hide the network behind a `Target` trait; fakes in tests, reqwest in the app.
Sketch the CLI and the report before writing the core.

examples.title: Why averages lie about latency
examples.note: The mean of 59 ms suggests a healthy service, but the p99 shows that one request in a hundred took over a second. Percentiles describe what real users experience at each level of "unluckiness", which is why the tool reports them and why SLOs are written as "p99 under 300 ms".
examples.output:
mean       59 ms   <- looks healthy
p50        22 ms
p95        26 ms
p99      1240 ms
p99.9    1260 ms
31 users in 1000 waited over half a second

check.q: Most of the 1,000 requests take about 20 ms, but 3% take over a second. What does the p99 line show?
check.explain: The mean (59 ms) and the p95 look healthy, but the slowest 1% are over a second. Percentiles show the tail that averages hide.

examples.title: Validating the plan before any request is sent
examples.note: `validate` consumes the plan and gives it back only if it makes sense, so the rest of the program can assume a valid plan. Each mistake has its own error variant, which the CLI can turn into a precise message ("concurrency 50 is higher than the 10 requests") instead of failing halfway through a run.
examples.output:
ok: http://localhost:3000/health x1000 at concurrency 50
rejected: TooConcurrent { concurrency: 50, requests: 10 }
rejected: BadUrl("localhost:3000")
rejected: NoRequests

check.q: Why does `validate` take the plan by value and return it inside `Ok`?
options: The rest of the program then only ever receives a plan that has passed validation.
It lets the plan be modified during validation.
Validation is faster on owned values.
check.explain: Consuming the unchecked plan and handing back a checked one means invalid plans can't sneak past. Each mistake gets its own error variant for a precise message.

mistakes: **Reporting average latency.** Report percentiles; the tail matters most.
**Counting 500 responses as successes.** Track status codes separately from errors.
**Testing the core against a real server.** Put the network behind a trait and use fakes.
keys: Measure throughput, latency percentiles, statuses and errors.
Validate plans before sending anything.
A Target trait separates the core from the network.
Design the CLI and report first.

idea: The core of the load tester has two parts: a **runner** that performs N requests with at most C in flight, and the **statistics** that turn outcomes into a summary. Both are pure logic once the network is behind the `Target` trait.

The runner is a natural fit for Tokio: spawn the requests as tasks and cap how many run at once with a **`Semaphore`** of C permits (or, equivalently, keep a `JoinSet` topped up to C tasks). Each task records its own latency with `Instant::now()` around the call. Collect outcomes as they finish, and measure the **wall-clock** time of the whole run to compute throughput. With a fake target that sleeps for a scripted latency, tests can check precise properties: all N requests ran, concurrency never exceeded C, and the total time is about N/C × latency.

For statistics, sort the successful latencies once and read percentiles by **nearest rank**; count statuses in a `BTreeMap` so reports list them in order. Edge cases matter for a tool people trust: no successful responses (percentiles are `None`), one request, all errors. Each gets a test.
how: Share the target with `Arc`; spawn one task per request.
Limit in-flight requests with `Semaphore::new(concurrency)`.
Time each call with `Instant`; time the whole run for throughput.
Sort latencies once; nearest-rank percentiles; `BTreeMap` for status counts.
Test with a fake target: counts, peak concurrency, timing, edge cases.

examples.title: A concurrency-limited runner, measured with a fake target
examples.note: All 200 requests ran, never more than 10 at a time, and the run took about 20 rounds of 20 ms, as the arithmetic predicts. The fake target made these properties checkable in milliseconds, including the error and 503 paths. The real app swaps in a reqwest-based target with the same trait.
examples.output:
completed 200 requests: 8 errors, 8 responses with status 503
peak concurrency: 10 (limit 10)
wall time close to 200/10 x 20 ms = 400 ms: true
throughput above 150 req/s: true

check.q: 200 requests run against a fake target with a Semaphore of 10 permits. What peak concurrency is reported?
check.explain: Every task waits for a permit before calling the target, so no more than ten requests are ever in flight. The fake target records the peak to prove it.

examples.note: Five small tests pin down the behaviour users rely on: no data means no percentiles rather than a panic, errors never count as latencies, one request is its own p50 and p99, input order doesn't matter, and status counts come out sorted. With these in place, the statistics can be refactored or optimised without fear.

test tests::all_errors ... ok
test tests::empty_run_has_no_percentiles ... ok
test tests::nearest_rank_on_a_hundred_values ... ok
test tests::single_request_is_every_percentile ... ok

check.q: What should `summarize` return for p50 when every request failed?
options: The latency of the fastest error.
`None`, because there are no successful latencies to rank.
check.explain: Errors aren't latencies. Returning `None` lets the report say "no data" instead of printing a misleading 0 ms.

mistakes: **Spawning all requests without a limit.** That's a burst of N, not concurrency C. Use a Semaphore.
**Timing from before acquiring the permit.** Queue time isn't request latency; start the clock after.
**Untested edge cases.** Empty runs and all-error runs are exactly when users need correct output.
keys: A Semaphore caps requests in flight; JoinSet collects outcomes.
Time each request and the whole run separately.
Nearest-rank percentiles over sorted latencies.
Fake targets make the core fully testable.

idea: "Shipping" turns working code into a tool other people can install and trust. Three pieces matter. **The interface**: wire the clap struct to the core, print a readable **human report** by default and a **machine-readable JSON report** with `--json`, so the tool fits both terminals and CI pipelines. Use distinct **exit codes** (0 success, 1 thresholds missed, 2 usage error) so scripts can react.

**Continuous integration**: a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` and `cargo test` on every push and pull request, on Linux, macOS and Windows, catches regressions before users do. Caching (`Swatinem/rust-cache`) keeps it fast.

**Releases**: tag a version (`git tag v0.1.0 && git push --tags`) and let a workflow build binaries for each platform and attach them to a GitHub Release, so users without Rust can download and run the tool; `cargo install --git ...` or publishing to crates.io serves Rust users. A README with an example command, a sample report, and an honest "limitations" section completes the portfolio piece: it shows you can deliver, not just code.
how: Human report by default, `--json` for machines; exit codes for scripts.
Optional thresholds: `--max-p99 300ms` fails the run (exit 1) when missed.
CI: fmt, clippy with `-D warnings`, tests, on three OSes, with caching.
Release on tags: build per-platform binaries and attach them to a GitHub Release.
README: install, usage, sample output, limitations.

examples.title: One summary, two report formats, and a threshold

Requests    1000 (4 errors, 0.4%)

Latency     p50 11 ms | p95 38 ms | p99 412 ms
Statuses    200x990 503x6

{"url":"http://localhost:3000/health","requests":1000,"errors":4,"throughput_rps":812.4,"p50_ms":11,"p95_ms":38,"p99_ms":412,"statuses":{"200":990,"503":6}}

examples.title: A release workflow that builds binaries on every tag
examples.note: Pushing a tag such as `v0.1.0` triggers three parallel builds, one per platform, and each uploads its binary to the same GitHub Release. `--locked` makes the build use exactly the versions in Cargo.lock. Tools like `cargo-dist` can generate a more complete version of this workflow, including installers.

check.q: What does pushing a tag like `v0.1.0` trigger in the release workflow?
options: Builds for each platform, each uploading its binary to the same GitHub Release.
A rebuild of the documentation only.
check.explain: The workflow runs on tags matching `v*`. A matrix builds Linux, macOS and Windows binaries in parallel and attaches them to the release.

mistakes: **Only a human-readable report.** CI can't parse it; offer `--json`.
**Exit code 0 when thresholds fail.** Pipelines need a non-zero code to stop.
**Releases that require a Rust toolchain.** Attach prebuilt binaries for each platform.
keys: Human and JSON reports from one struct; meaningful exit codes.
CI runs fmt, clippy and tests on every change.
Tagged releases publish binaries for each platform.
A clear README turns the project into a portfolio piece.

idea: **testlens** analyses JUnit XML reports from many CI runs to find tests that can't be trusted. JUnit XML is the de facto interchange format: pytest, Jest, Maven, Gradle, Go and cargo-nextest can all emit it. A report contains `<testsuite>` elements holding `<testcase classname=".." name=".." time="..">`, where a child `<failure>` or `<error>` means it failed and `<skipped/>` means it was skipped; no child means it passed.

The analysis needs a precise definition of **flaky**: a test that both passed and failed **on the same code**. That rules out tests that started failing because of a real change, which is a regression, not a flake. In practice, comparing runs of the same commit is ideal; with mixed commits, looking at the **pattern** helps: `P P F P F P` (many flips) suggests flakiness, `P P P F F F` (one flip, then consistent failure) suggests a regression. Require a **minimum number of runs** before judging, so one failure on a brand-new test isn't labelled.

Model it with types: a `Verdict` enum, a `CaseResult` with a stable id (`classname::name`), and a `Classification` enum (`Stable`, `Flaky`, `Broken`, `Regressed`, `NotEnoughData`) that the report and the exit code both use.
how: Parse `testcase` elements; failure or error child = failed, skipped child = skipped.
Id each test by `classname::name` so it matches across runs.
Flaky = passed and failed on the same code; count flips to spot regressions.
Require a minimum number of non-skipped runs before classifying.
One `Classification` enum drives the report and the exit code.

examples.title: Classifying a test from its history
examples.note: The same "it has both passes and failures" observation splits into two very different findings: `wrong_password` flips back and forth (flaky, 66% pass rate, four flips), while `apply_coupon` passed and then failed consistently from run 4 onward (a regression to investigate, not to retry). Skipped runs don't count, so the SSO test and the two-run new test don't have enough data to be judged.

check.q: `cart::apply_coupon` passed three times, then failed three times. How is it classified?
check.explain: One flip followed by consistent failure points to a change that broke the test, not to flakiness. That needs investigating, not retrying.

examples.title: Stable ids across runs
examples.note: Test names alone collide (two suites can both have `test_valid_password`), so the id combines class and name, and normalises the retry suffix some runners add so a retried test is still recognised as the same test. Getting identity right is what makes cross-run statistics meaningful.
examples.output:

Some("tests.test_login")         test_valid_password (attempt 2)      -> tests.test_login::test_valid_password
Some("tests.test_admin")         test_valid_password                  -> tests.test_admin::test_valid_password

check.q: Why does the id normalise names like "test_valid_password (attempt 2)"?
options: Because parentheses are invalid in XML.
To hide retries from the report.
So a retried test is recognised as the same test across runs.
check.explain: Statistics across runs only work if each test keeps one identity. Some runners add retry suffixes, which would split one test into several.

mistakes: **Calling every intermittent failure "flaky".** A consistent failure after a change is a regression.
**Judging tests with very few runs.** Require a minimum before classifying.
**Using the test name alone as an id.** Names repeat across suites; include the class.
keys: JUnit XML is the common format for test results.
Flaky means passed and failed on the same code; flips reveal the pattern.
Stable ids make results comparable across runs.
One Classification enum drives every output.

idea: With the model defined, the work is parsing and aggregation. **roxmltree** is a fast, read-only XML parser that builds a tree you can query: `Document::parse(text)?` then `doc.descendants().filter(|n| n.has_tag_name("testcase"))`, reading attributes with `node.attribute("name")` and checking children for `failure`, `error` and `skipped`. It returns a descriptive error for malformed files (with a position for most syntax errors), which the tool should report with the file name and then **skip** rather than abort: one corrupted artefact shouldn't hide the other 49 runs.

Aggregation folds every run into per-test statistics: a `HashMap<String, TestStats>` where each entry collects the verdict history (in run order), pass/fail counts and durations. From those, compute each test's classification, pass rate and **median duration**, and also suite-level facts a QA lead cares about, such as the slowest tests.

Parsing must be robust to real-world variations: nested `<testsuites>`, missing `time` attributes, `time` values with commas in some locales, `<error>` used instead of `<failure>`, and `<system-out>` noise. Tests with small inline XML documents pin each variation down.
how: `roxmltree::Document::parse(&text)?`; iterate `descendants()` for `testcase` nodes.
`attribute("time").and_then(|t| t.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(0.0)` for optional numbers.
Report and skip malformed files; never abort the whole analysis.
Fold runs into `HashMap<String, TestStats>` keeping history in order.
Derive classifications, pass rates and medians from the stats.

examples.title: Aggregating several CI runs into per-test statistics
examples.note: Run 3 was truncated (its `testsuite` never closes), so roxmltree reported why parsing failed and the tool skipped that run instead of giving up. The remaining runs aggregated into per-test histories: `login::retry` failed once out of three, a flaky candidate, and is also the slow one. The comma in `0,25` was normalised, and a missing `time` defaulted to zero.

run 3: skipped, invalid XML (the root node was opened but never closed)
login::ok    [Passed, Passed, Passed]  pass 3/3  median 0.21s
login::retry [Passed, Failed, Passed]  pass 2/3  median 1.20s

check.explain: The broken run is reported and skipped, so only three runs count. The median of 1.10, 3.40 and 1.20 seconds is 1.20.

examples.title: Parser tests for real-world variations

check.q: What should the parser do with a `<testcase>` containing an `<error>` element?
options: Count it as failed, the same as `<failure>`.
Count it as passed with a warning.
check.explain: JUnit uses `<failure>` for assertion failures and `<error>` for unexpected exceptions. Both mean the test didn't pass.

mistakes: **Aborting on the first bad report.** Report it with its position and continue with the rest.
**Treating only `<failure>` as failed.** `<error>` is a failure too.
**Losing run order.** Classification depends on the sequence; keep histories ordered.
keys: roxmltree parses XML into a queryable tree with descriptive errors.
Be lenient with real-world variations and test each one.
Aggregate runs into per-test histories, counts and durations.
Skip bad inputs, never the whole analysis.

idea: testlens earns its place when it runs automatically. In CI, it becomes a **quality gate**: after the test step, download the last N reports, run testlens, and **fail the pipeline** when a new flaky test appears. That requires deliberate **exit codes** (0 clean, 1 new flaky or regressed tests, 2 bad input or usage) and an **allow-list** file of known flaky tests being worked on, so the gate catches new problems without blocking every build on old ones. Each allow-list entry should name an owner or ticket, so it doesn't become a graveyard.

The CLI follows the usual pattern: a directory or glob of reports, `--min-runs` to require enough data, `--json` for dashboards and bots, and `--fail-on-flaky` to enable the gate. The human report should lead with what to act on: the number of flaky and regressed tests, then a table sorted by impact (lowest pass rate, most runs), then the slowest tests.

Document the tool like a product: what problem it solves, a one-command quick start, the classification rules in plain words, the exit codes, and a GitHub Action snippet. That README is often the first thing a hiring manager reads.
how: Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 actionable findings, 2 usage or input errors.
Allow-list file for known flaky tests, with owners or tickets.
`--min-runs`, `--json`, `--fail-on-flaky` flags.
Report: summary line, impact-sorted table, slowest tests.
README: problem, quick start, rules, exit codes, CI snippet.

examples.title: The gate decision with an allow-list
examples.note: Known flaky tests listed in the allow-list (with ticket numbers in comments) are reported but don't fail the build, while the new flaky test and the regression produce exit code 1 and stop the pipeline. When only known problems remain, the gate passes, so the team can adopt testlens without first fixing every historic flake.

check.explain: Allow-listed tests are reported but don't block the build. The two new problems do, so the gate fails with 1.

check.q: What should each allow-list entry include, according to the lesson?
options: An owner or ticket, so known flaky tests don't sit there forever.
The date the test was written.
check.explain: An allow-list without owners becomes a graveyard. A ticket reference keeps each entry accountable.

mistakes: **A gate that fails on every known flake.** Teams disable it. Use an allow-list with owners.
**Exit code 1 for both findings and crashes.** Distinguish actionable findings from input errors.
**Reports that bury the action.** Lead with counts and the worst offenders.
keys: Exit codes turn the analyser into a CI quality gate.
Allow-lists separate new problems from known, owned ones.
Human reports lead with actions; JSON feeds other tools.
Document rules and exit codes clearly.

idea: **logwatch** reads authentication logs and raises an alert when one IP address fails to log in too often within a short time, a classic brute-force signal, like a minimal fail2ban. Start with one well-defined format: OpenSSH lines in `/var/log/auth.log` (Debian/Ubuntu) or `/var/log/secure` (RHEL), such as `Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.9 port 51240 ssh2`. On systemd machines the same lines are available from `journalctl -u ssh -o short`.

The detection **rule** has two parameters: N failures from one IP within a window of W seconds. Use a **sliding window** (the last W seconds before each event), not fixed buckets ("per minute"), because a burst that straddles a bucket boundary would be missed. Decide the details explicitly: alert once per burst rather than on every further failure, and **reset** an IP's history after a successful login so a user who mistyped twice isn't flagged later. Timestamps need care: syslog lines omit the **year**, so the parser must assume the current year and handle the December-to-January rollover.

There are **ethical and legal limits**: monitor only systems you own or are explicitly authorised to monitor, treat IP addresses as personal data where privacy law says so, and keep the tool detection-only (alerts, not automatic attacks back). Blocking, if added, should go through the system's firewall with allow-lists for your own addresses.
how: Support one log format well; read files or `journalctl` output.
Rule: N failures per IP within a sliding window of W seconds.
Alert once per burst; reset an IP after a successful login.
Parse syslog timestamps with an assumed year and handle rollover.
Monitor only authorised systems; detection first, blocking via the firewall.

examples.title: Syslog timestamps without a year
examples.note: Three failures two seconds apart straddle midnight on New Year's Eve. With rollover handling the gaps are 1 and 2 seconds, so a burst rule would fire; parsed naively, January 1st lands in the same year as the December lines and the gap becomes almost minus a year, hiding the attack. Attackers don't stop for holidays, so this edge case is worth handling.
examples.output:
gaps between events: [1, 2] seconds
without rollover handling the last gap is -31535998 seconds
garbage line parses to None

check.q: Three failures happen at 23:59:58, 23:59:59 on Dec 31 and 00:00:01 on Jan 1. With rollover handling, what are the gaps?
check.explain: Syslog lines have no year. Noticing the jump backwards in months and moving to the next year keeps the events two seconds apart, so a burst rule still fires.

examples.title: Sliding windows catch what fixed buckets miss
examples.note: The burst of seven failures in 16 seconds split into four in the first minute and three in the second, so per-minute buckets never reached five. The sliding window looks at any five consecutive failures and saw them within 11 seconds. A slow trickle of one failure every 40 seconds correctly doesn't trigger the rule.
examples.output:
rule: 5 failures within 60 s
fixed one-minute buckets alert? false
sliding window alerts?          true
slow trickle, sliding window?   false

check.q: Seven failures arrive within 16 seconds, straddling a minute boundary. The rule is "5 failures within 60 s". Do fixed one-minute buckets alert?
options: `fixed one-minute buckets alert? only in release builds`
check.explain: The burst splits into four and three across the boundary, so no single bucket reaches five. A sliding window sees five within 11 seconds and alerts.

mistakes: **Fixed time buckets.** Bursts across boundaries slip through; use sliding windows.
**Ignoring the missing year in syslog.** New Year's Eve breaks naive parsing.
**Monitoring systems you don't own.** Get authorisation; keep the tool detection-first.
keys: One log format, parsed well, beats many parsed loosely.
N failures within a sliding window of W seconds per IP.
Alert once per burst; reset after successful logins.
Handle syslog's missing year; stay within ethical and legal limits.

idea: The detector combines two parts. The **parser** turns lines into events with a regular expression compiled **once** (in a `LazyLock<Regex>` static), because compiling a regex is far more expensive than matching; with the `regex` crate, matching runs in linear time, so hostile input can't make it hang. Lines that don't match (other services, other messages) return `None` and are ignored.

The **detector** keeps, for each IP, a `VecDeque<u64>` of recent failure timestamps: on each failure, push the new time to the back, pop times older than the window from the front, and alert when the queue holds N or more. This is a classic **sliding window**: each timestamp is pushed and popped once, so the work per event is constant on average. On a successful login from an IP, remove its history. Track which IPs are already **in alert** so a burst produces one alert, re-arming once the window has emptied.

Memory must stay bounded on a long-running service: an attacker can rotate through thousands of addresses. Remove an IP's entry when its queue empties, and optionally cap the map size. Test the detector with event sequences rather than files: exactly-at-the-boundary timing, reset after success, re-alerting after a quiet period, and many IPs at once.
how: `static RE: LazyLock<Regex>`; `RE.captures(line)?` → `Option<Event>`.
Per IP: `VecDeque<u64>`; push back, pop expired from front, alert when `len() >= n`.
Remove history on success; remove empty queues to bound memory.
Alert once per burst; re-arm when the window clears.
Test with sequences: boundaries, resets, re-alerts, many IPs.

examples.title: Parser and sliding-window detector end to end
examples.note: The attacker's fifth failure within the window raised exactly one alert, and the sixth was folded into the same burst. Kev's single mistyped password was cleared by his successful login, so his address isn't tracked any more, and the cron line didn't match the regex and was ignored.
examples.output:
ALERT 203.0.113.9: 5 failures in 11 s
8 events, 1 ignored line; IPs still tracked: ["203.0.113.9"]

check.q: The attacker fails six times within 15 seconds, with the rule at 5 failures per 60 s. How many alerts are printed?
check.explain: The fifth failure raises one alert, and the sixth is part of the same burst, so the detector stays quiet. Kev's single mistake was cleared by his successful login.

examples.title: Detector tests built from event sequences
examples.note: The tests use plain timestamps instead of log files, so each scenario is one readable line per event. The boundary test documents a decision (an event exactly W seconds old has expired), and the others cover resets after success, independence between addresses (including IPv6) and a slow trickle that must never alert.
examples.output:
running 4 tests
test tests::ips_are_independent_including_ipv6 ... ok
test tests::slow_attempts_never_alert ... ok
test tests::success_resets_history ... ok
test tests::window_boundary_is_exclusive ... ok
test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
examples.label: cargo test output

check.q: With a 10-second window, failures at t=0 and t=5 are stored. Is the t=0 failure still counted at t=10?
options: It depends on the IP address.
Yes: events never expire until a success.
No: the test defines an event exactly W seconds old as expired.
Yes: it expires only at t=11.
check.explain: The detector pops timestamps where `ts - t >= window`. The test documents that boundary decision so it can't change by accident.

mistakes: **Compiling the regex inside the loop.** Compile once in a `LazyLock` static.
**Unbounded per-IP state.** Remove empty or reset entries so memory stays bounded.
**Alerting on every failure after the threshold.** One alert per burst; re-arm later.
keys: A compiled regex turns lines into events; non-matching lines are ignored.
A per-IP VecDeque implements the sliding window in constant time per event.
Reset on success, de-duplicate alerts, bound memory.
Test with event sequences, not files.

idea: A detector is only useful if it runs continuously. **Following** a log like `tail -f` means: open the file, seek to the end, read new lines as they're appended, and sleep briefly when there's nothing new. Real logs also **rotate**: logrotate renames `auth.log` to `auth.log.1` and creates a new file, or truncates the existing one. A robust follower notices when the file got **shorter** than its read position (truncation) or when the path now refers to a **different file** (its inode changed), and reopens from the start. Crates like `notify` replace polling with filesystem events.

**Alerts** should be machine-readable: one JSON object per line on stdout (`{"ts":..,"ip":..,"failures":..}`) composes with `jq`, log shippers and systemd's journal; an optional webhook (Slack, Discord, Teams) uses reqwest with a timeout and must never block detection, so it runs in its own task or thread with a bounded queue. A **benchmark** on a large synthetic log (millions of lines) shows the parser and detector keep up with a busy server.

Deploy it as a **systemd service** running as an unprivileged user with read access to the log (the `adm` group on Debian), with sandboxing options such as `ProtectSystem=strict` and `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, and `Restart=on-failure`. Document what it does, what it doesn't do, and that it should only watch systems you're authorised to monitor.
how: Follow: seek to end, read new lines, sleep when idle.
Detect truncation (file shorter than position) and rotation (inode changed); reopen.
Alerts as JSON lines; webhooks off the detection path with timeouts.
Benchmark with a synthetic log of millions of lines.
systemd unit: dedicated user, `adm` group, sandboxing, restart policy.

examples.title: Following a file through appends and a truncation
examples.note: The follower skipped the line that existed before it started, held back a half-written line until its newline arrived, and noticed when the file was truncated (as `logrotate` with `copytruncate` does), reopening from the start so the next line wasn't lost. The real tool polls forever and also compares inodes to catch rename-style rotation.
examples.output:
new line: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9
new line: Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.9
  (file truncated: reopening from the start)
new line: Accepted publickey for kev from 198.51.100.7

check.q: What does the follower do when it reads a line without a trailing newline?
options: It seeks back and waits, so the half-written line is processed once it's complete.
It processes the partial line immediately.
check.explain: Writers may flush half a line. Waiting for the newline avoids parsing a truncated log entry.

examples.title: Running logwatch as a hardened systemd service
examples.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/logwatch.service
[Unit]
Description=logwatch: SSH brute-force detector
After=network-online.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/logwatch /var/log/auth.log --failures 5 --window 60s --webhook-env LOGWATCH_WEBHOOK
EnvironmentFile=-/etc/logwatch.env
User=logwatch
Group=adm
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/log
CapabilityBoundingSet=

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# $ sudo useradd --system --no-create-home logwatch
# $ sudo systemctl enable --now logwatch
# $ journalctl -u logwatch -f -o cat | jq .
# {"ts":"2026-11-04T06:12:06Z","ip":"203.0.113.9","failures":5,"window_s":60}
examples.note: The service runs as its own unprivileged user in the `adm` group, which can read the log but nothing else matters: the filesystem is read-only to it, home directories are hidden and it can't gain privileges. The webhook URL comes from an environment file rather than the command line, so it doesn't appear in process listings. Alerts go to the journal as JSON lines.

check.q: Why does the systemd unit run logwatch as its own user in the `adm` group?
options: systemd requires every service to be in `adm`.
It can read the logs but nothing else, so a bug can't damage the system.
check.explain: Least privilege: the `adm` group grants read access to logs, and the sandboxing options make the rest of the filesystem read-only.

mistakes: **Assuming the log file never changes identity.** Handle truncation and rotation.
**Sending webhooks inline.** A slow endpoint would stall detection; use a separate task with timeouts.
**Running as root.** Use a dedicated user with read access and systemd sandboxing.
keys: Follow files like `tail -f`, handling partial lines, truncation and rotation.
Emit alerts as JSON lines; send webhooks asynchronously.
Benchmark on synthetic logs to prove it keeps up.
Deploy as a sandboxed, unprivileged systemd service.

idea: **taskhub** is a REST API for tasks, built the way production services are. The first step is the **contract**: the resources (a task with id, title, done, due date, created time), the routes (`GET /tasks`, `POST /tasks`, `GET/PATCH/DELETE /tasks/{id}`, `GET /health`), the request and response shapes, the **status codes** (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 404 Not Found, 422 for validation errors) and a single **error format** (`{"error": "..."}`) used everywhere. Writing this down first means the handlers, the tests and the README all agree, and a front-end developer could start before the server exists.

**Pagination** is part of the contract from day one: `GET /tasks?page=2&per_page=20` returns `items` plus `page`, `per_page` and `total`, with defaults for missing parameters and a cap on `per_page` so one request can't ask for a million rows. Filtering (`?status=open`) follows the same pattern.

Structure the code in **layers**: **routes** (HTTP only: extract, call, convert to responses), a **service** (business rules such as "a title can't be empty" or "a done task can't be un-done after 30 days") and a **repository** (SQL only). Each layer depends on the one below through plain functions or a trait, so the rules can be tested without HTTP and the SQL without the rules.
how: Write the contract: routes, shapes, status codes, one error format.
Paginate with `page`/`per_page`, defaults and a maximum; return `total`.
Validate query parameters into a typed struct with defaults.
Layers: routes → service → repository, each testable alone.
Keep HTTP types out of the service and SQL out of the routes.

examples.title: Pagination parameters parsed, defaulted and clamped
examples.note: Missing parameters took their defaults, a page of 0 became 1, and a request for 5,000 items per page was capped at 100. An unknown status value was rejected with a clear message, which the API returns as a 422 in its standard error format. axum's `Query` extractor uses this same `serde_urlencoded` parsing.
examples.output:
?                                  -> page 1 per_page 20 status None: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 0
?page=3                            -> page 3 per_page 20 status None: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40
?page=0&per_page=5000              -> page 1 per_page 100 status None: LIMIT 100 OFFSET 0
?status=done&per_page=10&page=2    -> page 2 per_page 10 status Some(Done): LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10
?status=archived                   -> 422 {"error":"unknown variant `archived`, expected `open` or `done`"}
57 tasks at 20 per page = 3 pages

check.q: The query string is `?page=0&per_page=5000`. What window does the API use?
options: `?page=0&per_page=5000              -> page 1 per_page 5000 status None: LIMIT 5000 OFFSET 0`
`?page=0&per_page=5000              -> page 0 per_page 5000 status None: LIMIT 5000 OFFSET 0`
`?page=0&per_page=5000              -> page 1 per_page 100 status None: LIMIT 100 OFFSET 0`
check.explain: `normalised` raises page 0 to 1 and clamps `per_page` to the maximum of 100, so one request can't ask for thousands of rows.

examples.title: Layers you can test separately
examples.note: The service enforces the rules (trimmed titles, non-empty, a length limit, existing ids) without knowing anything about HTTP or SQL, and here it runs on an in-memory repository. In the real app the routes translate `ServiceError::Validation` into 422 and `NotFound` into 404, and a SQLite repository implements the same trait.
examples.output:
Ok(Task { id: 1, title: "Write the README", done: false })
Err(Validation("title must not be empty"))
Err(Validation("title must be at most 200 characters"))
Ok(Task { id: 1, title: "Write the README", done: true })
Err(NotFound(42))
stored: Some(Task { id: 1, title: "Write the README", done: true })

check.q: Which layer should check that a task title isn't empty?
options: The service layer, so the rule applies no matter how the task is created.
check.explain: Business rules belong in the service, testable without HTTP or SQL. The route translates its errors into status codes.

mistakes: **Designing the API while writing handlers.** Write the contract first; it keeps everything consistent.
**Unbounded list endpoints.** Paginate with a maximum page size from the start.
**Business rules inside handlers.** Put them in a service layer you can test without HTTP.
keys: A written contract defines routes, shapes, status codes and errors.
Paginate with defaults, caps and a total count.
Routes, service and repository each have one job.
Each layer is testable on its own.

idea: The repository wraps SQLite. A `rusqlite::Connection` isn't `Sync`, so the simplest correct sharing for a small service is **`Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`** in the app state: each handler locks, runs a short query and unlocks. Because rusqlite is synchronous, heavier services move database calls into `spawn_blocking` or use a pool (r2d2, deadpool) or an async driver like sqlx; for a portfolio API with modest traffic, a mutex is honest and fast enough.

Map rows to structs in one helper (`fn row_to_task(row) -> Result<Task>`) so every query returns the same shape. Use **parameters** everywhere, `LIMIT ?1 OFFSET ?2` for pagination and a separate `COUNT(*)` for the total. For **PATCH**, accept optional fields and update only those present: `UPDATE tasks SET title = COALESCE(?1, title), done = COALESCE(?2, done) WHERE id = ?3`, then check `changes()` (zero rows means 404).

Errors flow through one type: `ApiError` with `From<rusqlite::Error>` so `?` works in handlers, and `IntoResponse` so each variant becomes the right status and the standard JSON body. Finally, test the whole stack with **`oneshot`**: build the router on an in-memory database and send real requests, asserting status codes and bodies.
how: State: `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`; lock briefly, never across `.await`.
One `row_to_task` mapper; parameters for every value.
Pagination: `LIMIT ?1 OFFSET ?2` plus `COUNT(*)`.
PATCH with `COALESCE(?n, column)`; `changes() == 0` means not found.
`ApiError`: `From<rusqlite::Error>` + `IntoResponse`; test with `oneshot` on `:memory:`.

examples.title: The SQLite repository with pagination and partial updates
examples.note: Page 2 with two items per page returned tasks 3 and 4 along with the total of five, which is all the API needs to build its pagination response. `COALESCE` let one PATCH statement update only the fields that were sent, and an update touching zero rows became `None`, which the handler turns into a 404. `.optional()` turns "no rows" into `None` for single-row lookups.
examples.output:
page 2 of 5: [Task { id: 3, title: "Dockerfile", done: false }, Task { id: 4, title: "README", done: false }]
patch done only:  Some(Task { id: 3, title: "Dockerfile", done: true })
patch title only: Some(Task { id: 3, title: "Multi-stage Dockerfile", done: true })
patch missing id: None
get missing id:   None

check.q: Task 3 is patched with `done = true` only, using `COALESCE(?1, title)`. What does the result show?
options: `patch done only:  Some(Task { id: 3, title: "", done: true })`
`patch done only:  Some(Task { id: 3, title: "Dockerfile", done: true })`
check.explain: `COALESCE(NULL, title)` keeps the existing title, so only the fields that were sent change.

examples.title: The full HTTP stack tested with oneshot on an in-memory database
examples.note: Each request went through routing, extraction, the handler, SQLite and error conversion, without a network or a database file, so a test suite like this runs in milliseconds. Because `ApiError` converts from `rusqlite::Error`, handlers use `?` on database calls, and every error response shares the `{"error": ...}` format promised in the contract.

check.q: What lets handlers use `?` on rusqlite calls?
check.explain: `?` converts the database error into the API's error type, which then becomes a 500 response with the standard JSON body.

mistakes: **Holding the Mutex across `.await`.** Lock, query, drop; or use `spawn_blocking` or a pool.
**Reading the inserted row with a second query when not needed.** `last_insert_rowid()` gives the id.
**Testing only the happy path.** Assert 404 and 422 bodies as well.
keys: `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>` is a simple, correct start for SQLite.
One row mapper; parameters, LIMIT/OFFSET and COUNT for pages.
PATCH with COALESCE; zero changed rows means 404.

idea: Shipping a web service adds operational features. **Configuration** comes from environment variables (`TASKHUB_ADDR`, `TASKHUB_DB`, `RUST_LOG`), the convention for containers and the twelve-factor app; parse them once at start-up into a typed `Config` with defaults, and **fail fast** with a clear message if a value is invalid, rather than discovering it on the first request.

**Request logging** with `tower_http::trace::TraceLayer` records the method, path, status and latency of every request through `tracing`, and a request-id layer lets you follow one request through the logs. **Graceful shutdown** matters for deployments: on SIGTERM (what Docker and Kubernetes send), the server stops accepting new connections, lets in-flight requests finish, and exits; `axum::serve(listener, app).with_graceful_shutdown(signal)` does this.

The **Dockerfile** uses a multi-stage build: compile in a full Rust image, then copy only the binary into a minimal runtime image (distroless or debian-slim) running as a non-root user, typically under 30 MB. CI builds and tests on every push, and an **OpenAPI-style README** documents each endpoint with example requests and responses. Together, they show employers you understand the whole life of a service, not just the handlers.
how: Typed `Config` from env vars with defaults; exit early on invalid values.
`TraceLayer::new_for_http()` for request logs; `RUST_LOG` filters them.
`axum::serve(..).with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal())` for SIGTERM/Ctrl+C.
Multi-stage Dockerfile, minimal runtime image, non-root user, volume for the database.
CI and a README with every endpoint, example requests and status codes.

examples.title: Configuration from the environment, validated at start-up

Invalid values produce one precise message naming the variable, so a misconfigured deployment fails immediately at start-up instead of misbehaving later. Taking the variables as an iterator (`std::env::vars()` in production) makes the loader testable without touching the real environment.

check.explain: `SocketAddr` needs an IP and a numeric port. The loader fails fast with a message naming the variable, instead of misbehaving later.

After that, a new request failed to connect. Without graceful shutdown, every deployment would cut off requests in progress.

**Killing the process on deploy.** Handle SIGTERM with graceful shutdown.
**Shipping the build image.** Multi-stage builds give small, non-root runtime images.

Graceful shutdown finishes in-flight requests.

idea: **kvlog** is a persistent key-value store in the style of **Bitcask**, the engine behind Riak. Its core idea is simple: never modify data in place. Every `set` and `remove` is **appended** to a log file as a record, and an in-memory **index** maps each key to the position of its latest record. Reads are one index lookup plus one disk read; writes are one sequential append, which is the fastest thing a disk can do. Removes append a **tombstone** record.

Because old values are never overwritten, the log grows with every update. **Compaction** fixes that: write the live records (the latest value of each key) to a new file, then atomically replace the old one. On start-up, **opening** the store replays the log from the beginning to rebuild the index.

The on-disk **record format** must make crashes survivable. Each record carries a header with a **checksum** (CRC32) over its contents, the kind (set or remove) and the key and value lengths, followed by the bytes. If the machine loses power mid-write, the last record may be **torn** (incomplete) or corrupted; on replay, a record whose length runs past the end of the file or whose checksum doesn't match marks the end of the valid log, and the store truncates there. Durability depends on **fsync**: calling `file.sync_data()` after a write guarantees it reached the disk, at a cost, so stores often offer a choice between syncing every write and syncing periodically.
how: Append-only log of set and tombstone records; in-memory index of key → position.
Reads: index lookup then one read; writes: one append.
Replay on open to rebuild the index; compact to reclaim space.
Record = `[crc32][kind][key_len][val_len][key][value]`, little-endian.
On replay, stop at a torn or corrupted record and truncate; `sync_data()` for durability.

examples.title: A real CRC32 and why it catches corruption
examples.note: The implementation reproduces the standard CRC32 check value, so it matches zlib and the `crc32fast` crate (which a real project would use for speed). A single flipped bit or two swapped bytes changes the checksum, so a corrupted record is recognised on replay instead of being returned as a wrong value. The simple rotate-and-xor checksum from the original sketch would miss some of these errors.
examples.output:
crc32("123456789") = cbf43926 (the standard check value is cbf43926)
record: 22 bytes, valid: true
one flipped bit detected: true
swapped bytes detected: true

check.q: Why does each record carry a CRC32 checksum?
options: So a corrupted or half-written record is detected on replay instead of being returned as a wrong value.
check.explain: Disks and power failures can corrupt bytes. A checksum mismatch marks where the valid log ends.

examples.title: Recovering from a torn final record
examples.note: The last record was cut off four bytes short, as if the power failed during the write. Replay kept the two complete records, reported where the valid log ends, and after truncating there, new writes appended cleanly. Without truncation, the next record would be glued to the torn bytes and the log would be unreadable from that point.
examples.output:
recovered [("a", "apple"), ("b", "banana")]
file is 40 bytes; truncate to 29 and carry on
after the next write: [("a", "apple"), ("b", "banana"), ("c", "cranberry")]

check.q: The last record was cut off mid-write. After truncating to the valid length and appending "c" = "cranberry", what does replay return?
check.explain: Truncating at the end of the last complete record removes the torn bytes, so the new record follows cleanly. "cherry" was never fully written.

mistakes: **Updating values in place.** A crash mid-write corrupts data; append instead.
**No checksums.** Corruption is returned as data; verify every record.
**Assuming a write is durable when `write` returns.** It's in the OS cache until `sync_data`.
keys: Append-only log plus an in-memory index: fast writes and reads.
Tombstones record removals; compaction reclaims space.
Checksums and length checks detect torn and corrupted records.
Durability needs fsync; trade it off deliberately.

idea: The engine turns the record format into a working store. **`open`** reads the file from the start, decoding records one by one: a set inserts `key → (offset, length)` into the index, a tombstone removes the key, and a torn or corrupted tail is truncated. Storing positions rather than values keeps memory proportional to the number of keys, not the data size; small stores may keep values in memory, as the original sketch does.

**`set`** appends a record and updates the index; **`get`** looks up the position, seeks and reads the value; **`remove`** appends a tombstone and removes the key (returning whether it existed). Track **stale bytes**, the space taken by superseded records, so the store knows when compaction is worthwhile (for example when more than half the file is stale).

**Compaction** writes every live record to a new file (`data.compact`), calls `sync_all`, then **atomically renames** it over the old file, so a crash leaves either the old file or the new one, never a mix; the index is rebuilt with the new offsets. Tests prove persistence by **reopening**: set values, drop the store, open it again from the same path, and check everything is still there, including removals and the result of a compaction.
how: Index `HashMap<Vec<u8>, (u64, u32)>`: key → offset and length of the value.
`set`: append, then update the index; count superseded bytes as stale.
`get`: index lookup, `seek`, `read_exact`.
Compact: write live records to a temp file, `sync_all`, `rename` over the original.
Test by dropping and reopening the store.

examples.title: An engine with an offset index and atomic compaction
examples.note: Fifty overwrites of `counter` plus a removed key left most of the file stale. Compaction rewrote only the two live records into a new file and renamed it over the old one, shrinking the log to a few dozen bytes. Reopening from disk restored exactly the latest values, and the removed key stayed removed.

before compaction: 892 bytes, 860 stale, 2 live keys
after compaction:  32 bytes, 0 stale
reopened: counter=Some("49") name=Some("Ada") temp=None

check.q: `counter` was set 50 times, plus one live and one removed key. How big is the file after compaction?
check.explain: Compaction rewrites only the latest value of each live key (two records) into a new file, so all stale space is gone.

examples.title: Persistence tests that reopen the store
examples.note: Each test writes through one store, lets it go out of scope (closing the file), and checks the data through a freshly opened store, which is the only way to prove that what's in memory also reached the log. The cases cover overwrites, removals of present and absent keys, and a key set again after removal, where replay order must decide.

running 3 tests
test tests::removals_survive_reopen ... ok
test tests::set_after_remove_wins ... ok
test tests::values_survive_reopen ... ok
test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

check.q: Why do the persistence tests let the store go out of scope and open it again?
options: To test that the file can be deleted.
Only a fresh open from disk proves the data reached the log; in-memory state can hide a broken replay.
Rust requires closing files before reading them.
Opening twice makes the tests faster.
check.explain: Reopening exercises the replay code, which is what actually runs after a restart or a crash.

mistakes: **Writing compaction output over the live file directly.** A crash mid-compaction loses data. Write elsewhere, sync, rename.
**Testing without reopening.** In-memory state can hide a broken replay.
**Counting stale space wrongly.** Superseded sets and tombstones both count; test the numbers.
keys: Open replays the log into an index of positions.
Set and remove append; get reads one value from disk.
Compaction rewrites live data and atomically renames.
Reopen in tests to prove persistence.

idea: A storage engine becomes a product with a **command-line client** and honest documentation. The CLI uses clap subcommands (`set`, `get`, `rm`, `compact`, `stats`) and conventional behaviour: values print to stdout, errors to stderr, a missing key exits with code 1 so scripts can test for it (`if kvlog get user:1 >/dev/null; then ...`), and `stats` reports keys, file size, stale bytes and whether compaction is recommended.

**Benchmarks** with criterion measure what users care about: writes per second (with and without `sync_data` per write, which can differ by a factor of a hundred or more), random reads, and open time for a large log. Publish the numbers with the hardware they were measured on.

**Document the guarantees and limits** plainly: single process only (no file locking yet, so two writers would corrupt the log), the index must fit in memory, durability depends on the sync setting, keys and values up to 4 GB each. Then publish: fill in Cargo.toml metadata (description, license, repository, keywords), run `cargo publish --dry-run` to check the package, and `cargo publish`. A crate on crates.io with docs on docs.rs is a strong portfolio signal.
how: clap subcommands; stdout for values, stderr for messages, exit 1 for missing keys.
`stats` reports size, live keys, stale bytes and a compaction hint.
criterion benchmarks for writes (synced and not), reads and open time.
README: guarantees, limits, benchmark results with hardware.
Cargo metadata, `cargo publish --dry-run`, then `cargo publish`.

Returning `(stdout, stderr, code)` from `run` keeps the dispatch testable; `main` would print them and return the exit code.

**Hiding limits.** Say clearly that the store is single-process and needs the index in RAM.
**Benchmark numbers without context.** State the hardware and whether writes were synced.

idea: **lifewasm** runs Conway's **Game of Life** in the browser, with the simulation in Rust compiled to WebAssembly. The rules are tiny: on a grid of cells, each alive or dead, the next generation is computed from each cell's eight neighbours. A live cell with two or three live neighbours survives; a dead cell with exactly three becomes alive; every other cell is dead next turn. Simple rules produce rich behaviour: still lifes, oscillators, gliders that travel across the grid.

Represent the grid as a **flat `Vec<u8>`** of `width × height` cells, indexed by `row * width + col`. A flat buffer is cache-friendly and, crucially, JavaScript can read it **directly from WebAssembly memory** without copying, which is what makes large grids fast. Make the edges **wrap around** (a torus), so a glider leaving the right edge reappears on the left: neighbour coordinates are computed with `(row + height - 1) % height` and similar, avoiding bounds checks and special cases.

Split the work between the languages by strength: **Rust** owns the state and computes generations (`tick`), plus mutations like toggling a cell or inserting a pattern; **JavaScript** draws cells on a `<canvas>`, handles clicks and buttons, and drives the animation with `requestAnimationFrame`. The boundary stays narrow: a few calls per frame and a pointer to the cell buffer.
how: Rules: survive with 2 or 3 neighbours; birth with exactly 3; otherwise dead.
Flat `Vec<u8>`: index `row * width + col`.
Wrap-around neighbours with modular arithmetic.
Rust: state, `tick`, `toggle`, patterns. JavaScript: canvas, input, animation loop.
Expose a pointer to the cells so JS reads them without copying.

examples.title: Wrap-around neighbour counting on a flat grid
examples.note: On a torus the four corners are mutual neighbours, so each corner cell sees three live neighbours and the cells beside the corners see one or two, even though they look far apart on the flat printout. Adding `height - 1` instead of subtracting 1 keeps the arithmetic in unsigned integers, so there's no underflow and no special case for edges.
examples.output:
#...#   neighbours [3, 2, 0, 2, 3]
.....   neighbours [2, 1, 0, 1, 2]
.....   neighbours [2, 1, 0, 1, 2]
#...#   neighbours [3, 2, 0, 2, 3]
cell (1, 2) lives at index 7 of 20

check.q: On a 5×4 torus, one cell is alive in each corner. How many live neighbours does the top-left corner see?
check.explain: With wrap-around edges, the four corners touch each other, so each corner cell sees the other three.

examples.title: What JavaScript sees: a pointer and a length
examples.note: JavaScript builds a `Uint8Array` over WebAssembly memory at the address the pointer gives, so drawing reads Rust's buffer directly; the Rust `from_raw_parts` view here does the same thing to show it. One byte per cell keeps this simple; packing eight cells per byte would use less memory but make the drawing code more complex.
examples.output:
·■■■····
·■■■····
16 bytes shared, 6 alive, no copying

check.q: How does JavaScript read the cells without copying them?
options: WebAssembly copies the cells into a JS array automatically.
It builds a `Uint8Array` over WebAssembly memory at the pointer Rust exports.
JavaScript calls a Rust function once per cell.
Rust sends the cells as a JSON string every frame.
check.explain: A flat `Vec<u8>` is one block of memory, so JS can view it directly. That's what makes large grids fast to draw.

mistakes: **A `Vec<Vec<u8>>` grid.** Rows scattered in memory are slower and can't be shared with JS as one view.
**Bounds-checking edges with many `if`s.** Modular arithmetic handles wrap-around uniformly.
**Drawing from Rust through many JS calls.** Let JS read the buffer and draw in one pass.
keys: Three rules produce the whole Game of Life.
A flat buffer is fast and shareable with JavaScript.
Wrap-around edges via modular arithmetic.
Rust simulates; JavaScript draws and handles input.

idea: The `Universe` type implements the simulation. **`tick`** computes the next generation into a **second buffer** and then swaps them: every cell's next state must be computed from the *current* generation, so updating in place would corrupt neighbours not yet visited. Keeping two buffers and swapping (`std::mem::swap`) avoids allocating a new vector every frame. **`toggle(row, col)`** flips a cell (for mouse clicks), and **`insert(pattern, row, col)`** stamps a known shape, often described in the community's **RLE** format (`bo$2bo$3o!` is a glider: `b` dead, `o` alive, `$` end of row, numbers repeat).

**Test natively** before involving a browser: well-known patterns have exact, documented behaviour. A **blinker** (three in a row) oscillates with period 2; a **block** (2×2) never changes; a **glider** returns to its original shape after 4 generations, shifted one cell diagonally. These tests catch every off-by-one error in neighbour counting and wrap-around.

Then add the **wasm-bindgen layer**: annotate the struct and an `impl` block with `#[wasm_bindgen]`, exposing `new`, `tick`, `toggle`, `width`, `height` and `cells_ptr`. Keeping the logic in plain methods and the annotations thin means `cargo test` keeps working on your machine while `wasm-pack build` produces the browser package.
how: Two buffers; compute next from current; `std::mem::swap` after each tick.
`toggle` and `insert` for interaction and patterns; parse RLE for real patterns.
Test with still lifes (block), oscillators (blinker) and spaceships (glider).
Compare a pattern after N generations with a shifted copy.
Thin `#[wasm_bindgen]` layer over tested methods.

examples.title: Known patterns prove the simulation correct
examples.note: The block stayed still, the blinker flipped between horizontal and vertical, and the glider moved exactly one cell down and right every four generations. On a 6×6 torus, 24 generations carry the glider all the way around and back to its starting cells, which only works if wrap-around neighbour counting is right on every edge.

running 4 tests
test tests::blinker_has_period_two ... ok
test tests::block_is_still ... ok
test tests::glider_moves_one_cell_diagonally_every_four_ticks ... ok
test tests::glider_wraps_around_the_edges ... ok
