check.explain: The glider cycles through four phases. On a 6×6 torus, 24 generations carry it all the way round, which tests wrap-around on every edge.

examples.title: Inserting a pattern from RLE and watching it run
examples.note: The RLE string `bo$2bo$3o!` (dead-alive, two dead then alive, three alive) decoded into a glider and was stamped onto the grid. Four generations later the same shape sits one cell further down and right. The two buffers are swapped after every step, so the simulation allocates nothing while it runs, which matters at 60 frames per second.

check.q: Why does `tick` write into a second buffer and swap, instead of updating cells in place?
options: Every cell's next state must come from the current generation; updating in place would mix generations.
It makes the simulation run backwards.
check.explain: In-place updates would let already-updated neighbours affect later cells. Swapping also avoids allocating a new vector each frame.

mistakes: **Updating cells in place during a tick.** Neighbours then mix generations. Use a second buffer.
**Allocating a new Vec every tick.** Swap two buffers instead.
**Testing only in the browser.** Known patterns make precise native tests.
keys: Compute into a second buffer and swap each generation.
Toggle and RLE insertion make the universe interactive.
Still lifes, oscillators and gliders are exact test oracles.
A thin wasm-bindgen layer sits on tested methods.

idea: Shipping lifewasm means a **live demo** anyone can open. Build with **`wasm-pack build --target web --release`**, which compiles to WebAssembly, runs wasm-bindgen and optimises with `wasm-opt`, producing `pkg/` with the `.wasm` module and its JavaScript glue. A static `index.html` imports it as an ES module, so no bundler is required.

**Measure and shrink** the module, because size is load time. Release-profile settings make a large difference: `opt-level = "s"` or `"z"` (optimise for size), `lto = true` (link-time optimisation removes unused code across crates), `codegen-units = 1`, and `panic = "abort"` (drops unwinding machinery). Avoid pulling in heavy dependencies and formatting machinery in hot paths. `twiggy` shows what takes space in a `.wasm` file. A Game of Life core can be under 20 KB.

**Deploy to GitHub Pages** with a workflow: on every push to `main`, install Rust and wasm-pack, build, and upload the site folder with `actions/upload-pages-artifact` and `actions/deploy-pages`. The README then leads with the **live demo link** and an animated GIF, followed by how it works (Rust computes, JS draws, shared memory), how to build locally, and what you'd add next (patterns library, speed control, bit-packed cells). It's a portfolio piece people can try in five seconds.
how: `wasm-pack build --target web --release`; serve `index.html` + `pkg/`.
`[profile.release] opt-level = "s"`, `lto = true`, `codegen-units = 1`, `panic = "abort"`.
Inspect size with `ls -lh` and `twiggy top`.
GitHub Pages workflow: build, `upload-pages-artifact`, `deploy-pages`.
README: demo link and GIF first, then design, build steps and next ideas.

examples.title: Deploying the demo to GitHub Pages on every push
examples.code:
# .github/workflows/pages.yml
name: Deploy demo
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
concurrency: { group: pages, cancel-in-progress: true }
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: { name: github-pages, url: "${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}" }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with: { targets: wasm32-unknown-unknown }
      - run: curl https://rustwasm.github.io/wasm-pack/installer/init.sh -sSf | sh
      - run: cargo test                          # native tests first: patterns must still pass
      - run: wasm-pack build --target web --release
      - run: mkdir site && cp index.html site/ && cp -r pkg site/ && rm site/pkg/.gitignore
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with: { path: site }
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
# Settings > Pages > Source: "GitHub Actions". The demo appears at https://<user>.github.io/lifewasm/
examples.note: The workflow runs the native pattern tests before building, so a broken simulation never gets deployed. It then copies only the page and the generated package into a `site` folder and publishes it; removing `pkg/.gitignore` (which wasm-pack creates) avoids confusion if the folder is ever committed. The Pages source must be set to "GitHub Actions" once in the repository settings.

check.q: Why does the Pages workflow run `cargo test` before `wasm-pack build`?
options: So a broken simulation is never deployed: the native pattern tests must pass first.
It warms up the Rust cache.
check.explain: The fast native tests act as a gate in the same workflow, before anything is published.

examples.title: Release settings for a small .wasm file
examples.code:
[package]
name = "lifewasm"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]

[dependencies]
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"

[profile.release]
opt-level = "s"        # optimise for size ("z" is smaller still, sometimes slower)

examples.note: The debug build is over a megabyte, mostly debug information and unoptimised code; the release build with size settings and wasm-opt shrinks to about 16 KB, small enough to load instantly on a phone. `twiggy` confirms that the simulation itself dominates what remains. (Sizes are typical; yours will vary slightly with versions.)

check.q: Which release setting removes unused code across crates to shrink the .wasm file?
check.explain: Link-time optimisation sees the whole program at once and drops what's unused. Combined with `opt-level = "s"` and wasm-opt, the module shrinks to about 16 KB.

mistakes: **Deploying a debug build.** It's dozens of times larger. Always `--release` with size settings.
**A demo link buried at the bottom of the README.** Put the link and a GIF first.
**Deploying without running tests.** Run native tests in the same workflow first.
keys: wasm-pack builds a ready-to-serve package; no bundler needed.
Size settings and wasm-opt shrink the module dramatically.
GitHub Actions deploys the demo to Pages on every push.
Lead the README with a live link and a GIF.
